1: But the earthquake in the days of Uzziah king of Judah is said to belong to that time when Uzziah, who is called by another name Azariah, trying to claim for himself a priesthood not lawful for him, was struck with leprosy on his forehead; of this earthquake we also read at the beginning of Amos: The words of Amos, who was among the shepherds of Tekoa, which he saw concerning Israel in the days of Uzziah king of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam son of Joash king of Israel, two years before the earthquake. In short, after this wicked king died, at whose impiety the whole earth was shaken, Isaiah saw the great vision which he wove into his book.

The prophet Amos, who follows Joel and is the third of the twelve prophets, is not the same man whom we read of as the father of the prophet Isaiah. For that one is written with the first and last letters of his name, aleph and sade, and is interpreted strong and robust; this one, however, with ain and samech, and is interpreted a people torn away; the middle letters, mem and uau, are common to both. But among us, who do not have so great a difference of vowel letters, and of the letter s, which among the Hebrews is threefold, both these and other names seem to be the same, which among the Hebrews are distinguished by the diversity of their letters and by their own peculiarities. This prophet, then, whom we now have in hand, was from the town of Tekoa, which lies six miles toward the southern region from holy Bethlehem, which gave birth to the Savior of the world; and beyond it there is no village at all, not even rustic huts like ovens, which the Africans call mapalia. So great is the vastness of the desert, which stretches as far as the Red Sea and the borders of the Persians, the Ethiopians and the Indians. And because on the dry and sandy ground no crops whatever are produced, everything is full of shepherds, so that they may make up for the barrenness of the land by the multitude of their flocks. Of this number of shepherds was also the prophet Amos, unskilled in speech, but not in knowledge. For the same Holy Spirit who spoke through all the prophets was speaking in him. Hence we translate from the Hebrew.

The words of Amos, who was among the herdsmen of Tekoa, which he saw concerning Israel. But the Seventy, intending I know not what, translated: The words of Amos, which came to be in Accarim of Tekoa, which he saw on behalf of Jerusalem. And it should be known that this prophet prophesied, not on behalf of Jerusalem, which is not found at all in the Hebrew, but concerning Israel, that is, the ten tribes, which are called Israel and were in Samaria. And indeed Aquila and Symmachus and Theodotion translated this likewise. The first, then, the prophet Hosea, speaks to the ten tribes, which are called Ephraim, Samaria, the house of Joseph and Israel. The second, Joel, utters his prophecy to Jerusalem and the two tribes, which are called Judah and Jerusalem and Jacob, making no mention at all of Israel. The third, Amos, preaches by no means to Jerusalem, which was ruled by the tribe of Judah, but to Israel in Samaria. This can be proved from his whole volume, and above all from what is written: Amaziah the priest of Bethel sent to Jeroboam king of Israel, saying: Amos has rebelled against you in the midst of the house of Israel. And a little after, Amaziah said to Amos: You who see, go, flee into the land of Judah, and eat bread there; and there you shall prophesy, and in Bethel you shall not again prophesy any more, for it is the king's sanctuary and the house of the kingdom. To whom Amos answered: I was not a prophet, nor the son of a prophet, but a shepherd stripping the berries of brambles; and the Lord took me as I followed the flock, and said to me: Go, prophesy to my people Israel; not, surely, to Judah and Jerusalem, as is wrongly found among the Greeks and Latins, but to Israel, that is, the ten tribes, which, because of the multitude of the people, had kept the original name. But in the place where the Seventy translated in Accarim, Theodotion put the Hebrew word itself: in nocedim, which Aquila rendered ἐν ποιμνιοτρόφοις, that is, among the herdsmen, Symmachus and the Fifth edition ἐν τοῖς ποιμέσιν, that is, among the shepherds. And I think that here too, because of the likeness of the letters daleth and res, they were deceived, and read nocerim as though for nocedim, and from there put down the word Accarim, although the letter nun at the beginning of the name leaves no excuse for the error. But up to the present I have not read that Accarim is Hebrew. And those who interpret it barrenness, that is, στείρωσιν, express Ekron, the city of the Philistines, rather than Accarim, which is not read anywhere at all. The words, therefore, of Amos, who was from the town of Tekoa, of the number of the shepherds, since the region itself is also a pastoral one, are contained in this volume, which he saw concerning Israel, not with the eyes of the flesh but with the gaze of the mind; for the prophets were called seers; otherwise, according to the letter, words are not seen but heard. Hence the people also saw the voice of God, and Moses, keeping silent, spoke to the Lord when he said to him: Why do you cry to me? In the New Testament also we read: What we have seen and heard, what we have seen with our eyes, and our hands have handled, of the Word of life. For the Word of God, which in itself is invisible, the apostles see and handle with their hands. Because the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us. And he saw these words:

In the days of Uzziah king of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam son of Joash king of Israel, two years before the earthquake. At the time when Sardanapalus reigned among the Assyrians and the cities of Cilicia, of whom the distinguished orator wrote: "Uglier, he says, in his vices than in his name"; and among the Latins Procas Silvius, whom Amulius succeeded in the kingdom after driving out his brother Numitor; and when Amulius had been killed, Romulus, having gathered a band of shepherds and robbers, founded the city of his own name. This, moreover, is Uzziah king of Judah, surnamed Azariah, who, having tried to claim for himself a priesthood not due to him, was struck with leprosy on his forehead, when not only the punishment of the man who had committed sacrilege but also the earthquake, which the Hebrews record happened at that time, showed the wrath of the Lord. Jeroboam, however, is not the son of Nebat, who made Israel sin, but the son of Joash, son of Joathan, son of Jehu, the great-grandson of that same Jehu, under whom Hosea and Joel and Amos prophesied. Uzziah, then, is interpreted κράτος Κυρίου, that is, the dominion or strength of the Lord; Jeroboam, δικασμὸς λαοῦ, that is, the judging or the cause of the people, although some, reading it with the Greek letter chi, suppose it to mean the division of the people; Joash, Κυρίου χρόνισμα, that is, the delay of the Lord, or temporality. The words of Amos, therefore, at the time when the people of Israel had been torn away from the Lord and were serving golden calves, or had been torn away from the kingdom of the stock of David, sang out with a clear voice like a blaring trumpet, which is what Tekoa is interpreted. And they sang concerning Israel, which was once the most upright of God, that is, εὐθύτατος Θεοῦ. In the days of Uzziah king of Judah, in which, because of the temple and the holy of holies, the strength of the Lord remained, and ruled by its own dominion the people who confessed him. But the name of Jeroboam, who had been the cause of the division of the people, signifies that Israel remained for a long time in the error of idolatry before the universal captivity shook it; and this, in the two years, shows the twofold distress of the ten tribes and of the two, so that, if they were willing to repent, they might not feel the earthquake thereafter.

And he said: The Lord will roar from Zion, and from Jerusalem he will give his voice. And the beautiful places of the shepherds have mourned, and the top of Carmel has been dried up. LXX: And he said: The Lord has spoken out from Zion, and from Jerusalem he has given his voice; and the pastures of the shepherds have mourned, and the top of Carmel has withered. It is natural that all craftsmen speak in the examples of their own craft, and that each one should bring forward likenesses from the pursuit in which he has spent his life: for example, he who is a sailor and a helmsman compares his sadness to a storm, calls a loss a shipwreck, names his enemies contrary winds; and again he calls prosperity and gladness a most gentle breeze and favourable winds, calm seas and waters like plains. On the other side, whatever a soldier says sounds of shield, sword, breastplate, helmet, lance, bow and arrows, death, wound and victory. In the mouth of the philosophers Socrates and Plato, Xenophon and Theophrastus, Zeno and Aristotle, the Stoics and the Peripatetics are always turning up. The orators extol to the sky with praises Lysias and Hyperides, Pericles and Demosthenes, the Gracchi, the Catos, the Ciceros and the Hortensiuses. The poets, if they are epic, celebrate Homer and Vergil in frequent speech; if lyric, Pindar and Flaccus. Why have these things been said? Clearly so that we may show that the prophet Amos too, who was a shepherd from among shepherds, and a shepherd not in cultivated places planted with trees and vines, or at least among woods and green meadows, but in the broad vastness of the desert, in which the ferocity of lions and the slaughter of flocks are found, used in his discourses the terms of his own craft, so as to name the terrible and fearful voice of the Lord the roaring and growling of lions. Comparing the overthrow of the Israelite cities to the solitude of the shepherds and the dryness of the mountains, he says: The Lord will roar from Zion, and from Jerusalem he will give his voice. Will roar is said in Hebrew iesag. And it is fittingly said that he will roar from Zion and give his voice from Jerusalem, where the temple and the worship of God were, in order to teach that God dwells not in the cities of Israel, that is, in Bethel and in Dan, where the golden calves were, nor in the metropolis Samaria and in Jezreel, but in the true religion, which at that time was practised in Zion and Jerusalem. When he roars from Zion and gives his voice from Jerusalem — for the law shall go forth from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem —, all the beautiful things of the shepherds and of the kings of Israel have mourned, and the top of Carmel, which once abounded in rich pastures, has been dried up. Carmelus it is called in Greek and in Latin, but in Hebrew it is named Chermel; and there are two mountains which are called by this name. One, in which Nabal of Carmel, the husband of Abigail, lived, toward the southern region. The other near Ptolemais, which was formerly called Acco, overhanging the sea, on which the prophet Elijah, on bended knees, obtained the rains. If, then, he is speaking of the Chermel in which Nabal lived, it suits rather the flocks of the shepherds, because it is near the wilderness. But if of the one which is close to the shore, it pertains to the kings and to the pride of the kings of Israel, who, he says, when captivity is impending, are to be laid waste like deserted mountains. Another interpretation: when the Lord, from Zion and Jerusalem, from the watchtower of the Church, which, set upon a mountain, cannot be hidden, and in which there is the vision of peace, has given his voice through the Old and the New Testament and through the teachers of the Church, and has sounded as it were a clear trumpet, then all the beautiful things of the shepherds, that is, the doctrine of the heretics, which seemed composed in fine language, and the knowledge of circumcision — for this is what Chermel means —, by which they promise themselves the knowledge of the true circumcision, will mourn and be dried up, and the thousands of the peoples, who because of their simplicity are called flocks, will wither with sudden drought.

You must slay the allurements to vice while they are still only thoughts and dash the little ones of the daughter of Babylon against the stones where the serpent can leave no trail. Be wary and lay claim to the Lord's promise: "Let them not have dominion over me: then shall I be upright and I shall be innocent from the great transgression." For elsewhere also the Scripture testifies, "I will visit the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation." That is to say, God will not punish us at once for our thoughts and resolves but will send retribution upon their offspring or upon the evil deeds and habits of sin, which arise out of the offspring. As he says by the mouth of Amos, "For three transgressions of such and such a city and for four I will not turn away the punishment thereof."

Thus says the Lord: For three crimes of Damascus, and for four, I will not turn him back, because they threshed Gilead with iron carts. LXX: And the Lord said: For three impieties of Damascus, and for four, I will not turn away from them, because they sawed with iron saws the women with child in Gilead. For the threshing sledges, which in Hebrew are called arsoth, and were translated by Theodotion iron wheels, which we have rendered iron carts, the Seventy translated iron saws. It is, moreover, a kind of cart which rolls on iron, toothed wheels underneath, so that, when the grain has been shaken out, it may crush the stubble on the threshing floors and break up the chaff into fodder for the beasts of burden, because of the scarcity of hay.

We have spoken briefly about the causes of the different translation; now let us pass on to the sense of what has been said. First the word of God is directed against Damascus, in which Hazael reigned, who, at the time when Amos was prophesying, was pressing hard upon Israel, that is, the ten tribes, so much so that, after Ahab king of Israel had been overcome at Ramoth-gilead, he slaughtered and crushed the whole region which was called Gilead, and which had fallen as an inheritance to the half-tribe of Manasseh, like threshing sledges threshing grain on the threshing floors. This the prophet Elisha speaks of more fully in the volume of Kings, where we read it written: And he stood with him, and was troubled until his face was flushed; and the man of God wept. Hazael said to him: Why does my lord weep? And he answered: Because I know what evils you are going to do to the sons of Israel: you will set their fortified cities on fire, and you will kill their young men with the sword, and you will dash the little ones, and you will rip up the women with child. And Hazael said: For what am I, your servant, a dog, that I should do this great thing? And Elisha said: The Lord has shown me that you will be king of Syria. But as for what follows in the prophet:

And what is said at the beginning: For three crimes of Damascus, and for four, I will not turn him back, and according to the Seventy: Shall I not turn away from him?, that is, from the people of Damascus, or Aram, that is, the Syrian, can have this sense according to the history: If he had persecuted my people once, or a second time, I would grant pardon; but now, since he has shown himself cruel a third and a fourth time, so that he crushed the captive multitude with iron carts, ought I not to chastise him with blows? Ought I not to turn the face of my clemency away from him? But according to tropology we can say this: the first sin is to have thought what is evil; the second, to have consented to perverse thoughts; the third, to have carried out in deed what you have resolved in your mind; the fourth, not to repent after the sin, and to be pleased with oneself in one's own offence. This all the heretics do, who not only think and do evil, but by their doctrine deceive all the simple, and, after the manner of the people of Damascus, which is interpreted drinking blood, drink the blood of those whom they have deceived. For sins of this kind, says the Lord, is it not right that I should chastise them with blows and turn my face away from them? So that those who do not see the truth of my dogmas may be overwhelmed with darkness by the turning away of my face. For they have crushed, or cut asunder, with iron carts the women with child of Gilead. These are the women with child of whom the Lord speaks in the Gospel: Woe to those who are with child, and to those who give suck in those days. The women with child are the souls of believers, who at the beginning of faith can say: From fear of you, Lord, we have conceived and been in labour; and if they have not been cut up and pierced with iron by the carts and the iron and toothed wheels, of which the psalmist says: The sons of men, their teeth are weapons and arrows, they can also say what follows: And we have brought forth; we have made the spirit of your salvation upon the earth. And consider at the same time that they cannot cut up men of mature age, but only those who are still in the womb, or who cannot take solid food and are still nourished with the milk of infancy. These women with child, moreover, are of Gilead, which is interpreted transfer or migration of the testimony. For they have migrated from the Church into heresy, and have transferred the testimonies of God which they had received before to foreign borders.

This is what the prophet also says: 'For three and four sins I will not turn her back, says the Lord.' And he says this eight times. Now Amos speaks this, that is: you thought, I pardoned: you did it, I pardoned: you did not do penance, I pardoned: were you obliged even to teach evils? This is what is said, For three and four sins I will not be angry with you, says the Lord.

Again, where in the Hebrew there is Benadad, and it is a single name, the Seventy translated the sons of Ader, deceived by the likeness of the letters res and daleth. In that place too where we said, from the house of pleasure, which in Hebrew is mebbeth eden, and all translated it likewise, the Seventy translated from the men of Charran, taking daleth, the middle letter of the name, for res, and, according to their custom, putting the Greek chi before ain, the first Hebrew letter. Cyrene also, which in Hebrew is called cira, they translated ἐπήκλητον, that is, called or named, because of the likeness of the word, since carae can be said for calling, and they understood the proper name as a common noun.

And I will send fire into the house of Hazael, and it will devour the houses of Ben-hadad. And I will break the bar of Damascus, and I will destroy the inhabitant from the plain of the idol. LXX: And I will send forth fire into the house of Hazael, and it will devour the foundations of the son of Ader. And I will break the bars of Damascus, and I will destroy the inhabitants from the plain of ὢν. He gives us to understand that Hazael, in the reigns of Uzziah and Jeroboam, had already died in Syria, and that his son Ben-hadad had succeeded him in the kingdom, from whom afterwards all the kings of Aram, that is, of Syria and Damascus, held the name Ben-hadad. Hence he fittingly did not say: I will send fire into Hazael, but into the house of Hazael, that is, into his royal house, over which his son Ben-hadad presided at that time.

But the Lord will send fire into the house of Hazael, which they themselves call Hazael, that is, vision of God; a fire to consume the wood and stubble in them, and to devour the foundations of the son of Ader. For we ought to speak according to the Seventy as well, lest we seem to have set them out to no purpose: Ader is interpreted εὐπρέπεια, which we can call comeliness, because all the discourse of the heretics, being elegant and well composed and having the beauty of worldly eloquence, deceives its hearers the more easily.

And I will break, he says, the bars of Damascus, and I will destroy the inhabitant from the plain of the idol: that is, all the strength of the Syrians, who, as with a kind of cart and with bars, kept off the onsets of their adversaries. But the plain of the idol, which in Hebrew is called auen, and which both the Seventy and Theodotion rendered ὢν, Symmachus and the Fifth edition translated iniquity; Aquila ἀνωφελοῦς, that is, useless, to show the vain help of idols, since the people of Damascus is taken captive when the Assyrian comes. For we read that Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria, after killing Rezin king of Damascus, of whom Isaiah also speaks, carried away the whole people of Syria, which was called Aram, to Cyrene, and for this reason it is now said:

And him who holds the sceptre from the house of pleasure and luxury, and the people of Syria will be carried away to Cyrene, says the Lord. LXX: And I will cut down the tribe from the men of Charran, and the people of Syria, the named one, will be led captive, says the Lord. So that we understand: I will break and I will destroy; and the people of Syria, last of all, will be carried away into the borders of Egypt.

And by the bars of Damascus, as it were very strong and very firm bolts, let those be understood who are equipped with the art of dialectic and with the arguments of the philosophers. For example: he is called the door who conceived and brought forth a false dogma, like Arius in Alexandria; its bars and its very firm bolts are Euticius and Eunomius, who try to strengthen it with syllogisms and enthymemes, or rather with sophisms and pseudomena and sorites, which were wickedly invented by others. And when the bars of Damascus have been crushed and broken, he will also destroy the inhabitants from the plain of ὢν, which is interpreted labour or pain. For all the heretics have tried with excessive labour and with the pain of seeking to find some order and consistency for their heresy. And I will cut down the tribe from the men of Charran, which in our tongue is rendered holes. For they have no windows through which the light of truth may enter in to them, but certain holes and hidden passages through which harmful and unclean animals come in. And Aram will be led captive, a people lofty and exalted, which has been lifted up into pride and promises itself heavenly things, so that it may be taken captive for its own salvation and, according to the Hebrew, be carried away to Cyrene, where the calling of God is.

According to tropology it seems that it should be explained by us thus: Gaza, which in Hebrew is called Aza, means strength or dominion; Solomon, peaceful; the Idumean, bloodthirsty and earthly; Azotus, that is, Esdod, fire of the breast, or of the paternal uncle, although some, wrongly reading dor for dod, think it means fire of generation; Ashkelon is interpreted murderous fire, or hung up and weighed; Ekron, στείρωσις, that is, barrenness, and ἐκρίζωσις, which is interpreted uprooting. Gaza, therefore, which promises itself the strength and dominion of its own knowledge, is accused of having shut up in Idumea captives from the household of Solomon. These I take to be the teachers of the Jews, and all who follow the letter that kills and will not receive the spirit that gives life, but want whatever they interpret and understand to be earthly, and do not hear, with the disciples, the Lord expounding parables and saying to them: Those who have ears to hear, let them hear, especially since the Apostle understands a plain history as referring to the two testaments: one upon Mount Sinai, which is Hagar, and is in slavery with her children; the other upon Jerusalem the free, which is our mother. He says, then, that he will send fire upon the walls of Gaza and upon all its arguments, with which it strives to surround and defend its lies. And when he has sent fire upon the walls, its houses, or foundations, will be devoured, whatever it could have that was firm and built by the art of dialectic. From Azotus also, which itself too belongs to the foreigners, he will take away the inhabitant, whose breasts, because he follows the letter, are full not of milk but of fire, and who falsely claims to have the fire of the paternal uncle, or whose whole generation is to be consigned to the fires. And he will take away the sceptre, or the tribe, from Ashkelon, where the murderous fire is. For just as the fire of the Lord will save those whose hearts it has penetrated, so that fire which fell from heaven like lightning, which kindles the arrows of the devil, will kill whomever it breathes upon. He will move his hand also upon Ekron, where there is barrenness and uprooting. For whoever does not receive the spiritual understanding will hear through Hosea: Give them, Lord. What will you give them? Give them a barren womb and dry breasts. And so as to take in everything at once in a single word, he says that he will destroy all the remnant of the Philistines, either the city of Gath, in which is the winepress of the devil, or all the remaining Philistines, who are called falling by the cup. For when they have become drunk, they will fall down and wallow in their own vomit.

Thus says the Lord: For three crimes of Gaza, and for four, I will not turn him back, because he carried away a complete captivity, to shut it up in Idumea. And I will send fire into the wall of Gaza, and it will devour its houses; and I will destroy the inhabitant from Azotus, and him who holds the sceptre from Ashkelon, and I will turn my hand upon Ekron, and the remnant of the Philistines will perish, says the Lord. LXX: Thus says the Lord: For three impieties of Gaza, and for four, I will not turn away from them, because they led captive the captivity of Solomon, to shut it up in Idumea; and I will send forth fire upon the walls of Gaza, and it will devour its foundations, and I will destroy the inhabitants of Azotus, and the tribe will be taken away from Ashkelon, and I will bring my hand upon Ekron, and the remnant of the foreigners will perish, says the Lord. The Lord threatens in the law that he will requite the sins of the fathers upon the children to the third and fourth generation; not by an equality of judgment, so that some sin and others are punished, but by the greatness of his clemency, since he always awaits repentance; and what is committed in the first generation he does not rebuke and correct until the third and fourth generation has come. Something of this kind the apostle Paul also says to the Romans: Or do you despise the riches of his goodness and forbearance and patience, not knowing that the kindness of God leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of the just judgment of God, who will render to each one according to his works. What he says, then, is this: I waited a long time for them to repent, and for that reason I was unwilling to punish them when they sinned, so that at some time they might turn and receive healing. But because they do the same things a third and a fourth time, I am compelled to change my sentence and to correct the offenders with blows. Let us see, however, what the Philistines and their cities sinned, whom the Seventy always translated foreigners; for wherever in the Old Testament we read ἀλλοφύλους, that is, foreigners, we must take it not as a common name for all foreign nations, but properly as the Philistines, who are now called the people of Palestine. What did Gaza do to provoke the Lord to anger and vengeance? It carried away the complete captivity of the people of the Jews, and shut it up in Idumea, so as to sell to the Idumeans those whom it had taken from the Jews. For complete captivity the Seventy translated the captivity of Solomon, taking the Hebrew word salma, which means perfect and complete, for the name of Solomon. Accordingly Aquila translated ἀπηρτισμένην and ἀναπεπληρωμένην, Symmachus and Theodotion τελείαν, which signifies not Solomon but perfect and complete, so that none of the captives remained who was not handed over to the Idumeans.
Hence he says that he will send fire upon the walls and houses, or foundations, of Gaza, to devour and swallow up everything.

And because we read of five cities of the Philistines, which were struck with plagues on account of the wrong done to the ark, after Gaza he passes to Azotus, which is called Esdod, and again to Ashkelon, and with a terrible voice he threatens that he will destroy the inhabitants of Azotus, and him who holds the sceptre from Ashkelon, that is, the royal power, or the tribe of Ashkelon, so that no one may remain there, not even men of the last age, who support their trembling limbs with a guiding staff. And again he moves his hand to strike Ekron. And having enumerated four cities, he takes in the remaining cities of the Philistines in a single word: And the remnant of the Philistines will perish, by whom we must understand either the city of Gath, or all the villages which lie under the aforesaid cities.

Tyre means tribulation, or one who hems in; and every perverse doctrine strives to seize the truth, and to shut it up in earthly senses, and it did not remember the covenant of its brothers, that we ought to ascend from the letter to the spirit, from earthly things to heavenly ones; and that it is a precept for us to write out the sacred Scripture in our heart threefold. But God will send fire upon all the fortifications of Tyre, which will devour not only its walls but also its foundations. Concerning the captivity of Solomon, in place of which the Hebrew has consummate and perfect, we have spoken above.

Thus says the Lord: For three crimes of Tyre, and for four, I will not turn him back, because they shut up a perfect captivity in Idumea; and they did not remember the covenant of brothers, and I will send fire upon the wall of Tyre, and it shall devour its houses. LXX: Thus says the Lord: For three impieties of Tyre and for four I will not turn away from her, because they shut up the captivity of Solomon in Idumea, and they did not remember the testament of brothers. And I will send forth fire upon the walls of Tyre, and it shall devour its foundations. The same three and four impieties or crimes which he had imputed to Damascus, to Gaza, and to Azotus, and to Ashkelon, and to Ekron, and to the remaining cities of the Philistines, he heaps upon Tyre as well, and he reproaches it for having shut up a consummate and perfect captivity in Idumea, concerning which we spoke above: And they did not remember the covenant of their brothers. We ask how the Tyrians are brothers of the Jews? He here calls brothers those who are friends and joined by close ties, because Hiram, the prince of Tyre, had friendship with David and Solomon, to such a degree that he, for the building of the temple and of the palace, brought cedar wood on rafts as far as Joppa; and they bestowed grain and oil on the Tyrians, and gave them twenty cities in Bashan as a gift; which he refused to accept, because they were full of grass.

Therefore he says that he will send fire upon its walls, and that it will devour its houses or foundations, which the prophet Ezekiel, in the vision of Tyre, records that Nebuchadnezzar king of the Chaldeans did, where he says: He will surround you with fortifications, and he will heap up a mound round about. And again: Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon made his army serve a great service against Tyre. Every head was made bald, and every shoulder stripped of hair, and wages were not paid to him, nor to his army, for Tyre, for the service with which he served me against her, because his army heaped up a mound for taking Tyre, which formerly was an island. And history relates that Alexander of Macedon also did this, so as to make out of the island a peninsula, which the Greeks call χεῤῥόνησον.

Whatever we have said about Esau and Jacob, let us refer to the Jews and the Christian people. For they, earthly and bloodthirsty, persecuted their brother Jacob, who supplanted them and took away their birthright, and they persecuted him with the sword, so that they confiscated the substance and possessions of the believers, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles; and they violated mercy and the rights of nature, and forgot their mother Rebekah, which means patience, who bore them together in Christ; and holding on to their ancient fury and wrath, to this day in their synagogues they blaspheme the Christian people under the name of Nazarenes, and provided only that they may kill us, they are willing to be burned with fire. But the Lord will send fire into Teman, into the deserted and dry places of Judea — which are by no means watered by the showers of the prophets —, and it will devour all their fortifications, or the foundations of its walls, so that, with every sense of the letter collapsing, the Church may be built up upon the foundations of Christ the Lord. In place of mercy the Seventy translated womb, and in place of fury, horror, and in place of indignation, onset, led by the ambiguity of the words, because rehem signifies both womb and mercy, aphpho both his fury and his horror; and ebrath is said both for indignation and for onset. Moreover armanoth, which we have translated houses, Aquila and Symmachus translated βάρεις, that is, houses, and Theodotion, inhabitants; the Seventy alone, both here and above, said foundations.

Thus says the Lord: For three crimes of Edom and for four I will not turn him back; because he pursued his brother with the sword, and violated his mercy, and held his fury beyond measure, and kept his indignation to the end; I will send fire into Teman, and it shall devour the houses of Bozrah. LXX: Thus says the Lord: For three impieties of Idumea and for four I will not turn away from them, because he pursued his brother with the sword, and violated the womb upon the earth, and seized his horror for a testimony, and kept his onset for ever; and I will send forth fire into Teman, and it shall devour the foundations of its walls. Edom is the same as Esau, so called because of the cooking of the red lentil, for the food of which he lost his birthright. He is called by another name Seir, hairy and shaggy. Hence the mountains of the Idumeans are called the mountains of Seir, and from Edom, in the Greek language, it is called Idumea. He pursued his brother with the sword, namely the sons of Jacob, concerning which it is written more fully in the blessings of Isaac, with which he blesses first Jacob and afterwards Esau; so that the hatred of the brothers was preserved in their descendants, and the Idumean nation persecuted its brothers to such a degree that it did not even grant them passage into the holy land when they were coming out of Egypt; and not only did he pursue his brother with the sword, but he violated his mercy, or his womb, or, as Symmachus translated more plainly, his own bowels; so that he forgot his brotherhood, and hardened the bowels of mercy, and did not know that he was a brother, and despised the womb of Rebekah, who in one birth had brought forth twin infants. And what follows: And he held his fury beyond measure, and kept his indignation to the end, shows an ancient hatred, because they were never joined to one another in peace.

In all places the Scriptures call Esau cunning and crafty, and one who layeth up anger, and keepeth wrath, as it is said, "He keepeth his anger for ever, and he layeth up his wrath for ever and ever."
13 Ascetic Discourses, Discourse 4 -- On Faith: First Discourse on Simplicity

Hence he threatens punishment for their crimes, and says: I will send fire into Teman, which is a region of the Idumeans, and it lies toward the southern quarter, which is what Teman means; this province is called not only Teman but also Daron and Nageb, because it faces the east wind and the south wind and the south-west wind. And as for what he says: It shall devour the houses of Bozrah, it signifies, not another city, as some think, but Idumea, ὀχυρωμένην and fortified, according to that which we read in Isaiah: Who is this who comes from Edom, with garments dyed from Bozrah; this one beautiful in his robe, walking in the multitude of his strength?

Now between the cruelty of Damascus and that of the sons of Ammon there is this difference, that they crushed Gilead with iron carts, or the pregnant women of Gilead with iron saws; but these ripped up the pregnant women of Gilead, to enlarge their border. In the people of Damascus, who drink blood, are understood the heretics, who not only have broken the people of God away from the Church, but have also crushed them and ground them with iron teeth, of whom it is written: Who devour my people as a meal of bread? In the sons of Ammon, which means people of grief, or my people, we understand the schismatics, who do indeed separate a deceived multitude from the Church of God, and break off and divide untrained souls which have lately conceived the word of Christ; yet they do not do this with the cruelty with which the heretics slaughter all whom they have deceived, but, remaining in the same rule of faith, they desire to enlarge their borders and to send down to posterity a name of glory. Therefore the Lord threatens that he will set on fire the walls of Rabbah, that is, of the multitude, in the day of howling and of battle, of commotion and of whirlwind, and that their king, the author of the schism, will go captive, and that the princes will submit their necks to the yoke of the Church.

Thus says the Lord: For three crimes of the sons of Ammon and for four I will not turn him back, because he ripped up the pregnant women of Gilead, to enlarge his border; and I will kindle fire on the wall of Rabbah, and it shall devour its houses with howling in the day of battle, and with a whirlwind in the day of commotion; and Melchom shall go into captivity, he and his princes together, says the Lord. LXX: Thus says the Lord: For three impieties of the sons of Ammon and for four I will not turn away from them, because he cut up the pregnant women of the Gileadites, that he might enlarge his borders; and I will kindle fire upon the walls of Rabbah, and it shall devour the foundations with shouting in the day of battle, and it shall be shaken in the day of its consummation; and the kings shall go into captivity, their priests and their princes together, says the Lord. The divine word rebukes the sons of Ammon, who were begotten of the stock of Lot, and dwell in Arabia, where Philadelphia now is, because under Saul, king of Judea, Nahash the Ammonite, their prince, laid waste Jabesh-gilead, and ripped up its pregnant women, that he might enlarge his borders and subject all Gilead to his rule.

The [false teachers] are also to be admonished to consider well, how sacred Scripture is set up as a kind of lantern for us in the night of this life. When the words are not rightly understood, darkness is the result. And obviously, their perverse mind would not hurry them into a false understanding unless they were first inflated with pride. For while they think themselves wiser than others, they scorn to follow others in matters which these understand better. What is more, in order that they may extort from the untutored crowd a reputation for knowledge, they make every endeavor to discredit what these rightly understand and to confirm their own perverse views. Therefore, it is well said by the prophet, "They have ripped up the women with child of Gilead to enlarge their border." Now Gilead is interpreted as meaning "a heap of testimony." Since the whole congregation of the church together serves by its confession of it, as a witness to the truth, the church is not ineptly expressed as Gilead, for it witnesses to all truth concerning God by the mouth of all the faithful. But souls are said to be with child when they conceive an understanding of the Word by divine love, so that when they come to full term, they will bring forth the understanding conceived by them in showing forth their deeds. Again, "to enlarge the border" is to extend one's own reputation. Thus "they ripped up the women with child of Gilead to extend their border"—that is to say, heretics by their perverse preaching slay the minds of the faithful who have already conceived some measure of the understanding of truth, and so they extend their reputation for knowledge. The hearts of little ones, already big with conception of the Word, they cleave with the sword of error, and thereby make a reputation, as it were, for their teaching. When, therefore, we endeavor to instruct these people not to entertain perverse views, we must first admonish them not to seek their own interests. For if the root of pride is cut away, the branches of false assertions become withered.

Hence he threatens that he will kindle fire on the walls of Rabbah, which was the metropolis of the Ammonites, so that its houses may be devoured amid the shouting and howling of the conquering army; in the day of commotion and of whirlwind, when, Nebuchadnezzar conquering, its captives will be led away, and the idol of the Ammonites, which is called Melchom, that is, their king, will be carried off to the Assyrians; and its princes, that is, its priests, will be led away together. Priests is not in the Hebrew, but princes. So the Seventy added priests, so that, if you wish to know who these princes are, you may hear: priests.
2: Now to prove that in the present place Moab is to be understood of the pride of the philosophers, of whom it is said: I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the understanding of the understanding I will reject, a few examples from the prophet must be unfolded: Amos says: Thus says the Lord: For three impieties of Moab and for four I will not turn away from him, because he burned the bones of the king of Edom to ashes — for truly, whatever there is in the world of perverse doctrines, whatever pertains to earthly knowledge and is thought to be robust, this is overthrown by the dialectical art and, like a fire, dissolved into ashes and embers, so that what was thought to be strongest is proved to be worth nothing —; Isaiah too rebukes the pride of Moab, saying: We have heard the insolence of Moab, he is exceedingly insolent; I have taken away his pride; Jeremiah also, prophesying against all the nations, speaks specifically to Moab: Because you trusted in your fortifications, and a little after: You had confidence in your glory, and again: How do you say: We are strong?, and then: Near is the day of Moab, that it should come, and its malice is exceedingly swift, and more plainly: Say: How has the glorious staff been broken, the rod of magnificence?, and again: The horn of Moab is broken; and these things are said so that, under the name of Moab, the foolish pride of the world that lifts itself up to heaven may be crushed.

Thus says the Lord: For three crimes of Moab and for four I will not turn him back, because he burned the bones of the king of Idumea even to ashes. And I will send fire into Moab, and it shall devour the houses of Kerioth, and Moab shall die in the noise, in the blast of the trumpet, and I will destroy the judge from the midst of it, and I will slay all its princes with him, says the Lord. LXX: Thus says the Lord: For three impieties of Moab and for four I will not turn away from them, because he burned the bones of the king of Idumea into ashes; and I will send forth fire into Moab, and it shall devour the foundations of its cities, and Moab shall die in weakness with shouting, and with the voice of the trumpet; and I will destroy the judge out of it, and I will slay all its princes, says the Lord. Not only the sons of Ammon, but Moab too was begotten of the seed of Lot, who was the son of Abraham's brother. And so that God may show himself to be the Lord of all, and that all souls belong to his dominion, who is their maker, he avenges the injury done even to the king of the Idumeans, or rather the crime which was committed against him by the Moabites, in that they burned his bones even to ashes, and did not end their savagery and rage even at his death. The Hebrews relate that the bones of the king of Idumea, who was already buried, and who had gone up with Joram king of Israel and Jehoshaphat king of Judah against Moab, were afterwards torn up and burned by the Moabites in revenge for their grief.

But just as one ought not to carry off the perfect captivity, or that of Solomon, and shut it up in Idumea, so as to make lowly and earthly men out of lofty and heavenly ones, which Gaza and Tyre are recorded to have done, so we ought not to burn the bones of the king of Idumea and dissolve them into ashes and embers. The Jews transfer the spiritual understanding into Idumean flesh, and the royal sense, which is engaged in the letter, and is most solid and most firm, they enervate and break down with certain genealogies and superfluous traditions, and reduce to dust; and not only do they do this, but all the heretics, who would have God, after the manner of a human likeness, sit on a high and lofty throne and set his feet upon the earth, so that, of course, they may not dangle; and have a nose with which to smell the odor of a good fragrance, eyes with which to see, hands through which to work, feet by which to walk, ears with which to hear, a mouth with which to speak, teeth with which to grind his food. Whoever reads that Judah went in to Tamar the harlot and begot two sons of her, if he follows the shamefulness of the letter and does not ascend to the beauty of the spiritual understanding, burns the bones of the king of Idumea. Whoever thinks that Hosea took a wife of fornication, and perceives nothing more in the saying than is contained in the simple words, burns the bones of the king of Idumea.

For this reason, therefore, they say, God declares that he will send fire into Moab, either the metropolis of the Moabites, from which the whole province was named, or the whole province, so that it might devour the houses of Kerioth, which is the name of a city; although the Seventy translated of its cities, that is, of Moab; and that it will perish in the noise and in the howling of the conquering army, of which the one is called in Hebrew saon, the other therua; and in the blast of the trumpet or horn, for this is what sophar signifies. And when Moab has perished, the counsel of its princes and judges will be vain, its cities and its leaders being overthrown alike.

And for that reason the Lord sends fire into Moab, which means from the father, because he was indeed born of God, but has abandoned him. And it will devour its cities, or towns, which is what Kerioth means. Hence also Kiriath-jearim is turned into our language as village of the forests. And Moab will die in no other way than in shouting, and noise, and howling, and the blast of the horn, so that they may be overwhelmed by the lofty senses which in the holy books are compared to the blasts of the horn. Then the divine word destroys both the judges and the princes, and all who preside over earthly works, and it commands the teachers of the Church: Go up onto a high mountain, you who bring good tidings to Zion; lift up your voice, you who preach to Jerusalem.

Thus says the Lord: For three crimes of Judah, and for four I will not turn him back, because he has cast away the law of the Lord, and has not kept his commandments; for their idols have deceived them, after which their fathers had gone, and I will send fire into Judah and it shall devour the houses of Jerusalem. LXX: Thus says the Lord: For three impieties of the sons of Judah, and for four I will not turn away from them, because they have rejected the law of the Lord, and have not kept his precepts; and they have been deceived in their vanities, which their fathers followed, and I will send forth fire into Judah, and it shall devour the foundations of Jerusalem. To the other cities and nations mentioned above, Damascus, Gaza and Azotus and Ashkelon and Ekron, and the remaining towns of the Philistines, to Tyre also and Idumea, and to the sons of Ammon and Moab, he does not reproach that they cast away the law of God and despised his commandments; for they did not have the written law, but the natural one. Hence he says that they violated their own bowels and the bowels of mercy, and crushed the pregnant women of Gilead with iron carts, and carried off the captivity of Solomon, or the perfect captivity, and shut it up in Idumea, and did not remember the covenant of their fathers, and pursued their brother with the sword; and that they burst forth into such, I will not say cruelty, but rage, that they burned the bones of the king of Idumea, and would not allow death to be the last of all evils. But Judah, in which, at the time when these things were being said, there were the religion of God and the temple and the ceremonies, and which had received the law, and the precepts, and the judgments, and the testimonies, and the commandments — on the difference among which there is a fuller discussion in the eighteenth (19th) psalm and in the hundred and eighteenth (119th) —, is rebuked and convicted by the Lord; and he is going to receive fitting punishments, because he cast away his law and did not keep his commandments. And because he cast these away and despised them, his idols deceived him in due order and course. For he could not have been deceived by idols before, unless he had rejected the law of the Lord and had not done his commandments. These are the idols after which their fathers went in Egypt, fashioning images of the Egyptian ox, and adoring Baal-peor, and worshipping Ashtaroth and the Baalim.

Whatever we have said about Judah is referred to the Church, in which there is the true confession, and the peace of the Lord, and the vision of truth. And in this it is reproved, that it has despised the law of God and has not done his commandments, and that each one, adoring his own vices and sins, has begun to have as God that by which he has been overcome, as the apostle Peter says: For by what one is overcome, of this he is also the slave. The miser worships gold, the glutton his belly, the lustful man his member and Baal-peor; the wanton woman, who, living in pleasures, is dead, adores venereal pleasures.

Hence the Lord threatens that he will send fire into Judah also, to devour the houses and the foundations of Jerusalem, not of that Jerusalem in which the vision of peace abides, but of those which have arisen in various cities under the name of Jerusalem.

Hence the Lord will send fire into Judah, and it will devour the most wicked houses and the vicious foundations, which have destroyed the glory of Jerusalem; and at the same time we learn that the Creator of all has care not only of Judah and Israel but of all the nations; and that, according to the Apostle, those who have sinned without the law perish without the law, and those who have committed offences under the law are judged by the law of the Lord.

Many, truly, are the shoes of the sinful soul, by which it is bound and cramped. For each man is cramped by the cords of his own sins. Accordingly, Abraham swears to the king of Sodom, "I will not take of all that is thine, from a thread to a shoe-latchet." On account of these being defiled and polluted on the earth, every kind of wrong and selfishness engrosses life. As the Lord reproves Israel by Amos, saying, "For three iniquities of Israel, yea, for four, I will not turn him back; because they have given away the righteous for silver, and the needy for a pair of shoes, which tread upon the dust of the ground."

He might also have been betrayed by any stranger, did I not find that even here too he fulfilled a psalm: "He who did eat bread with me has lifted up his heel against me." And without a price might he have been betrayed. For what need of a traitor was there in the case of one who offered himself to the people openly and might quite as easily have been captured by force as taken by treachery? This might, no doubt, have been well enough for another Christ but would not have been suitable in one who was accomplishing prophecies. For it was written, "The righteous one did they sell for silver." The very amount and the destination of the money, which on Judas's remorse was recalled "from its first purpose of a fee" and appropriated to the purchase of a potter's field, as narrated in the Gospel of Matthew, were clearly foretold by Jeremiah: "And they took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of him who was valued, and gave them for the potter's field."

But we, who have shown in Hosea that under the name of Israel, and of Samaria, and of Ephraim, and of the sons of Joseph — of which tribe was Jeroboam, who separated the people from the kingdom of David and from Jerusalem and from the temple of God — the heretics are signified, let us understand now too, after Judah and Jerusalem, which is interpreted as the Church, that the prophetic discourse is directed at the heretics, who sell a holy and righteous man, and a poor one too, for money. The poor and righteous man is the churchman who does not have knowledge of the Scriptures, but, content with simplicity, does the commandments that have been enjoined, of whom it is written: The poor man does not endure threatening. And to the Galatians: Only that we should be mindful of the poor. All these things the heretics do for riches, and for sandals, with which they tread the dust of the earth; for because they cannot stand with bare feet upon the holy ground — on which Moses stood, and Joshua the son of Nun; whence the apostles too are commanded to go with bare feet, so that they may have nothing of death and of skins, which are referred to the flesh —; therefore they strike the poor on the head. And the Savior commanded his disciples that if by chance, since they were still dwelling on the earth, anything mortal had clung to their works, they should shake the dust off their feet.

Thus says the Lord: For three crimes of Israel, and for four I will not turn him back, because he sold the righteous for silver and the poor for sandals, they who crush the heads of the poor upon the dust of the earth and turn aside the way of the humble; and a son and his father went in to the girl, to profane my holy name; and upon garments taken in pledge they reclined beside every altar, and they drank the wine of the condemned in the house of their God. LXX: Thus says the Lord: For three impieties of Israel, and for four I will not turn away from them, because he sold the righteous for silver, and the poor for the sake of sandals, which tread upon the dust of the earth; and they struck the heads of the poor with the fist, and turned aside the way of the humble, and a son and his father went in to the same girl, to defile the name of their God; and binding their garments with cords, they made awnings beside the altar, and they drank wine from false accusations in the house of their God. He puts Israel, that is, the ten tribes, last for this reason: because, as we said before, almost everything that follows was written to it, so that the prophetic discourse might keep the order of the book within one continuous text. Their first crime, then, or impiety, enumerated in three offences or four, is that for money they sold a man, and a righteous man, who is the more admirable in this, that he was not overcome even by poverty so as to do anything unjust; and if indeed, compelled by the necessity of hunger, they had sold the poor righteous man for a price, there would be some excuse for the crime; but as it is, for the cheapest of things, sandals, with which they tread dust and dung, they sold the precious soul of a man.

He does not leave him unpunished, but rather subjects to punishments Israel, that is, the tribes in Samaria. And that they themselves, sinning unguardedly, have all but consumed the tranquility owed by God to the weak, the turning away for three and four sins would show, which having suffered they must necessarily be subjected to terrible things, and be in every evil. Therefore, the divine David, fearing this thing, and knowing it to be a cause of destruction, implored, saying, "Do not turn Your face from me, and do not turn away in wrath from Your servant." For wrath always follows, and, as it were, accompanies the turnings away.

"They sell the righteous for silver, and the needy for a pair of sandals": They did not endure to speak rightly and justly, and to render for each of those being judged the justice that accords with the law. But if it happened that a man was righteous, sober and gentle, modest and unboastful; for such a one would be understood as both righteous and needy, or poor in spirit; being brought to judgment by one of the more powerful, this man is sold to his enemies, although the law clearly proclaimed, "You shall not take person in judgment;" and again, "You shall not slay the innocent and the just." For the one entrusted with judging is certainly established in the order of God, to whom alone judging is proper. "For there is one lawgiver and judge," according to the voice of the saint. Therefore, the one who falsifies the account of justice and shows partiality will certainly insult the divine dignity, and offends God who says, "Execute true judgment, and show mercy and compassion every one to his brother." He accuses them, therefore, of selling the just and the needy to their enemies, and of being accustomed to doing this for the sake of a few and most worthless gains, which would scarcely suffice for those who received them for the purchase of sandals.

How then is it that while forbidding the greater he was silent about the less? Because the example of the patriarch seemed injurious to many who indulged their flesh so far as to live with sisters in their life time. What ought to be my course? To quote the Scriptures, or to work out what they leave unsaid? In these laws it is not written that a father and son ought not to have the same concubine, but, in the prophet, it is thought deserving of the most extreme condemnation, “A man and his father” it is said “will go in unto the same maid.” And how many other forms of unclean lust have been found out in the devils’ school, while divine scripture is silent about them, not choosing to befoul its dignity with the names of filthy things and condemning their uncleanness in general terms! As the apostle Paul says, “Fornication and all uncleanness…let it not be once named among you as becometh saints,” thus including the unspeakable doings of both males and females under the name of uncleanness. It follows that silence certainly does not give license to voluptuaries.

These, according to the Seventy, strike the poor man on the head; according to the Hebrew, they crush the heads of the poor upon the dust of the earth, and they are lifted up into such pride that they are unwilling to walk with the humble. And lest this misdeed be thought small, a son and his father went in to one girl, to violate the holy name of God. Whatever, therefore, is done shamefully is referred to an injury against God, who says: Through you my name is blasphemed among the nations. This is what the Apostle also writes to the Corinthians: It is actually reported that there is fornication among you, and such fornication as is not even among the nations, so that someone has his father's wife. And you are puffed up, and have not rather mourned, so that he who has done this deed might be taken away from your midst. It often happens that a father defiles his son's wife, that is, a father-in-law his daughter-in-law; both of which are forbidden in the law: You shall not reveal the shame of your father, and you shall not uncover the shame of your daughter-in-law. And so the letter too has the greatest usefulness, if it is kept.

And the heretics strike the heads of the poor, although this is not read in the Hebrew, because they have turned aside the way of the humble. The way of the humble is that which says: I am the way, and the life, and the truth, which calls us to walk along it, and says: Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. But all the chiefs of the heretics swell with pride, of whom the Apostle also speaks: Lest, being puffed up, he fall into the judgment of the devil; who says: I will ascend into heaven, above the stars of heaven I will set my nest, I will be like the Most High. Hence the proud heretics God resists, but to the humble churchmen he gives grace. The son and the father, too, went in to one girl, to violate and profane the holy name of God. That the people of the Jews is our father, we often read, as Paul says: For I do not wish you to be ignorant, brothers, that our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea. And in another place: Ask your fathers, and they will declare to you, your elders, and they will tell you. And again: In place of your fathers sons have been born to you. Hence also, in the Church of the nations, it says: The sons of my mother have fought against me. We, therefore, are the sons, and the father is the people of the Jews. We sin and commit a crime when we go in with our parent to the observance of the sabbath, the injury of circumcision, the ceremonies of the abolished law; to whom the Apostle says: Behold, I Paul say to you, that if you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing. And again: Those who are justified in the law have fallen from grace. Whoever enters the Church in such a way as to keep the law within the Gospel, he goes in with his father to the girl, and commits debauchery, and violates the name of God. Hence those who say that it does the Jews no harm, after the coming of Christ, if they so believe in God as to keep the precepts of the law as well, defile father and son in one fornication.

They so multiplied their ill-gotten gains as to betray the rights of the needy for the basest profit (the meaning of the phrase "sandals trampling the dust of the earth," which was clear proof of their setting no store by justice, especially as they easily did so for base profit). "They pummeled the heads of the poor." Of the same people he says that they not only failed to vindicate their claim on justice but even belabored them without risk—hence his going on, "and strayed from the path of the lowly." Though their behavior was correct, they changed the verdict to a negative one, scorning them for their lowliness.

Cain was the first murderer. Afterwards a deluge engulfed the earth because of the exceeding wickedness of humanity. Fire came down from heaven upon the people of Sodom because of their corruption. Subsequently God elected Israel, but even Israel became perverse, and the chosen people were wounded. For while Moses stood on the mountain before God, the people worshiped a calf in the place of God. In the days of their lawgiver Moses, who said, "You shall not commit adultery," a man dared to enter a brothel and be wanton. After Moses, prophets were sent to heal Israel, but in their exercise of healing they deplored the fact that you could not overcome evil. One of them says, "The faithful are gone from the earth. Among men the upright are no more!" and again, "All alike have gone astray; they have become perverse; there is not one who does good, not even one." And again, "Cursing and theft, and adultery, and killing have overflowed" upon the land. "They sacrificed their sons and daughters to demons." They engaged themselves in auguries and enchantments and divinations; and again, "They fastened their garments with cords and hung veils next to the altar."

And because every outrage, once it has passed the boundary of shame, adds crimes to crimes and always advances to worse things, the ten tribes even reclined upon garments taken in pledge beside every altar, which the Hebrews interpret thus: upon the garments of those who were unwilling to go to the idols, which they had extorted by force, they reclined, feasting in the idol's temple. But according to the Seventy, so great was their contempt for God that they stretched out with cords beside the altar their garments in which they sleep, or in which they commit fornication, and made παραπετάσματα, that is, coverings, so that no one could see them committing fornication in the temple; and, serving drunkenness and lust, they bought even the very wine that they drank, not from their own labor, but from false accusations; and they did this in the shrine of their god, so as to defile those whom they thought gods with shamefulness and debaucheries. So speak, and so expound, those who follow the simple history.

But also, binding their garments with cords, they make coverings beside the altar, holding out the faith of Christ as a screen. For as many as have been baptized in Christ have put on Christ, and they set their garments, which they have bound with the cords of sins, before the eyes of those who look, so that their outrages may not be seen, and so that whoever looks at the altar may not suspect the debauchery. This all the heretics do, committing fornication under the Christian name, and spreading the testimonies of the Scriptures over their errors and lies as a screen. Hence the apostles too spread their garments on the foal of the ass, so that the Lord might sit more softly, and might mount the road paved from the law and the prophets. On the contrary, the heretics do not spread their garments beneath the footsteps of the Savior; but they bind them beside the altar and hold them out before their sins, so that they may drink the wine of false accusation, or of the condemned, who are condemned from the very fact that they have gone out of the Church. This is the wine of Sodom, of the fury of dragons and of asps; whoever drinks it cannot be healed. And they drink the wine, not in the house of God, where the temple is and Jerusalem, but in the house of their god, whom they have fashioned for themselves with artful speech.

But I destroyed the Amorite from before their face, whose height was the height of the cedars, and he was strong as an oak; and I crushed his fruit above, and his roots beneath. It is I who made you go up from the land of Egypt, and I led you out in the desert forty years, that you might possess the land of the Amorite; and I raised up of your sons for prophets, and of your young men Nazirites. LXX: But I took away the Amorite from before their face, whose loftiness was as the height of the cedar, and he was strong as an oak; and I dried up his fruit above, and his roots below. I led you out of the land of Egypt, and led you around in the desert forty years, that you might possess the land of the Amorites; and I took of your sons for prophets, and of your young men for sanctification. You indeed sold the just man for silver and the poor man for sandals, striking his head, or crushing the heads of the poor in the dust, and you turned aside the way of the humble, so far that father and son went in to one girl and violated, or profaned, my holy name; and your garments, polluted by brothels and fornication, you bound with the chains of sins, so that you committed adultery in the holy place and, joining injustice to drunkenness, drank another's wine, and did this in the house of your God. But I, on the contrary, in return for your evils, which you paid back to me, bestowed good things on you: so that, as you were coming out of Egypt, I destroyed before your face Sihon king of the Amorites, who was as lofty and as strong as a cedar and an oak; and I crushed his fruit above, and his roots below. I led you out of Egypt, and through forty years I made you come to the holy land by a long circuit, that you might possess the land of the Amorite, of which we spoke above, which Moses divided to the sons of Reuben and Gad and to the half-tribe of Manasseh; and after such great benefits I added this as well, that I took prophets to myself from your sons, and from your young men, or chosen ones, made Nazirites, whom the Seventy translated as sanctified. Nor indeed, where the praises of God are spoken of, must the order of the history be kept; but it often happens that what was done first is told last, and what was done last is set at the beginning. This the seventy-seventh (78th) psalm and the hundred and fourth (105th), where the power of the signs, not their order, is described, will be able to teach us, and so will the titles of the psalms, of which let us set down only two examples, those of the third psalm and of the fifty-first (52nd), where what was done earlier is narrated last, and what we read as last is placed at the beginning. For in the volume of Kings we read that what concerns Doeg the Edomite, which is the title of the fifty-first (52nd) psalm, was written before Absalom rose against his father, which is noted at the head of the third psalm in its title. So too the Amorite was destroyed, or blotted out, last, which is now told first; and his making them go up from Egypt, and afterwards leading them out into the wilderness for forty years, we read was done at the beginning, things which are told last here, the order being changed.

His roots too he cut down and broke in pieces, so that nothing of the evil tree might sprout afterwards; and the Lord himself made us go out from the world and, through forty years, a number which always belongs to affliction and fasting, to mourning and sorrow, come through tribulations and straits to the holy land, that we might first possess the land of the Amorite, and the region that was once his might become our possession; and that afterwards he might raise up prophets from our sons, all the holy men who received the prophetic spirit, of whom we read more fully in the first epistle to the Corinthians; and that from our young men, or chosen ones, he might take Nazirites and sanctified ones, who, offering their souls to God in sacrifice, do not touch wine, which can make men drunk and overturn the state of the mind, so that they may have the hair of Samson, in whose head, because the head of a man is Christ, his strength and victory resided.

Therefore, before God led us out of the land of Egypt, out of the iron furnace, he destroyed before our face the Amorite, who is called bitter, or λαλητὸς, that is, speaking, or famous and celebrated in frequent talk. Now this Amorite and king of the Amorites is called Sihon, an unfruitful and barren tree, not because it bears no fruit, but because it brings forth bad fruit, of which it is said: Every tree that does not bear good fruit will be cut down and cast into the fire. And of the false prophets we read: Who come in the clothing of sheep, and inwardly are ravening wolves; by their fruits you will know them, by their bad fruits, that is. Whether, then, it bears no fruit, or bears fruit but not good fruit, it is called an unfruitful tree. This Sihon, of whom it is written: Already the axe is laid to the roots of the trees, because he was an unfruitful tree, was cut down when the Lord struck him; his height is compared to the height of the cedars, of which we read: I saw the wicked man exalted on high and lifted up like the cedars of Lebanon; and I passed by, and behold, he was not; and I sought him, and his place was not found. And he fittingly says that he passed by, because from him who passes over from the world, and can say: Passing over, I will see this great vision, the cedar is taken away, and the place of pride cannot be found. His strength too, like that of the oak, a tree most hard and most strong. From its name Philo, the most eloquent man of the Hebrews, thinks that Esau was called δρύινον, that is, oaken and made of hard oak, although Esau can also be understood as ποίημα, that is, a thing made, so as to be referred to evil works. Of this strong and sturdy one he speaks in the Gospel: When a strong man armed guards his court, the things he possesses are in peace; but if one stronger than he comes upon him and overcomes him, he will take away all his armour, in which he trusted, and will distribute his spoils. And the Lord granted us that he should crush from above the fruits of this Amorite Sihon, whose name we said means an unfruitful tree, because they were bad, and take them away, lest anyone, thinking them good, should eat and perish.

[This was the reason why] the Lord accused the Israelites more severely and showed that they deserved greater punishment, because they sinned after receiving the honors that he had bestowed on them. He said, "You only have I known of all the families of the earth; therefore I will visit upon you your iniquities," and again, "I took of your sons for prophets and of your young men for consecration." And before the time of the prophets, when he wanted to show that sins received a much heavier penalty when they were committed by the priests than when they were committed by ordinary people, he commanded as great a sacrifice to be offered for the priests as for all the people. This explicitly proves that the priest's wounds require greater help, indeed as much as those of all the people together. They would not have required greater help if they had not been more serious, and their seriousness is not increased by their own nature but by the extra weight of dignity belonging to the priest who dares to commit them.

Is it not so, sons of Israel, says the Lord.

And you will give the Nazirites wine to drink, and you were commanding the prophets, saying: Do not prophesy. LXX: likewise. While I was bestowing such great benefits on you, so as to kill your adversaries and hand their land over to you, and to choose prophets and Nazirites from your sons and young men and consecrate them to my worship. Can you say that I did not do these things, and deny my clemency toward you, through which you live?

Samson and Samuel drank neither wine nor strong drink, for they were children of promise and conceived in abstinence and fasting. Aaron and the other priests when about to enter the temple refrained from all intoxicating drink for fear they should die. From this we learn that they die who minister in the church without sobriety. And hence it is a reproach against Israel: "You gave my Nazirites wine to drink."

You who broke out into such madness that you made my Nazirites drunk with wine, though they are commanded by the law not to drink anything that can intoxicate, and charged the prophets not to prophesy in my name. This is what Amaziah the priest of Bethel also commanded the prophet Amos, whom we now have in hand; and Jeremiah was ordered by the king not to speak the words of the Lord to the people, to such a degree that the king even burned his discourses in the fire. From this passage Tatian, the chief of the Encratites, tries to build up his heresy, asserting that wine must not be drunk, since it is commanded in the law that the Nazirites should not drink wine, and now those who give the Nazirites wine to drink are accused by the prophet. If they follow the letter in all things, and thrust Jewish fables upon the churches of Christ, then they ought also to let their hair grow, and not eat grapes, dried or fresh, and not go in over a dead father and mother; and if perhaps they have done these things, and have been overcome either by human frailty or by necessity, let them shave their heads, and let all the days of their consecration and their toil be void. But if they do not do these things, and cannot, after the manner of Jewish innkeepers, mix water with wine, shadows with the truth, the constraint of the law with the grace of the Gospel, let them understand that drunkenness to be the one by which the vigour of the soul is made drunk and overwhelmed with worldly cares, and understand that it is those who charge the prophets, saying: Do not prophesy, who, overcome by envy, forbid learned men to bring forth the word of doctrine. And while the Lord says: Go and say to this people, they on the contrary command that you not speak in the name of the Lord, above all if he who teaches looks not to shameful gain, glory and boasting, but to the profit of those who read and hear.

And the cart that is rolled is the one of which we read in Isaiah: The land of Moab shall be trampled down, as a threshing floor is trampled with carts. And in another place: I will make you, he says, like the new wheels of a cart with the teeth of saws, and you shall crush the mountains and grind the hills to pieces, so that, after you have crushed the mountains and hills, flight may perish from the swift, as Paul says: Do you not know that those who run in the stadium all run indeed, but one receives the prize. And in another place: You were running well; who hindered you, so that you should not obey the truth? Hence, fearing for himself as well, he says: Not that I have already received, or am perfect; but I run, if I may lay hold of that in which I also have been laid hold of by Christ. All these things he did, lest flight perish from the swift; and for this reason, when he had now reached the finishing mark and received the prize of victory, he said in security: I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith; for the rest, there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the just judge, will render to me on that day; and not to me only, but also to all who love his coming. If we flee with a quick step, sin will not be able to catch us; but if malice binds our feet, we shall speak with the prophet to God: Where shall I go from your spirit, and where shall I flee from your face? Of bad runners the Apostle speaks: It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who has mercy.

Behold, I will creak beneath you, as a cart loaded with hay creaks, and flight shall perish from the swift, and the mighty shall not hold his strength, and the strong shall not save his soul, and he who holds the bow shall not stand, and the swift of foot shall not be saved, and the rider of the horse shall not save his soul, and the strong of heart among the mighty shall flee naked in that day, says the Lord. LXX: Therefore behold, I will roll beneath you as a cart full of stubble is rolled, and flight shall perish from the runner, and the mighty shall not hold his might, and the fighter shall not save his soul, and the archer shall not endure, and the swift of foot shall not be able to be saved, and the horseman shall not save his soul, and his heart is found among the powerful, and he shall flee naked in that day, says the Lord. While I was bestowing benefits on you, and leading you out of the land of Egypt, and killing the Amorite before your face so that you might possess his land, and raising up prophets from your sons and Nazirites from your young men, you were making my Nazirites drunk with wine and saying to the prophets: Do not prophesy. Therefore, just as a cart weighed down with a load of stubble or hay howls far off with creaking and noise, so I, no longer bearing your sins, and handing them over to the fire like stubble, will cry out and say: Flight shall perish from the swift, whom the Hebrews understand as Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who had earlier fled into Egypt. Here, however, let us take not the princes themselves but their houses and their offspring.
