And the mighty shall not hold his strength — the mighty one they interpret as Baasha, who was most ready for wars —, and the strong shall not save his soul — this one here they take to be Omri —, and he who holds the bow shall not stand, or endure, they think was said of Jehu the son of Nimshi, who struck Joram king of Israel with an arrow. And the swift of foot shall not be saved: they understand Menahem, who, hastening in vain, sent gifts to the king of the Assyrians. And the rider of the horse shall not save his soul: this one they interpret as Pekah the son of Remaliah, who, joined with Aram, that is, the Syrian, laid waste much of Judea under Ahaz its king. And the strong of heart, among the mighty, shall flee naked in that day, says the Lord. Hoshea alone, who was the last king of the ten tribes and tried to call the straying people back to the worship of God, will come out of the fire as if naked. And he calls him naked because under him the ten tribes were taken captive. This is what the Hebrews hold, and as it was handed down to us by them, so we have faithfully set it out for our own people.

But now let us return to our own. God threatens that he will roll a cart weighed down with hay or stubble beneath them, so that, since they have no grain to be stored up in barns, their hay and stubble may be burned up in the fire. This is the hay of which the prophet says: Let them become like the hay of the buildings, which withers before it is plucked up. And: All flesh is hay. And the stubble is that over whose burning the prophet laments so mournfully, saying: Woe is me. For I have become like one who gathers stubble in the harvest, and like grapes at the vintage, when there is no cluster to eat, the first-ripe. Woe is me. O soul, for the reverent man has perished from the earth, and there is none among men who does what is right: all are judged in blood, and the rest. This is the hay and stubble of which the Apostle also speaks: Wood, hay, stubble, each one's work will become manifest, because in the day of the Lord it will be revealed in fire.

He sometimes compares himself with deep condescension, on account of our infirmity, to objects without sense, as he says by the prophet, "Behold, I will shriek over you as a cart creaks when laden with hay." For since the life of the carnal is hay (as it is written, all flesh is hay), in that the Lord endures the life of the carnal he declares that he carries hay as a cart. And to creak under the weight of the hay is for him to bear with murmuring the burdens and iniquities of sinners. When therefore he applies to himself very unlike resemblances, we must carefully observe that some things of this kind are sometimes spoken of concerning God, on account of the effect of his doings, but sometimes to indicate the substance of his majesty.
MORALS ON THE BOOK OF JOB 6:32.7
swift: Jeroboam I. Other kings are described afterwards.

There follows: And the mighty shall not hold his strength; not that he is mighty, but that he boasts of being mighty. Or he is the one who trusts in his own strength and not in the mercy of God, according to what is written: I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the understanding of the prudent I will reject; not that true wisdom can perish and the understanding of the truth be rejected, but that the wisdom of those perishes who seem wise in their own eyes and trust in their own learning. The strong one too, or the fighter, who will not save his soul, is he who by no means possesses the armour of the Apostle: having a shield, but not of faith; girded about the loins, but not in truth; clothed with a breastplate, but not of righteousness; bearing a sword, but not of salvation. A fighter of this sort does not sanctify the battle, nor can he fight the wars of the Lord, since he struggles against the truth on behalf of falsehood. Such a fighter cannot say: Blessed be the Lord my God, who teaches my hands for battle and my fingers for war. My mercy and my refuge.

The heretics too have archers, who, bending the bow in vain, will not be able to withstand the arrow of the Lord, who speaks through Isaiah: But I am like a chosen arrow in the quiver of the Lord. These are the archers of whom David also sings: Behold, sinners have bent the bow, they have made ready their arrows in the quiver, to shoot in the dark at the upright of heart. And the swift of foot, he says, shall not be saved: he who, because of the sharpness of his wit, runs about through the testimonies of the Scriptures and strives to crush the truth with the eloquence of orators or the sophisms of dialecticians; and in this he is tripped and falls, because he trusts not in the Lord but in his own feet. The rider of the horse, too, shall not save his soul, he who does not know what was said through the prophet: The horse is deceitful for salvation. And he does not know that it is written: All who mounted horses have slumbered. This man will not save his soul, but as he perishes he will hear: Some in chariots, and some on horses, but we will call upon the name of the Lord our God. They were hindered and have fallen, but we have risen and stand upright.

And the strong also of heart among the mighty shall flee naked. This passage can be explained in two ways: either that he can escape for this reason, that he has stripped off the old man and the skin tunics of sins, and was weighed down by no burden; or, on the contrary, that because he is naked and has lost the garment of Christ, of which it is said in the Apostle too: Put on Christ Jesus, and in another place: If indeed, being clothed, we are not found naked, his strength will profit him nothing, but in the day of battle and contest he will flee from his pursuers and, unable to resist without the armour of the Apostle, will turn his back to the enemy.
3: Hear the word which the Lord has spoken concerning you, sons of Israel; concerning every kindred which I brought out of the land of Egypt, saying: Solely you have I known of all the kindreds of the earth; therefore I will visit upon you all your iniquities. LXX: Hear this word which the Lord has spoken concerning you, house of Israel, and against every tribe which I brought out of the land of Egypt, saying. Nevertheless, you have I known of all the tribes of the earth; therefore I will take vengeance upon you for all your wickednesses. The prophetic word is directed to the sons of Israel, and who these sons of Israel are the following verse shows: Concerning every kindred, he says, which I brought out of the land of Egypt, which we must take to refer not only to the ten tribes but to all twelve, adding Judah and Benjamin. For he brought them all out of the land of Egypt, and he says: Solely — or, as Symmachus translated, Only —, you have I known of all the kindreds of the earth. And because I, who am the Creator of all, have known you alone, and have held you as my peculiar people, therefore upon you alone I will repay all your sins: For the mighty will suffer torments mightily; but he who is least is worthy of mercy. And in Ezekiel we read: Begin from my saints. And the judgment of God is said to have its beginning from his own house. Let this, meanwhile, have been said according to the history. Moreover, since hearing in the holy Scriptures is taken to mean not only that which we receive with the ears of the flesh, but also that of which the Lord says: He who has ears to hear, let him hear, and since for this reason all the people also saw the voice of God, the word of the Lord is properly addressed to those who see the Lord with their understanding, whom he brought out of the land of Egypt and out of the power of Pharaoh — so that they should by no means serve with mud and straw, building the cities of Egypt —; and whom he has known out of all the tribes of the earth, as the Apostle says: But now knowing God, or rather being known by him. And in another place: He who is ignorant will be ignored. The Lord, then, does not know all, but those who are worthy of his knowing them, as he says in the Gospel: Depart from me, workers of iniquity, I do not know you. For in that they are workers of iniquity, they are unknown to the Lord. Therefore, he says, because I have known you alone and have held you as mine, I will visit upon you all your iniquities. Whom the Lord loves, he reproves, and he chastises every son whom he receives. And he said well, I will visit, and not, I will strike, because the stroke of God is a visitation and a healing. And all your iniquities, he says, or your sins, I will visit, so that nothing may remain unstruck, and nothing fail to receive healing.

The word might be understood as having come against all of Israel, no longer taking Judah and Ephraim in part, but with the whole race gathered as if into one; for every tribe of Israel was brought up from Egypt. Therefore, with none being left out, he commands them to hear the things from God. And what were these things? For there are countless, he says, cities and countries throughout the whole world under heaven, and those in them are beyond number, but you from Israel out of all I have made chosen, I made myself manifest through many wonders, I delivered you from bitter and unbearable slavery, I declared you enviable and thrice-blessed, I have instructed you by law for what is pleasing to me, I have fortified you with my assistance, and I have brought you into the land promised to the fathers. But since you alone, he says, out of all who have been deemed worthy of so conspicuous a grace have not ceased grieving and have offended in many ways, for this reason I will henceforth demand of you an account of your folly, I will no longer tolerate those who sin and have an unreproved inclination for this. Therefore, to despise God and to disregard the master's will is a cause of destruction for anyone henceforth who has known him, or has been known by him, in the manner of spiritual kinship.

And each of us thinks, since he has not been an idolater, since he has not been immoral—would that we were pure in such areas—that after he has been set free from this life, he will be saved. We do not see that "all of us must appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each one may receive either good or evil according to what he has done in the body." We do not hear what has been said: "You especially have I known out of all the tribes on the earth. Therefore I will punish you for all"—not just some and not others—"of your iniquities."

For this very cause God accuses the Israelites more vehemently, and shows that they were worthy of greater chastisement, because they sinned after so many honors had come to them from Him, saying in one place: "But you only have I known of all the families of the earth, therefore will I punish you for your iniquities," and again, "and I raised up of your sons for prophets, and of your young men for Nazarites;" and before the times of the prophets, wishing to show that sins receive sorer punishment by far when they occur in the case of the Priest than in the case of the laity, He enjoins as great a sacrifice to be offered for the Priest as for the whole people, and this amounts to a proof on his part, that the wounds of the Priesthood need more assistance—that is, as great as those of all the people together, and they would not have needed a greater, except they were worse; and they are not worse in their nature, but are aggravated through the dignity of the Priest, who dares to commit them.

Will two walk together unless they have agreed? Will a lion roar in the forest unless he has prey? Will the lion's whelp give voice from his den unless he has seized something? Will a bird fall into the snare of the earth without a fowler? Will the snare be taken up from the earth before it has caught something? If the trumpet sounds in the city, will the people not be terrified? Will there be evil in the city which the Lord has not done, for the Lord God will not do a thing unless he has revealed his secret to his servants the prophets. The lion will roar, who will not fear? The Lord God has spoken, who will not prophesy? LXX: Will two walk together at all unless they have known each other? Will a lion bellow from his forest, having no prey? Will the lion's whelp give his voice from his den at all unless he has snatched something? Will a bird fall upon the earth without a fowler? Will a snare be set down upon the earth unless it has caught something? If the trumpet sounds in the city, will the people not fear? Will there be evil in a city which the Lord has not done, for the Lord God will not do anything unless he has revealed his instruction to his servants the prophets. The lion will bellow, and who will not fear? The Lord God has spoken, and who will not prophesy? I have read in the commentaries of a certain man, who wished to win assent to a difficult thing, that to the eight crimes, or impieties and sins, first of Damascus, second of Gaza and the other cities of Palestine, third of Tyre, fourth of Idumea, that is, Edom, fifth of the sons of Ammon, sixth of Moab, seventh of Judah, that is, the two tribes, eighth, which is the last, of Israel, that is, the ten tribes, as many threats are now given in return, and that the first answers to the first, that is, Damascus, the second to the second, that is, Gaza, and the rest to the rest. Whether this is true, he who wrote it will know for himself. Another, however, thinks that six examples are set forth, of two walking together on the road, and of a lion roaring in the forest, and of a lion's whelp giving its voice when it has seized something, and of a bird caught by a fowler, and of a snare which is fixed in the ground to catch prey, and of a trumpet sounding in the city, and that to these examples a likeness is given in return: as the things above have a cause and do not happen unless that cause has gone before, so no evil befalls in a city which has not been done at the Lord's command.

There are some who think that the first example contains a teaching: that two cannot walk together unless they have first agreed with each other in him who made both one, and the middle wall of the partition destroyed, and fashioned the two into one new man; and he made peace between them, and joined them with the bond of love, so that, when two are together, they may ask of the Father and obtain whatever they have asked. These are the two rods which are joined to each other in Ezekiel, and the two peoples, of the circumcision and of the Gentiles, of which the Lord speaks to Elijah: I have left for myself seven thousand men who have not bent the knee before Baal. And in another place God: I was found, he says, by those who did not seek me; I appeared to those who did not ask for me. But when the two have been brought together into one, they will cleave to the Lord, and one spirit will come to be: For he who cleaves to the Lord is one spirit. These two, then, who agree with each other and walk together in the way of Christ, can fear the assault of none of their adversaries.

He therefore accuses them, because they claimed that the prophets from Him did not convey words from above and from God; but rather they thought that things were being uttered from their own opinion, and that they were speaking things different from what seemed good to the Lord of all. For this reason He says, O foolish and senseless ones, will any of you become friends and walk the same path of life, not having known yourselves, or rather one another; that is, unless they have seen one another to be of the same character and like-minded? "For every creature loves its like, and a man will cleave to his like." And if this is true, how could I have accepted the prophets, as it were, into friendship and love, being holy Myself, if they too had not become holy? How then do you persecute the saints, to whom I have entrusted My words, whom I have accepted as good, as it were walking the same road of My wills? For whatever I might wish, this is also their will. Therefore, to rebuke the prophets is nothing other than to direct the rebuke against Me.

But if they are separated by discord, at once the roaring lion will attack them, of whom the apostle Peter also says: Your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour. This roaring lion does not move about in sown fields, not in vineyards, not in olive groves, nor among the fruit-bearing trees, which praise God, but where there are forests and untilled ground and wild beasts dwell. And not only will they lie open to the lion's bites, but the lion's whelp will seize them and lead them to his den, fleeing the light and making for the darkness. For everyone who sins loves the darkness and hates the light; of these we read in the psalm too: You have set darkness, and it became night; in it all the beasts of the forest will pass through. The lions' whelps roaring to seize their prey, and to seek their food from God. For the lion's whelp seeks not the prey which he already possesses, which is in his own power, but to snatch from the Church of Christ; of him it is written in Habakkuk: His foods are choice.

Those who study the habits of wild beasts say that the lion, when it is in need of food, roams about powerfully through mountains and glens and forests, turning its eye this way and that, and seeking to catch something of the animals grazing in the woods. But when it sees something suitable for food, then it comes near and makes its attack, roaring terribly and harshly. Why then, He says, do you accuse God, because He makes the threat before the attack of terrible things? And why do you gnash your teeth at the prophets themselves, because they too have cried out against your impiety? For I am like a lion, He says, which is accustomed to roar before the hunt, all but threatening the attack beforehand, and the prophets are like cubs, imitating my custom. But just as for the animals in the mountains the hunter's shout beforehand is not entirely unprofitable, scaring them to flight before they happen to be caught, so also for sinners the threat and prediction before the terrible things is exceedingly useful, leading them to repentance and avoidance of what is impending. God, therefore, compares himself to a lion that does not leap upon and bring things from his wrath upon some, unless he first makes known the threat, so that by repenting they might be saved, receiving the prediction of the things that will be as a medicine for salvation before the onset of the terrible things.

The third punishment of those whom discord has separated is that they lose the wings by which they were formerly borne on high, and fall headlong from heaven to earth, and are held by the fowler, who is better called ἰξευτὴς, because with clinging birdlime he catches free birds which of their own will come down to earthly things. Of these it is written in Proverbs: Not unjustly are nets spread for birds. For just is the ruin of sinners, who, though they had the wings of a dove and ought to have flown through the air, were pressed down to earthly things by the weight of their sins, and through their own vice stuck fast to the birdlime. Of this we read in the Apostle: He who cleaves to a harlot becomes one body with her. The fourth punishment of those in discord is that they are caught in the snare, which is set not in heaven but on the earth; the saint glories in having escaped it, and says: Our soul, like a sparrow, has been snatched from the snare of the hunters; the snare is broken, and we are set free. This is the broken snare of which the Apostle speaks to believers: God will crush Satan under your feet swiftly. And again we read in David: Beside the path they have set a stumbling block for me. For they cannot deceive any of the simple among believers unless they put forward the name of Christ, so that, while we think we are finding Christ, we go on to the Antichrist.

The discourse is now made by way of comparison. For fowlers most skillfully bring down the sparrows that have settled in the plants, and with snares, on the other hand, some crush what is caught. But the discourse now seems to signify through the sparrows those who are accustomed to think lofty things, the boastful in mind and arrogant in spirit, and not enduring to be brought down with the lowly; and through those caught in snares, the lovers of earthly things, and those who seek only carnal and fattening things. And God again compares himself to a fowler and a snare, bringing the proud down to the earth, and as it were crushing and hunting for punishment those who mind only the things on earth. But those from Israel were boastful, despising God and rejecting prophets and dishonoring the law; and they were no less also exceedingly greedy for the things in the world, and seeking only the things on earth, overcome by whose strange desires they did not accept the word of God, but opposed those who call to virtue.

I do not say these things in arrogance, but I have the prophet Amos standing at my side, crying and saying, "There is no evil in the city which the Lord has not done." Now evil is a many-faceted term. I wish that you shall learn the exact meaning of each expression, in order that on account of ambiguity you may not confound the nature of the things and fall into blasphemy. There is then evil, which is really evil; fornication, adultery, covetousness, and the countless dreadful things, which are worthy of the utmost reproach and punishment. Again there is evil, which rather is not evil but is called so, famine, pestilence, death, disease, and other of a similar nature. For these would not be evils. On this account I said they are called so only. Why then? Because, were they evils intended to become the sources of good to us, chastening our pride, goading our sloth and leading us on to zeal, making us more attentive.
HOMILY AGAINST THOSE WHO SAY THAT DEMONS GOVERN HUMAN AFFAIRS 1:4–5

The fifth punishment is that of those who have abandoned the peace which surpasses all understanding, and which the Lord, as he went to the Father, left to the apostles, saying: My peace I give to you, my peace I leave to you: that, though set in the city of the Lord, they are terrified by the sound of the trumpet. For whatever is said in the holy Scriptures is a threatening trumpet, piercing the ears of believers with a great voice. If we are righteous, we are summoned by the trumpet of Christ to blessedness; if sinners, we hear what torments we are going to suffer. But the evil which the Lord does in the city is not the contrary of virtue, but affliction and torment, of which we read: Sufficient to the day is its own evil, that is, tribulation and distress. And in the prophet we read: I am God, who made light and darkness, who make peace and create evils. For just as darkness is contrary to light and day, so war too is contrary to peace; it is not evil in itself, but seems to be evil to those who endure it. And that we may know that in the holy Scriptures evil is sometimes taken not as the contrary of virtue but as affliction, punishments and distress, let us take one more example, from Jonah: And God saw their works, that they had turned from their most wicked ways, and he repented over the evil which he had spoken of doing to them. The evil there is surely the overthrow of the Ninevites, which God had threatened through the prophet, and not the evil contrary to virtue, which belongs to sin, on account of which he was threatening torments to sinners.

Germanus: We often read in holy Scripture that God has created evil or brought it upon men, as is this passage: "There is none beside Me. I am the Lord, and there is none else: I form the light and create darkness, I make peace, and create evil." And again: "Shall there be evil in a city which the Lord hath not done?"

Theodore: Sometimes holy Scripture is wont by an improper use of terms to use "evils "for "affliction;" not that these are properly and in their nature evils, but because they are imagined to be evils by those on whom they are brought for their good. For when divine judgment is reasoning with men it must speak with the language and feelings of men. For when a doctor for the sake of health with good reason either cuts or cauterizes those who are suffering from the inflammation of ulcers, it is considered an evil by those who have to bear it. Nor are the spur and the whip pleasant to a restive horse. Moreover all chastisement seems at the moment to be a bitter thing to those who are chastised, as the Apostle says: "Now all chastisement for the present indeed seemeth not to bring with it joy but sorrow; but afterwards it will yield to them that are exercised by it most peaceable fruits of righteousness," and "whom the Lord loveth He chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom He receiveth: for what son is there whom the father doth not correct?" And so evils are sometimes wont to stand for afflictions, as where we read: "And God repented of the evil which He had said that He would do to them and He did it not." And again: "For Thou, Lord, are gracious and merciful, patient and very merciful and ready to repent of the evil," i.e., of the sufferings and losses which Thou art forced to bring upon us as the reward of our sins. And another prophet, knowing that these are profitable to some men, and certainly not through any jealousy of their safety, but with an eye to their good, prays thus: "Add evils to them, O Lord, add evils to the haughty ones of the earth;" and the Lord Himself says "Lo, I will bring evils upon them," i.e., sorrows, and losses, with which they shall for the present be chastened for their soul's health, and so shall be at length driven to return and hasten back to Me whom in their prosperity they scorned. And so that these are originally evil we cannot possibly assert: for to many they conduce to their good and offer the occasions of eternal bliss, and therefore (to return to the question raised) all those things, which are thought to be brought upon us as evils by our enemies or by any other people, should not be counted as evils, but as things indifferent.

But perhaps you say that the outcome of these matters grieves you not moderately. Will there then be an affliction in a city, perchance, which the Lord has not done? It is like as if one should say: Will there then be anyone among men able to afflict a city either with diseases or sieges or destructions of crops or even in some other such way? But if no one of men could do such things, and it lies rather in the authority and power of God, why are you angry with those who announce it beforehand? And yet it is necessary to repent, and by inclinations to this to appease him the one who is grieved and has the power to harm those who have sinned. Therefore, in these matters, we shall understand the 'evil' that comes from God in the cities not as wickedness—far from it!—but rather as an affliction, that is, the wrath and movement for whatever reason, which He might bring upon sinners, persuading them to turn back to what is more fitting. For it is written that, "With bit and bridle you shall restrain the jaws of those who do not draw near to you." For since He is good, and "wishes all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of truth," He somehow compels them by means of wrath toward what is better, and sometimes powerfully moves, with terrors and threats, those whom reason and the guidance of what is beneficial do not persuade.

As it is impossible for two people to share a journey at the same time, he is saying, unless indicating to each other where and why they are traveling, or for a lion to roar if there is no prey, or for a bird to fall without a hunter, or for all the other things mentioned, so it is impossible for any punishment to be imposed without God willing it. He calls punishment "evil," note, by use of a general custom: we are accustomed to use "troubles" of diseases, chastisements, untimely deaths, famines, wars, and the like, not because they are troublesome by nature but because they are troublesome to human beings and the source of distress and grief.

His permission, therefore, is usually spoken of in the Holy Scripture as His energy and work. Nay, even when He says that God creates evil things, and that there is no evil in a city that the Lord hath not done, he does not mean by these words that the Lord is the cause of evil, but the word ‘evil’ is used in two ways, with two meanings. For sometimes it means what is evil by nature, and this is the opposite of virtue and the will of God: and sometimes it means that which is evil and oppressive to our sensation, that is to say, afflictions and calamities. Now these are seemingly evil because they are painful, but in reality are good. For to those who understand they become ambassadors of conversion and salvation. The Scripture says that of these God is the Author.

It is, moreover, to be observed that of these, too, we are the cause: for involuntary evils are the offspring of voluntary ones.
An Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith, Book 4, Chapter 19

But if there were no evils in the world, much good would be lost to man, as well in respect of knowledge, as also in respect of desire and love of good: for good is better known in contrast with evil; and while evil results come about, we more ardently desire good results: as sick men best know what a blessing health is.

There follows: The Lord God will not do a thing unless he has revealed his secret, or his correction, to his servants the prophets; not that God reveals to the prophets everything that he does in heaven or has already done before, but what he is going to do on earth. He revealed to Noah his servant that he was going to bring on the flood. He revealed to Abraham and Lot his servants that Sodom and Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboiim were going to burn. He revealed to Joseph the interpretation of the dream of the seven years of famine in Egypt, and to the prophet Jonah the overthrow of Nineveh, so that those who heard of the punishments to come might either repent and avoid the torments, or, if they scorned them, be punished more justly. So now too the Lord reveals through Amos his servant and prophet what he is going to do to the ten tribes, so that, if they are turned to better things and abandon their idols, they may be freed from the danger that threatens. And note that God, merciful and kind, always foretells what is to come, so that he may not be forced to inflict punishments. And what the heretics slanderously charge against the Creator, as though he were severe and savage, cruel, and nothing but a judge, because there is no evil in a city which he does not do, this we refer to the greatness of his mercy, in that he does not inflict punishments unless he has foretold them beforehand. And he who foretells does not wish to punish sinners.

The Lord reveals to the prophets all things that are necessary for the instruction of the faithful; yet not all to every one, but some to one, and some to another. 
And although God revealed in general to the prophets what He was one day to do regarding the salvation of the human race, still the apostles knew some particulars of the same, which the prophets did not know. Thus we read (Ephesians 3:4-5): "As you reading, may understand my knowledge in the mystery of Christ, which in other generations was not known to the sons of men, as it is now revealed to His holy apostles." Among the prophets also, the later ones knew what the former did not know; according to Psalm 118:100: "I have had understanding above ancients," and Gregory says: "The knowledge of Divine things increased as time went on" (Hom. xvi in Ezech.).
National calamity is traced to national sin, specially to neglect of the poor.

The lion, he says, will roar, and who will not fear? The Lord God has spoken, who will not prophesy? The word who is taken in this passage not for the impossible, but for the rare. For he will not fear, and he will not prophesy, who because of his hardness has scorned to hear the Lord. And the sense according to the history is this: If at the voice of the lion all things tremble and the whole nature of living creatures is terrified, shall we, when God commands us to speak and announce to the people the punishments to come, not prophesy? Shall we not speak? I know that a certain man has left it written in his commentaries that the roaring lion is to be understood as the devil, roaring at those who are going to perish, but that God, who speaks through the prophets, is to be referred to the Lord the Savior; so that, as they hear the lion's roaring in the bad sense and are taken captive unto death, so the saints may hear the Lord commanding in the good sense, and be saved.

"Lord, you have been our refuge." Therefore we have recourse to you. Our healing shall be from you, for our evil is from ourselves. Because we have abandoned you, you have abandoned us to ourselves. May we therefore be found in you, for in ourselves we had been lost. "Lord, you have been our refuge." Why, my brethren, should we doubt that the Lord will make us gentle if we submit ourselves to be tamed by him? You have tamed the lion, which you did not create. Will your Creator be unable to tame you? What is the source of your power to tame such savage beasts? Are you their equal in bodily strength? By what power then have you been able to tame such huge beasts? The so-called beasts of burden are wild by nature, for if untamed they could not be endured. But because you are not accustomed to see them except when handled by men and under the curb and control of men, you might think that they were born tame. At any rate, consider the savage beasts. The lion roars; who does not fear? And yet, whence your knowledge of the fact that you are more powerful? Not in bodily strength but in the inner reason of the mind. You are more powerful than a lion, because you have been made to the image of God. The image of God tames a wild beast. Is God unable to tame his own image?

"A lion will roar, and who will not be afraid? The Lord God has spoken, and who will not prophesy?" It is not the prophets, he says, who bring on the things that come from wrath; how could they? For they are also human in nature, just like you, but they have been honored by God by learning all the things that He might wish to fulfill, and to bring upon cities and lands either good things, perhaps, or things that are accustomed to cause pain. But perhaps you say to this: Let them learn, if you wish; let them be enriched by you with the knowledge of future events; let all the mysteries be made clear to them; but let them speak to no one, nor let them sound anything in the ears of those who reject them. What then is the reply to this from God? A lion will roar and who will not be afraid? For if, he says, when the lion roars, the most powerful of beasts, there would not be anyone so hard-hearted and arrogant as not to receive fear, how, when God, who is above all, speaks and commands them to announce what they learn, would they not fear the one who has commanded them? For they are not, like you, scornful and unyielding, holding in no account the things that seem good to the Lord of all.

Make it heard in the houses of Azotus, and in the houses of the land of Egypt; and say: Gather yourselves upon the mountains of Samaria, and see the many madnesses in the midst of her, those who suffer calumnies in her inner chambers; and they did not know how to do what is right, says the Lord, treasuring up iniquity and plunder in their houses. LXX: Announce to the regions among the Assyrians, and to the regions of the land of Egypt; and say: Gather yourselves upon the mountain of Samaria, and see many wonders in the midst of her, and the oppression in her; and she did not know what things are to come before her, says the Lord, who treasure up iniquity and misery in their regions. We said above that the prophet Amos prophesies especially, indeed in the great part of the volume, to the ten tribes, which are called Israel and Ephraim, and Samaria. And so now too he is commanded to announce to Azotus and to the land of Egypt the things that follow. In place of Azotus the Seventy, intending I know not what, put the Assyrians, although Azotus in the language of the Hebrews is called Esdod, and the Assyrians, Assur. For the houses too, which are called armanoth, they translated regions, which are called sadoth, and the words have nothing of likeness. Say, he says, that all the nations which are in the neighbourhood should gather and see the crimes of Israel, lest they think the judgment of God unjust. As if he were saying: First see what they do, and then approve my sentence. And he fittingly added: Upon the mountains of Samaria, whether of the city, which is now called Sebaste and was then called Samaria, or of the whole province, which is situated in mountainous country: And see the many madnesses in the midst of her, that in place of God they worship calves and sacrifice their sons, and, not content with this crime, they bring calumnies against the poor in their inner chambers, and do not know at all how to do what is right, treasuring up for themselves not gold and money, which are sometimes gained by labour, but iniquities and plunder in their houses; so that, because they abandoned the worship of God and worshipped idols, he delivers them, God does, to a reprobate mind, to do what is not fitting. And since, once and for all, according to the laws of tropology, Samaria is referred to the heretics, who falsely claim to be the guardians of the commandments of God, the divine word commands that they preach among the nations which have no knowledge of God, in whose teaching there is a burning fire, and tribulation and anguish, that they may consider the false Samaria, and go up to the mountains of her pride, and see the many madnesses in the midst of the city, while each one fashions what he wishes and worships his own fiction: as Marcion a God who is good and idle; as Valentinus thirty αἰῶνας (aeons) and a Christ last of all, whom he calls ἔκτρωμα, that is, an abortion; as Basilides, who calls the almighty God by the monstrous name ἀβράξας (Abraxas), and says that this same name, according to the Greek letters, and the number of the yearly course, is contained in the circle of the sun, whom the heathen, under the same number in other letters, call Μείθραν (Mithras). And the Iberian follies marvel at Balsamus and Barbelo. Are these not madnesses, and many madnesses, when each one fashions whatever has fallen into his mind? They also suffer calumny in her inner chambers, that is, all the simple among the believers are oppressed, while under the name of truth they worship a lie; and they do not know at all how to do what is right, because they have lost the path of truth, nor do they believe in him who says: I am the truth; and they treasure up for themselves the dogmas of iniquity, and they seize and shut up in their houses those whom they have been able to deceive by false error. But if it please us to read Assyrians — which, however, is not found in the Hebrew —, let us say that these are the ones of whom it is written: I will bring it upon the great mind, the prince of the Assyrians, who said: By my strength I will do it, and so on, so that the heretics are taken captive by the Assyrian and held in the land of Egypt, from which, coming now to the Church, they have been set free.

Therefore thus says the Lord God: The land shall be afflicted and surrounded, and your strength shall be pulled down from you, and your houses shall be plundered. LXX: Therefore thus says the Lord God: Tyre, and your land round about, shall be deserted, and he will pull down your strength from you, and your regions shall be plundered. In place of Tyre, which in the Hebrew is written with two letters, sade and res, and is called Sor, as Aquila and the Seventy likewise translated it, the Hebrew who instructed me in the holy Scriptures interpreted tribulation; nor do we reject his opinion, because Symmachus too, who is not accustomed to follow the κακοζηλίαν (affectation) of words but the order of the understanding, says siege and encircling of the land. In place of siege, which he calls πολιορκία, strength was put by Theodotion, who thought that what should be read was not Sar and Sor, which means tribulation or Tyre, but sur, which properly refers to a very hard rock, which in Greek is called ἀκρότομος, and which we in Latin can call flint. Let us speak, then, of each in turn. The LXX said: Tyre, and your land all around. And the sentence seemed to hang unfinished; so they added on their own: Shall be deserted; nor is it an error of the translators, where, because of the ambiguity of the word, both tribulation and Tyre can be said. And the sense is: Upon the mountains of Samaria my people has committed many madnesses, practising calumny, and utterly ignorant of what is right, and treasuring up for itself iniquity and plunder; therefore it shall be afflicted, or crushed, and their land shall be surrounded by the Assyrian army, and there shall be pulled down from you, he says, O Samaria, O ten tribes, O once my people, your strength; and there shall be plundered in your houses what you gathered by calumny from the tears of the wretched. The heretics too will either be afflicted in the day of judgment, and all their strength will be worn down, and what they had gained from plunder will be plundered, so that the peoples whom they had deceived may be set free; or certainly they will be afflicted daily by churchmen, and surrounded by the testimonies of the Scriptures, and there will be pulled down from them the strength of the syllogisms and the subtleties of words by which they had confirmed their dogma. And their houses will be plundered, so that those who had been carried off from the Church may return to the Church.

If you have any hope of salvation; if you have the least thought of God, or any desire for good things to come; if you have any fear of the chastisements reserved for the impenitent, awake without delay, lift up your eyes to heaven, come to your senses, cease from your wickedness, shake off the stupor that enwraps you, make a stand against the foe who has struck you down. Make an effort to rise from the ground. Remember the good Shepherd who will follow and rescue you. Though it be but two legs or a lobe of an ear, spring back from the beast that has wounded you. Remember the mercies of God and how He cures with oil and wine. Do not despair of salvation. Recall your recollection of how it is written in the Scriptures that he who is falling rises and he who turns away returns; the wounded is healed, the prey of beasts escapes; he who owns his sin is not rejected. The Lord willeth not the death of a sinner but rather that he should turn and live.

Thus says the Lord: As if a shepherd should rescue from the mouth of the lion two legs, or the tip of an ear, so shall the sons of Israel be rescued who dwell in Samaria in the region of the couch and on the pallet of Damascus. LXX: Thus says the Lord: As if a shepherd should tear away from the mouth of the lion two legs, or the tip of an ear, so shall the sons of Israel be torn away who dwell in Samaria over against the tribe and in Damascus. At the beginning of Amos, where we discussed those little verses: The Lord will roar from Zion, and from Jerusalem he will utter his voice; and the beautiful places of the shepherds mourned, and the top of Carmel was dried up, we said that he used the language of his own craft, so that, because as a herdsman of flocks he had known nothing more terrible than the lion, he compared the wrath of the Lord to lions. According to this sense, then, now too he takes an example from what he had often seen, and so he tells that the small remnant of the ten tribes is to be rescued from the hands of the Assyrians: as if a shepherd, when all the other limbs have been devoured, should snatch two legs or the tip of an ear from the lion's jaws; and, having set down the example for the comparison, so, he says, shall the sons of Israel be rescued, namely the ten tribes that dwell in Samaria, in the region of the couch and on the pallet of Damascus. This seems to me to be explained thus: We read in Isaiah that Rezin king of Aram, that is, of the Syrians, who reigned in Damascus, and Pekah son of Remaliah, king of Israel, having made a league, came fighting against Judah; concerning whom the Lord commands Ahaz king of Judah and Jerusalem not to fear the two half-burnt firebrands, when, as a sign of full liberty, both the conception and the childbearing of a virgin are shown to him. The sons of Samaria, then, dwell in the region and quarter of the couch, resting on the help of the Syrians, and promising themselves victory on the pallet of Damascus, so that, as one who is weary is refreshed on a couch, so they might strengthen their broken forces by the help of a neighbouring nation. Hence also in the same Isaiah it is said, by a type of things to come, that a child is to be born who, before he knows how to call father and mother, will take the spoils of Samaria and the power of Damascus, which, that is, were fighting against Jerusalem with their forces joined. For the region of the couch and the pallet of Damascus the Seventy translated: Over against the tribe and in Damascus, so that according to tropology we may refer the tribe to Judah, and Damascus to the calling of the nations, out of whom one flock of the Lord has been made, whose sheep the savagery of lions often mangles, and from whose jaws scarcely two legs or the tip of an ear is carried off. In the leg is shown the way of teachings, in the ear the mysteries of the words. Hence also the apostles are commanded to walk with bare feet, without shoes and without any skin of a dead animal. And to believers it is said: He who has ears to hear, let him hear. In the Apocalypse of John too we read: He who has ears, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. And more plainly through the prophet: Put, he says, your words in the ears of your heart. This path both the heretics and their masters the demons hasten to obstruct and to interweave with nets, so that we may fall in the way which is Christ. But if there comes a churchman and man of God, and a Samson, which means sun, he kills the lion, and going down into the pit of hell, which cools the waters, in the time of snow, of storm and of winter, he strangles the lion, so that with secure foot and safe ears we may be able to follow the Lord and to hear his words.

God's other titles fall into two distinct groups. The first group belongs to his power, the second to his providential ordering of the world, a twofold providential ordering—involving, and not involving, incarnation. Clear cases of titles that belong to his power are "Almighty" and "King"—whether it be of "glory," "the ages," "of the forces," or "of the beloved" or the "rulers"16—"Lord Sabbaoth," which means "lord of the armies," "forces" or "masters." To his providential ordering belong "God"—be it "of salvation," "retribution," "peace," or "righteousness," or "of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob" or all the spiritual "Israel," which has the vision of God. For since we are controlled by three conditions—fear of punishment, hope for salvation and glory too, and the practice of the virtues which results in these last—the name which mentions retribution deals with fear, the one which mentions salvation with hope, and that which refers to virtues disciplines us to practice them. The intention is that by, as it were, carrying God inside one, a person may have some success here and press on all the harder to perfection, toward that affinity with God which comes from the virtues.

Hear and testify in the house of Jacob, says the Lord God of hosts, that in the day when I begin to visit the transgressions of Israel upon him, I will visit also upon the altars of Bethel; and the horns of the altar shall be cut off and shall fall to the ground; and I will strike the winter house with the summer house; and the houses of ivory shall perish; and many houses shall be scattered, says the Lord. LXX: Priests, hear: testify to the house of Jacob, says the Lord God Almighty, that in the day when I avenge the iniquities of Israel upon him, I will avenge also upon the altars of Bethel; and the horns of the altar shall be undermined and shall fall upon the ground. I will confound and strike the winged house upon the summer house, and the houses of ivory shall perish; and many other houses shall be added, says the Lord. What is put at the beginning of the section according to the Seventy, priests, is not found in the Hebrew, but in place of this word is read ares, which Aquila interpreted as pallet; and I think that the Seventy put the Hebrew word itself, which some, not understanding it, read in place of ares as ἱερεῖς, that is, priests. Now the prophetic word commands that they first hear, and then testify in the house of Jacob, that is, among the ten tribes, what the Lord has said.

When the Lord begins to visit the transgressions of Israel, which formerly beheld God with the mind, he will visit also upon the altars of Bethel, not the one altar which the Church has, but the very many altars of the heretics. For they have as many altars as schisms. He will cut off also the horns of the altar which in their pride they boast that they possess as the one altar. And their horns, that is, their arrogance, will fall to the ground; and he will strike the winter house, those heretics who toil in continence and fasts, in dry fasts and sleeping on the ground, among whom are Tatian and Mani; and the summer house, such as the Nicolaitans and the Eunomians, and the new followers of an old heresy, who for the gluttony of the belly admit every pleasure. And the houses of ivory will perish, which are put together with an artful tooth and the splendour of rhetorical polish. And many houses will be scattered, which are dispersed through the whole world. For when the one truth rises, many lies will be destroyed. For the winter house the Seventy translated οἶκον τὸν περίπτερον, which we have interpreted winged, because it has little doors over the windows, and as it were wings for keeping off the severity of the cold.

When I begin, he says, to visit the transgressions, or impieties, of the house of Israel, and to render to them what they deserve, and the time of captivity has come, then the altars of Bethel shall be destroyed, where the golden calves were, and the horns of the altar shall be cut off, the altar which was split apart when Jeroboam too stretched out his hand, and they shall crash to the ground, broken, as the Assyrian lays waste.

And I will strike, he says, the winter house with the summer house, which we can take simply according to the letter: that they were of such great wealth that they had double houses, winter ones and summer ones, of which some faced the north and others the south, so that according to the variety of the seasons they might secure a temperate measure of cold and heat and of the sky. We can call the winter house the kingdom of Israel, in which there was coldness of religion and of the worship of God, and various whirlwinds of the winds, and savage storm; and the summer house, Judah and Jerusalem, in which was the temple, and burnt offerings were offered morning and evening, and the warmth of religion flourished. And the houses of ivory, he says, shall perish, which can also stand according to the history. For we read that Ahab king of Israel abounded in such great luxuries that he made himself a house of ivory. For 'of ivory' we find in the Hebrew houses of tooth, that is, of elephant. Of these it is also written in the forty-fourth (45th) psalm: From the houses of ivory, out of which the daughters of kings have delighted you in your honour.
4: Hear this word, you fat cows, who are on the mountain of Samaria; who do calumny to the needy, and crush the poor, who say to your masters: Bring, and we will drink. The Lord God has sworn by his holy one that behold, days shall come upon you, and they shall lift you up on poles, and your remnants in boiling pots; and you shall go out through the openings, one against another, and you shall be cast into Armon, says the Lord. LXX: Hear this word, you cows of Basanitis, who are on the mountain of Samaria, who oppress the poor and trample the needy, who say to your masters: Give us, that we may drink. The Lord swears by his holy ones that behold, days shall come upon you, and they shall take you up in arms; and those who are with you, in pots, pestilent traders; and you shall be cast out naked, one facing another, and you shall be cast upon mount Remmam, says the Lord. In place of fat cows, the Seventy put of Basanitis; Aquila and Theodotion the Hebrew word itself, Basan; we, following the interpretation of Symmachus, who says αἱ Βόες εὔτροφοι, that is, fattened kine, have interpreted fat cows. Now he speaks to the princes of Israel and to all the nobles of the ten tribes, who gave themselves up to luxuries and plunder, that they should hear the word of God, and know that they are not ploughing oxen but fat cows from the herd, or such as are fed in the pastures of Bashan, which are places most fertile in grass; and by this he signifies that they were made ready not for agriculture but for sacrifice and for eating. You are fat cows on the mountain of Samaria, and you crush all the lowly, and you say to your masters, that is, to the shepherds, by whom we understand the kings: Give us and we will drink, that is, only give the command, and we will lay everything waste. But from the fact that he put: Give us and we will drink, and did not say: Give and we will eat, he signifies their drunkenness in wine and luxury, which overturn the state of the mind.

Now the word of the Lord which the cows of Bashan are commanded to hear is, according to the tropology we have begun, addressed to the heretics, who, serving the belly and gluttony, are rightly called very fat cows, or cows of ignominy; for this is what Bashan means, that is, αἰσχύνη; and if we wished to call it confusion, we should be interpreting Babylon rather than Bashan. These fat cows, or cows of ignominy and dry, for Bashan is understood in this sense too, are on the mountain of Samaria, to which it is also said in Hosea: Take away your calf, Samaria. And again in the same prophet: For your calf was a deceiver, Samaria; and they are on the mountain of Samaria for this reason, that they are always lifted up into pride and promise themselves lofty things. Samaria also means watch, not because they keep watch over the words of the Lord, but because they boast that they are the watchmen of his precepts. Who do calumny to the needy and crush the poor. By the needy and the poor understand the churchman, who, content with the simplicity of the truth, does not seek the furniture of the heretics, and the brilliance of eloquence, and the riches of arguments. These cows say to their masters: Bring and we will drink. Their masters we can call either the princes of perverse dogmas, such as Valentinus, and Marcion, and Arius, and Eunomius, or those who through many books strengthen what others have wickedly invented. To these the cows of Basanitis say: Bring us and we will drink. For unless those give, these have nothing to devour, or rather nothing to drink so as to be drunk. But that we may know that waters and cups signify teaching, the Lord speaks to the Samaritan woman: Everyone who drinks of this water will thirst again; but whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him will not thirst for ever. Therefore whoever drinks of the waters of the Samaritan woman, that is, of the heretics, will always thirst and will not be able to cool the burning of a parched throat, as Isaiah cries aloud about this very thing: As one who is thirsty dreams that he drinks, and when he has risen he still thirsts, and his soul has hoped in vain; so shall all the nations be that fight against Jerusalem. For truly whoever drinks of the waters of the heretics, and fights against Jerusalem, the Church of God, drinks in his sleep, and his soul is mocked by empty images. And when he thinks himself satisfied, then he will have the beginning of thirst. Hence also it is said to the churchman: Drink waters from your own vessels, and your waters from the springs of the wells, and let them be for you alone.

And the Lord your God swears by his holy one against the cows that are slaves to fattening and feasts, or he swears by his holy ones, that days shall come upon them, days of judgment and of punishments; so that, carrying them in their arms, they may put them, and those who are with them, into cauldrons, or carry them; and either the cows themselves are pestilent traders, or those who come to carry them; and they are cast out naked, seeing one another, and are cast upon mount Remmam, says the Lord God. For we must speak also according to the LXX, lest we seem to have set them out in vain. When the day of judgment and of vengeance comes against the heretics, then they will be carried away in arms, that is, with their own arms, with which they had fought against the Church, or, conquered by the armour of God and overcome by his fighters, they will be put into cauldrons, so that those who were formerly pestilent traders may be burnt and boiled through; for they traded to this end, that they might hand over to death those whom they had deceived. These are they of whom it is said: The sons of Eli, sons of pestilence, who sat in the chair of the pestilent. And when they have been boiled through and burnt, they will come out naked, having none of the things which they formerly presumed for themselves. And they will see their ignominy, and will be cast upon mount Remmam, which means loftiness, so that they may be crushed in their own pride. Some interpret Remmam as the vision of someone, that is, ὅρασίν τινὸς. For they were not able to see all things, but promised themselves the knowledge of some part, so that they are cast down in that which they believed they knew. According to the letter, we can understand that, when the days of captivity come upon the cows of Samaria, the enemies overcome them in battle and crush them with their arms, and drive them, overcome in the encounter, into fortified cities, which are compared to boiling pots; so that, as Jerusalem, holding its peoples shut in and besieged, is likened to a boiling pot full of flesh, so also the cities of Samaria are compared to boiling pots, which by famine and pestilence force the peoples shut in them to go out, and to go into captivity seeing one another, and to be transferred to Armon, the mountains of Armenia, which border on the Medes and the Persians.

And so the Lord swore by his holy one, whether by himself, or by the Son, or by the temple, or by everyone who is holy and is called the temple of God, that a day is to come not far off, nor after many ages, but already imminent: the day of captivity and distress, in which the cows are lifted up on poles, and their remnants in boiling pots, for which both in the Hebrew and in Aquila is written in cauldrons of little fish. For the poles too, which in Hebrew are called sannoth, Aquila interpreted shields, Symmachus and the LXX arms, Theodotion alone δόρατα; following him, we have interpreted poles or spears. This signifies that they are taken in battle, and carried and borne away by right of victory, while he nevertheless keeps the metaphor of the cows that he had begun, so that, as he had said that they were fat cows, he tells that their flesh is to be carried on poles or shields. And as a boiling cauldron wraps up small fish all together, so also the cows of Bashan are to be overwhelmed, without any order, by the miseries of captivity.

And what follows: And you shall go out through the openings, one against another, can be explained thus: The way of captivity lies open to you, and when your cauldrons have been burnt out, you shall go out one against another; according to the idiom of the Hebrews, who, for what we say mutually or in turn, say woman and woman, that is, one against another. And you shall be cast, he says, into the places of Armenia which are called Armona. Finally Symmachus interpreted: And you shall be cast into Armenia, for which the Seventy translated mount Remmam, Aquila mount Armona, Theodotion mount Mona, the Fifth edition the lofty mount.

Come to Bethel, and act impiously; to Gilgal, and multiply transgression; and bring your victims in the morning, your tithes on three days. And sacrifice praise from what is leavened, and call for voluntary offerings, and proclaim them. For so you have willed, sons of Israel, says the Lord God. Therefore I also have given you numbness of teeth in all your cities, and want of bread in all your places; and you have not returned to me, says the Lord. LXX: You entered into Bethel, and acted unjustly; in Gilgal you multiplied acting impiously, and you brought in your sacrifices in the morning, your tithes on the third day. And they read the law outside, and called upon confessions. Proclaim that the sons of Israel have loved these things, says the Lord God. And I will give you numbness of teeth in all your cities, and want of bread in all your places; and you have not returned to me, says the Lord. First let us lay the foundations of the history: O wretched Israel, captivity is already near you, already the Assyrian army is pressing upon you; do what you please, act impiously; commit fornication freely with idols, so that the more shameless you have been, the more just my sentence upon your torments may appear. Come, he says, into Bethel, in which you set up the golden calf, and act impiously against God. Come to Gilgal, the place of idolatry, of which I spoke through Hosea: All their wickedness is in Gilgal. And again in the same prophet: In vain were they sacrificing oxen in Gilgal. And when you have come to Gilgal: Multiply transgression. For whatever you do there is transgression against God, to whom you have preferred idols. And bring your victims in the morning, so that there may be no delay in crime. Your tithes on three days, or, as Symmachus translates, your tithes on the third day. The explanation of this passage seems to us to be this: in Leviticus it is commanded in the law that certain sacrifices are not to be kept over to the second day, and that others are not to remain to the third day, and that if they do remain they are unclean. The sense, therefore, is: Slaughter unclean victims every day, and offer defiled sacrifices, and sacrifice praise from what is leavened, which according to the precepts of Moses is not offered to God at all. For 'praise' Aquila translated εὐχαριστίαν, that is, thanksgiving, which in Hebrew is called thoda. And call, he says, for voluntary offerings, which the Hebrews call nadaboth, that is, spontaneous. A freewill sacrifice, moreover, belongs to rejoicing, and in Latin we can call it a banquet. And when you have done this, proclaim your impiety to all, so that you may be seen not only to have done it, but also to have taught others. These things I command, and I speak in the imperative mood, in order to satisfy your will, because so you have acted and so you have willed, sons of Israel, says the Lord God.

This we have said according to the Hebrew; let us pass on to the LXX translators, and discuss briefly what seems to us according to anagogy in each point; for the size of the books does not allow it, if we should wish to say both things in each edition. You entered into Bethel, that is, into the house of God, which is understood as the Church, and you acted impiously against the Lord, trampling on his precepts. And in Gilgal, which is interpreted revelation or wallowing-place, you multiplied impieties, claiming for yourselves the knowledge of the holy Scriptures, and while you are lifted up into pride, you have rolled down into the lowest depths of the mire. You also brought in your sacrifices in the morning, your tithes on the third day, transformed into an angel of light, and compressing the threefold understanding of the Scriptures — concerning which we have been commanded to write it threefold in our hearts — into the meaning of a single day. For we ought to understand holy Scripture first according to the letter, doing in ethics whatever is commanded; secondly according to allegory, that is, the spiritual understanding; thirdly according to the blessedness of things to come. But you, he says, despising the first and the second day, compose for yourselves certain spiritual fictions without a foundation, setting a roof on top of walls.

It is not enough to make a true solemnity of the heart. From this must follow good works. What value is there in partaking of his body and blood with our mouths if we oppose him with our wicked practices? And so Moses required that "unleavened bread with wild herbs" is to be eaten. One who eats bread without leaven does virtuous deeds without corrupting them with vainglory, and fulfills the precepts of mercy with no addition of sin, not perversely destroying what he properly accomplishes. In reproof of some who had mingled the leaven of sin with their good deeds, the Lord spoke by the voice of the prophet: "Come to Bethel and behave wickedly," and shortly after, "And make a sacrifice of praise of that which is unleavened." A person makes a sacrifice of praise of that which is unleavened when he makes ready a sacrifice for God of his misdeeds. Wild herbs are very bitter. The flesh of the lamb is to be eaten with wild herbs, so that when we receive our Redeemer's body we humble ourselves with weeping for our sins. Thus the bitterness of repentance purges our heart's stomach of all traces of a wicked life.

Nor are the heretics, of whom and to whom this is said, content with this limit of impiety, but they read the law of God outside, withdrawing from the Church, and tried to join confessions and testimonies to each of their dogmas, which they feigned with a perverse heart; or they sacrificed from what is leavened, concerning which it is said in the Gospel: Beware of the leaven, that is, the teaching of the Pharisees. And they did these things not by error, but by design; not by a chance will, but with the fullest affection for their forebears.

They had also mixed this leaven of sin into their good action, to whom the Lord spoke through the voice of the prophet in rebuke: "Come to Bethel and act impiously." And after a few words: "And sacrifice praise from what is leavened." For he offers praise from what is leavened who prepares a sacrifice to God from robbery.

Wherefore I too have given you numbness of teeth, as the LXX translated, whom we have followed in this place because of the simplicity of the word, or cleanness of teeth, as Aquila and Symmachus translated, so as to show by clean teeth the greatness of the famine. And I caused want of bread, not in one city, but in all your cities, nor in one place, but in all your places. And though I have done this, not punishing, but granting an occasion for repentance, not even so have you returned to me, says the Lord.

Hence the Lord threatens vengeance upon them: I will give, he says, you numbness of teeth, which in Greek is called γομφιασμός. For if anyone, according to Ezekiel, eats a sour grape, his teeth will be numbed; so that those who make ill use of the testimonies of the holy Scriptures, and eat them unripe and without their sweetness, lose the strength of their teeth, so that they cannot grind hard food and pass into the belly what would profit the whole body. This numbness of teeth and want of food I will give both in all your cities and in all your places, so that you may suffer a famine of the word of God, and of that bread which came down from heaven, and of which it is written in the psalms: Man ate the bread of angels. All of which I did, not out of cruelty and savagery, as the heretics slanderously claim, the ferocity of a stern judge, but that you might be converted to me, according to that which is written: In vain have I struck your sons; you have not received discipline.

I also withheld the rain from you, when there were still three months left until the harvest. And I rained upon one city, and upon another city I did not rain. One part was rained upon, and the part upon which I did not rain withered. And two and three cities came to one city to drink water, and they were not satisfied; and you did not return to me, says the Lord. LXX: And I held back the rain from you three months before the vintage; and I will rain upon one city, and upon one city I will not rain. One part will be watered, and the part upon which I shall not rain will dry up. And two and three cities will gather into one city to drink water, and they will not be satisfied; and you have not returned to me, says the Lord. Not only did I give numbness of teeth in all your cities, and want of bread in all your places, but I withheld the rain from you when there were still three months left until the harvest, the rain which is called the latter rain and is most necessary of all to the thirsty fields and ploughlands of Palestine, so that, when the grass was swelling toward the harvest and the wheat was bringing forth its ear, it withered from excessive drought. He means the spring season at the end of the month of April, from which three months remain until the wheat harvest: May, June, July. For 'harvest' the LXX, after their manner, translated 'vintage'; and if we accept this, it is altogether unusual and impossible throughout all the regions of the East. For we have never seen rains at the end of the month of June, or in the month of July, in these provinces, and above all in Judea. Indeed, in the books of Kings, rains were stirred up at Samuel's prayer in the days of summer and harvest as a great sign and portent. And it would have been superfluous now to threaten a drought in the month of July, in which he had never given rains. He withheld the rain, moreover, so that they should endure not only want of bread, but also the burning of thirst and a scarcity of drink. For in these places in which we now live, apart from small springs, all the waters are those of cisterns, and if the divine wrath holds back the rain, the danger of thirst is greater than that of famine, which Scripture records also happened in the days of the prophet Elijah for three years and six months. And lest they should perhaps think that this had befallen cities and peoples by the law of nature, and the course of the stars, and the changes of the seasons, he says that he rains upon one city and its fields, and holds back the rain from another, so that two and three cities go to another city, and yet are not satisfied with draughts of water. And though he has done these things, not as punishment, but as medicine, he rebukes those who persist in crime: and not even so did you return to me, says the Lord. The Lord also withholds, or holds back, the spiritual rains from the heretics, and all the dew of divine wisdom, and commands his clouds not to rain rain upon them three months before the harvest, or the vintage, so that they cannot attain to the fruit of the mystery of the Trinity. And just as this sun, which we see, completes its yearly course, until it returns to its former goal, in twelve months, each of which rolls on for thirty days; and the moon, which in Hebrew is called iare, in Greek μήνη, has in both languages given its name to the months from its own name, and is lit by the rays of the sun on the side on which it is near to it, receiving more or less light according to the variation of the times; so too the Church, adorned with the splendour of the true sun, fills up the number of the twelve apostles. Hence also the tribes in Israel are called twelve, and as a testimony of eternal memory twelve stones are taken from the bed of the Jordan, to be set up in the place of the second circumcision. The Lord, then, rains upon one city, the Church of the true confession, and upon another he does not rain, the one which is in the conventicles of the heretics. And while the one receives an everlasting rain, the other is dried up by a continual drought, so that those who thirst, compelled by want, may come to the city of the Lord, from which goes forth a most abundant fountain that waters the torrent of thorns. This is the fountain which says through Jeremiah: They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and have dug for themselves broken cisterns, which cannot hold waters. This fountain, proceeding from one fountain, runs down in a threefold union; and for these fountains of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit the psalmist sighs after the manner of a thirsting stag, saying: As the stag longs for the fountains of waters, so my soul longs for you, O God. And when two and three cities have gone to the one city in which the waters of hope, faith and charity abound, they will not be satisfied, because they have come to seek the divine grace not by will, but by necessity.

If we cannot gather spiritual fruits through our own labor, it is just that we dispense with holy zeal and most fervent charity those which have been collected by others. Since the Lord threatens that, because of the sins of the people, "I will cause it to rain upon one city and cause it not to rain upon another city," we ought to strive with great care that we may not be that city upon which the rain of the Word of God either does not come at all or, at least, only late and rarely. Without any doubt, if the dew or rain of the Word of God is provided too late, the fruits of souls will be the same as earthly fruits which do not receive rain.

I struck you with scorching wind and with mildew. The multitude of your gardens and of your vineyards, your olive groves and your fig groves, the caterpillar devoured, and you did not return to me, says the Lord. LXX: I struck you with burning heat and with mildew. You multiplied your gardens, your vineyards, and your figs, and your olive groves the caterpillar devoured, and not even so were you converted to me, says the Lord. Not only did I do the former things in order to correct you, but whatever was left over from the drought I struck with scorching wind and with mildew. For 'scorching wind' Aquila and Symmachus and Theodotion translated ἀνεμοφθορίαν; the Seventy πύρωσιν, which we can call burning. 'Mildew', moreover, all of them likewise translated ἴκτερον, except Theodotion, who alone translated ὠχρίασιν, which signifies pallor. And when, in defiance of the wrath of the Lord, they multiplied gardens and vineyards and fig groves and olive groves, the caterpillar consumed everything, of which more is said in Joel. And not even through blows and the weight of evils were they willing to come to the Lord. By this saying let the heretics be confounded, who interpret as cruelty the discipline and, so to speak, the medicine of the Creator. The Lord, moreover, strikes the heretics spiritually with that burning of which Paul the Apostle speaks: It is better, he says, to marry than to burn. And the prince of the apostles: Beloved, do not be as strangers in the burning which has come upon you for a trial. And with mildew, which, when the bile is spread abroad, changes the redness of the blood into pallor and allows nothing in the body to be sound, so much so that even the sweetest honey seems bitter. And those who once heard in the Church: Taste and see that the Lord is sweet, and themselves said: How sweet are your words to my throat, above honey to my mouth. Let them be called παραπικραίνοντες (embitterers), and let their waters and rains not drip sweetness, nor be from the land of promise, which we read is flowing with milk and honey, but let them be called mara, that is, bitterness. These have multiplied gardens for themselves, into which Naboth was willing to die rather than have his vineyard changed. He who, after all, is weak, let him eat herbs. And because the heretics, always swelling with pride and falling into the judgment of the devil, promise great things to themselves, and feign images of good things, in order to mix poisons with honey, they also boast that they have vineyards and olive groves and fig groves; but their vine is the vine of Sodom; their olive groves are not of good olives, but of wild olives, which the Apostle commands to be grafted onto the roots of good olives. Their fig groves too are such as to fill a basket with the worst figs, which Jeremiah testifies cannot be eaten for their bitterness. When the Lord comes to these, he curses them with an everlasting drought, so that they may never bear fruit, lest by the greenness of their leaves they deceive those who pass by. And so that we may understand that the gardens and vineyards and olive groves and fig groves of the heretics are to be taken in the bad sense, he added 'your' to each word, to show that they belong not to God, but to the heretics: Your gardens, your vineyards, your olive groves and your fig groves, all of which the caterpillar has laid waste, the last of all punishments; for it does not fly away like the locust, and, running here and there, leave things half-eaten, but stays on the crops that are to perish, and with slow movement and sluggish bites consumes everything. And though they suffered these things, not even so were they willing to return to the Lord.

I sent death upon you in the way of Egypt, I struck your young men with the sword, even to the captivity of your horses. And I made the stench of your camps rise into your nostrils, and you did not return to me, says the Lord. LXX: I sent forth death upon you in the way of Egypt, and I killed your young men with the sword, together with the captivity of your horses. And I brought out your camps in fire in my wrath, and not even so did you return to me, says the Lord. Israel is instructed by every kind of scourge and torment; hence also, at the time when they were asking help from the Egyptians, death is sent upon them, and their young men are struck with the sword, and the horses which they had multiplied for themselves against the precept of God a savage captivity shuts in, so that the stench of the camps and the foulness of a dying army fill the nostrils of the living. And though he did these things too, in order to rebuke the offenders and amend the erring, not even so did they return to him, says the Lord. He sends death in the way of Egypt not only at that time, but daily, so that whoever has trodden the Egyptian path may, as he dies, hear the Apostle teaching: For in that I died, I died to sin; but in that I live, I live to God. And in another place: If we have died with Christ, we shall also live together with him. And again: I always carry about the mortification of Jesus in my body. And once more: But I live, now not I, but Christ lives in me. By this death the Lord wishes to give us life, so that, dying to sin, we may live to God. And we die to sin when we mortify our members which are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, wantonness, idolatry and the rest. We read in Isaiah, at least according to the Seventy translators — otherwise the Hebrew has it differently —: I sent death upon Jacob, and it came upon Israel. Jacob is the name of the body being born; Israel, a name of blessing.
