For because he wrestled all night and conquered in the struggle, and at the rising of the morning star could say with the Apostle: The night is far spent, the day has drawn near, for this reason he received the name Israel, of one seeing God. Death, therefore, is first sent upon Jacob, so that we may mortify our members which are upon the earth, and through the mortification of the bodily members may come to the death of Israel, so that all the incitements of the passions in us may die. God strikes whatever is strong in evil and is lifted up in a perverse youth, lest it reach old age, and he hands the horses over to captivity, lest they slip down the precipices of hell; and he makes the stench of their camps rise into their nostrils, so that they may recognize their sins and perceive that they stink, and say with David: My scars have putrefied and are corrupted because of my folly. And though he did these things with the desire of one who heals, not even so did they return to him, says the Lord.

See how God, through His love of goodness, seeks repentance; and by means of the plan He pursues of threatening silently, shows His own love for man. "I will avert," He says, "My face from them, and show what shall happen to them." For where the face of the Lord looks, there is peace and rejoicing; but where it is averted, there is the introduction of evil.

Whence also, that there might be no doubt but that it was He who was the guest of Abraham on the destruction of the people of Sodom, it is declared: "Then the Lord rained upon Sodom and upon Gomorrha fire and brimstone from the Lord out of heaven." For thus also said the prophet in the person of God: "I have overthrown you, as the Lord overturned Sodom and Gomorrha." Therefore the Lord overturned Sodom, that is, God overturned Sodom; but in the overturning of Sodom, the Lord rained fire from the Lord. And this Lord was the God seen by Abraham; and this God was the guest of Abraham, certainly seen because He was also touched. But although the Father, being invisible, was assuredly not at that time seen, He who was accustomed to be touched and seen was seen and received to hospitality. But this the Son of God, "The Lord rained from the Lord upon Sodom and Gomorrha brimstone and fire." And this is the Word of God. And the Word of God was made flesh, and dwelt among us; and this is Christ. It was not the Father, then, who was a guest with Abraham, but Christ. Nor was it the Father who was seen then, but the Son; and Christ was seen. Rightly, therefore, Christ is both Lord and God, who was not otherwise seen by Abraham, except that as God the Word He was begotten of God the Father before Abraham himself.

[Passage quoted, Amos iv. ii.]

AND here the Lord Himself says that some God has caused the destruction of Sodom, since He Himself must plainly be a different Being from the One of Whom He speaks. Therefore two Lords stands out in the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah, when the Lord rained the fire of the Lord on them. You also, he says, will suffer a destruction such as Sodom underwent for its unnatural wickedness, and even so did not turn to Me. Scripture generally regards the future as past, so that we must understand the past to be meant in spite of the tense. The future "I will overthrow" must be understood for the past "I overthrew," and "ye will not turn," for "ye did turn."

This is levelled at the Jewish race, and only received its fulfilment in their case, after their plot against our Saviour, Their ancient holy place, at any rate, and their Temple are to this day as much destroyed as Sodom. Yet though they have suffered in accordance with the prediction, they have not hitherto turned to Christ, on Whose account they have suffered so much. And so the prophecy before us is justly inspired to say: "And neither so have ye returned to me, saith the Lord."
The Proof of the Gospel, Book 5, Chapter 23

I overthrew you as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, and you became like a brand snatched from the burning, and you did not return to me, says the Lord. LXX: I overthrew you as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, and you became like a brand plucked out of the fire, and not even so were you converted to me, says the Lord. It is the last remedy, both for the ten tribes and for the heretics and for all sinners, that, after he has sent death in the way of Egypt, and struck their young men with the sword, and consumed their horses, and made the stench of their camps rise into their nostrils, and still they have not returned to him, he should overthrow them as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah; and that, when they have been overthrown because of the likeness of their crimes to those of Sodom and Gomorrah, and the divine fire has burned up the worst buildings in them, they themselves should be delivered like a brand snatched from the burning. And just as Lot, when Sodom perished, was saved, losing his substance and a part of his body, which we understand to be his wife, so these, all losing the riches of Sodom, may escape naked, according to what we read in the Apostle: If anyone's work which he has built upon it remains, he will receive a reward; but if anyone's work is burned, he will suffer loss, yet he himself will be saved, but only as through fire. He, then, who is saved through fire is snatched like a brand from the burning. And to men of this kind, whom the Savior addressed in the Gospel, rebuking them: If you were sons of Abraham, you would do the works of Abraham, John the Baptist says: Brood of vipers, who showed you to flee from the wrath to come? Bear, therefore, fruit worthy of repentance, and do not presume to say within yourselves, We have Abraham as our father. For I say to you that God is able from these stones to raise up sons to Abraham? Therefore both Israel and all the heretics, because they had the works of Sodom and Gomorrah, are overthrown like Sodom and Gomorrah, so that they may be delivered like a brand snatched from the burning. And this is what we read in the prophet: Sodom shall be restored to its former state, so that he who by his own vice is among the Sodomites may, after the works of Sodom have burned up in him, be restored to his former state.

There are also other sorts of vengeance, with which some who have overpassed the bounds of wickedness are smitten in this life, as we read that Dathan and Abiram or Korah were punished, or above all, those of whom the Apostle speaks: "Wherefore God gave them up to vile passions and a reprobate mind:" and this must be counted worse than all other punishments. For of these the Psalmist says: "They are not in the labours of men; neither shall they be scourged like other men." For theyare not worthy of being healed by the visitation of the Lord which gives life, and by plagues in this world, as "in despair they have given themselves over to lasciviousness, unto the working of all error unto uncleanness," and as by hardening their hearts, and by growing accustomed and used to sin they have got beyond cleansing in this brief life and punishment in the present world: men, who are thus reproved by the holy word of the prophet: "I destroyed some of you, as God destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah, and you were as a firebrand plucked out of the burning: yet you returned not to Me, saith the Lord," and Jeremiah: "I have killed and destroyed thy people, and yet they are not returned from their ways."

In this he was probably suggesting to us the eventual sacking that happened in the time of Jeremiah by the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, who took the whole of Judea, set fire even to Jerusalem itself and its neighboring cities and towns, pulled down the divine Temple, took captive the survivors from the fighting, and as a glorious conqueror went back home with the captives, who finally returned to Judea at the completion of the period of 70 years.

Therefore I will do these things to you, Israel; but after I have done these things to you, prepare to meet your God, Israel; for behold, he who forms the mountains, and creates the wind, and announces to man his speech, who makes the morning mist, and treads upon the heights of the earth, the Lord God of hosts is his name. LXX: Therefore thus will I do to you, Israel; nevertheless, because I will do thus to you, prepare to call upon your God, Israel. For behold, he who establishes the thunder, and creates the spirit, and announces to men his Christ, making the morning and the mist, and ascending upon the heights of the earth, the Lord God Almighty is his name. Where we translated 'after', in the Hebrew is written eceb, and Aquila translated ὕστερον, that is, afterwards, and Theodotion 'at the last', and the Seventy 'nevertheless'; in the Hebrew it can be read thus: Therefore I will do these things to you, Israel, afterwards, that is, a long time after, and in the last ages, so that the verse begins again from another beginning: And since I am about to do this to you, prepare to meet your God, Israel. And again, in the place where the Seventy translated: Prepare to call upon your God, and we, following Theodotion, have put: Prepare to meet your God, Symmachus and the Fifth edition translated: Prepare to oppose your God, which in Hebrew is said hechin lacerath Eloiah. For 'mountains' also, which in Hebrew are called arim, the Seventy alone rendered βροντήν, that is, thunder. And why they said 'spirit' and we 'wind', which in Hebrew is called rua, the reason is plain: because by this word both wind and spirit are named. And as for what follows: Announcing to man his speech, while all translate it as we have rendered it, the Seventy alone translated: Announcing to men his Christ, deceived by the likeness and ambiguity of the word. For if we read 'his Christ', which in Hebrew is said Messio, it is written with these letters, mem, sin, iod, heth, and uau, which is what the LXX supposed. But if it is as in the Hebrew, according to Aquila τήν ὁμιλίαν αὐτοῦ, according to Symmachus τὸ φώνημα αὐτοῦ, according to Theodotion τὸν λόγον αὐτοῦ, according to the Fifth edition τήν ἀδολεσχίαν αὐτοῦ, all of which they translate as meaning that it is 'his speech', it will be written with these letters, mem, he, which is read ma, that is, 'that' or 'what'. Then sin, iod, heth, which we read sia, that is, speech. And the O, which is written with the single letter uau, signifies αὐτοῦ, that is, 'his'; and all mixed together it is read masio, having, compared with the word above, one letter more, he, the second letter. We have spoken of the variety of interpretation, which will be tiresome to the careless and welcome to the studious; now let us pass on to the sense of what is written.

I gave numbness to your teeth, and you did not return to me, says the Lord. I withheld the rain from you, and I rained upon one city, and upon another I did not rain, and two and three cities came to one to drink water, and they were not satisfied, and not even so did you return to me, says the Lord. I struck you with scorching wind, and with mildew your gardens and vineyards and olive groves and fig groves, and you did not return to me, says the Lord. I sent death upon you in the way of Egypt, and I struck your young men with the sword, and I made the stench of your camps rise into your nostrils, and you did not return to me, says the Lord. I overthrew you as the Lord overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, and you became as a brand snatched from the burning, and you did not return to me, says the Lord. Therefore I will do these things to you, O Israel, so that you who have despised what is past may at least be corrected by what I am about to bring upon you. And when he has said, I will do these things to you, he is silent about what he is going to do, so that while Israel hangs uncertain over each kind of punishment — which are the more terrible for this reason, that men suspect them all —, he may repent, lest God bring on what he threatens. But after I have done to you what I solemnly declare I will do, prepare to call upon the Lord your God. Everyone, after all, who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved. Or: prepare to meet your God, so that you may receive with all eagerness the Lord who comes to you.

But if we read according to Symmachus and Aquila: These things I will do to you, Israel, afterwards, and when I have done these things to you, prepare to oppose your God Israel, it is to be understood thus: In order to correct you I did the things which the preceding discourse describes; and because you were unwilling to return to me, I will do to you the things that are contained in my secret counsel. You killed the servants whom I had sent to you; last of all I will send my Son; but you, according to your custom, by which you have always resisted the will of God, prepare yourself to contradict and oppose your God, according to that which is written: Behold, this one is set for the fall and for the rising again of many, and for a sign which shall be contradicted. And he says this not to command what Israel ought to do, but to foretell what he will do of his own accord, as if rebuking and reproving him, so that, corrected, he may at least not do what has been foretold.

Since initial measures did not suffice, He proceeded to an overthrow similar to the Sodomites; this was the kind of thing, as he said, that was inflicted on them by divine wrath. Therefore prepare to call upon your God, O Israel: Since he did not benefit from being chastised, let him prepare himself for an encounter with God, accepting repentance and adopting a lifestyle calculated to appease Him.

And thus even the good movement of the free-will, whereby anyone is prepared for receiving the gift of grace is an act of the free-will moved by God. And thus man is said to prepare himself, according to Proverbs 16:1: "It is the part of man to prepare the soul"; yet it is principally from God, Who moves the free-will. Hence it is said that man's will is prepared by God, and that man's steps are guided by God.

[Passage quoted, Amos. iv. 12—v. 2.]

God now proclaiming the Christ by name the seventh time is said to "strengthen the thunder" and "to create the wind," the proclamation of the Gospel being called thunder from its being heard by all men, and similarly the spirit that Christ breathed on His apostles is meant; and also the Saviour's sojourn among men has clearly fulfilled the prophecy in which God is said to make "morning" and "mist" together, morning for those that receive salvation, but for the Jews that disbelieve in Him the contrary. On whom also Scripture foretells an extreme curse, adding a lamentation for the Jewish race, which actually overtook them immediately after their impiety against our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ. For of a truth from that day to this the House of Israel has fallen, and the vision once shewn by God and the rejection have been brought to pass, concerning the falling of their house in Jerusalem, and against their whole state, that it should not be possible for any one to lift them up, who will never more be lifted up. "There is," he says, "therefore no one to lift her up." For since they did not accept the Christ of God when He came, perforce He left them and turned to all the Gentiles, telling the cause of his turning, when He said with tears, as if almost apologizing:

"Jerusalem, Jerusalem, which killeth the prophets, and stonest them which are sent unto her, how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a bird gathereth her nestlings under her wings, and ye would not: behold, your house is left unto you desolate."
The Proof of the Gospel, Book 4, Chapter 16

It is the custom of Scripture to call firmament all that is strong and unyielding. It even uses the word to denote the condensation of the air: He, it says, who strengthens the thunder. Scripture means by the strengthening of the thunder, the strength and resistance of the wind, which, enclosed in the hollows of the clouds, produces the noise of thunder when it breaks through with violence.
The Hexaemeron, Homily 3: On the Firmament

When Christ came, the people of the old covenant denied him, but the devils confessed him. His forefather David was not ignorant of him when he said, "I will place a lamp for my anointed." Some have interpreted "lamp" as the splendor of prophecy; others have understood by the lamp the flesh he assumed of the Virgin, according to the words of the apostle: "But we carry this treasure in vessels of clay." The prophet was not ignorant of him when he said, "And declaring his Christ to men." Moses also knew him, and Isaiah and Jeremiah as well. None of the prophets was ignorant of him. Even the devils acknowledged him, for he rebuked them, and Scripture adds, "Because they knew that he was the Christ."

Nor does it escape my notice that heretics have been prone to object that the Holy Spirit appears to be a creature, because many of them use as an argument for establishing their impiety that passage of Amos, where he spoke of the blowing of the wind, as the words of the prophet made clear. For you read thus: "Behold, I am he that establishes the thunder and creates the wind and declare unto man his Christ, that make light and mist, and ascend upon high places, the Lord God Almighty is his name."

But if any one thinks that the word of the prophet is to be explained with reference to the Holy Spirit, because it is said, "declaring unto men his Christ," he will explain it more easily of the Lord's Sun of justice. For if it troubles you that he said Spirit, and therefore you think that this cannot well be explained of the mystery of the taking of human nature, read on in the Scriptures, and you will find that all agrees most excellently with Christ. Of [Christ] it is thoroughly fitting to think that he established the thunders by his coming, that is, the force and sound of the heavenly Scriptures, by the thunder, as it were, of which our minds are struck with astonishment, so that we learn to be afraid and pay respect to the heavenly oracles.

He it is who establishes the thunder, or makes firm the mountains, at whose voice the hinges of the heavens and the foundations of the earth are shaken. He it is who creates the spirit, which in this place we understand not as the Holy Spirit, as the heretics suppose, but as the wind, or the spirit of man, because no one knows what is in a man except the spirit which is in him; and the Spirit himself intercedes for us with unspeakable groanings. Or certainly by 'spirit' we ought to understand the soul, according to that which is written: You will take away their spirit, and they will fail, and they will return to their dust. And: Father, into your hands I commend my spirit, and saying this he breathed his last. And when he has created the spirit, he announces to men his own speech, or announces to man that man's speech, he who knows the secrets of the thoughts, and understands what the hidden mind ponders in silent thought, according to what we read in Jeremiah according to the Hebrew: The heart of all is perverse and unsearchable; who shall know it? I the Lord search the heart and test the reins. Which Scripture also attests in the hundred and thirty-eighth (139th) psalm: Your eyes saw my imperfect being. And the sense is: Before I was made, before I was shaped into limbs, while I was still contained in the seed, your eyes saw me. And Jeremiah hears from the Lord: Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you; and before you came forth from the womb, I sanctified you, and I set you as a prophet among the nations. And the evangelist: But Jesus, seeing their thoughts. But if we read: Announcing to man his speech, it is to be taken according to what was said above, where he says: The Lord God will not do a thing unless he has revealed his secret to his servants the prophets. And he who announces the thoughts of man and his speech, or his own, is the one who makes the dawn and the daybreak, and fills all things with clouds, and treads upon the heights of the lands, whose name is the Lord God Almighty. In place of this one reads in the Seventy: And announcing to men his Christ; on this pretext the heretics want the Holy Spirit to be created, from the order that follows: Creating the spirit, and announcing to men his Christ, so that the one is created and the other is announced among the peoples. To them we shall reply according to their own sense and the common edition: He who is the creator of all things, and establishes the thunder, or fashions the mountains, consequently brings the winds out of his treasuries, and, as the founder of the universe, promises his Son Christ to men. But after Christ has been announced, then the light of truth is opened to us, not to perfection, because now we see in part and know in part, and contemplate the things that are to come through a mirror and an image. Hence there follows: Making the morning and the mist, and ascending upon the heights of the earth. For the Lord is high in the high places, and he who is high does not dwell in low things; but the creator of the mountains ascends upon the mountains, in those who have their citizenship in the heavens, and, walking in the flesh, do not live according to the flesh but according to the spirit.

This is Amos the third in order, who also was privileged to tell of the coming of the Lord Christ and in these words: Lo! I am he that confirms the thunder and that creates the wind and that announces to men his Anointed.
5: Hear this word, which I raise over you as a lament. The house of Israel has fallen; it will not again rise. The virgin Israel is cast down into her land; there is no one to raise her up. LXX: Hear this word, which I will take up over you as a lament. The house of Israel has fallen; it will not any more rise again. The virgin Israel is cast down upon her land; there is no one to raise her up. As far as concerns the order of the letter and the truth of the history begun, the ten tribes, which are called Israel, once led into captivity, by no means returned afterwards to their own land. And the people of Israel is called a virgin, not because it remained in the purity of virginity, but because it was once joined to the Lord like a virgin. Hence the prophet is also commanded to take up a lament over it, because it will by no means be restored to its former rank. But as far as concerns the spiritual understanding, the prophet takes up a lament over every Israel which used to discern God with the mind and afterwards ceased to serve him, according to that which is commanded to Ezekiel, that he should devour the book in which there was written, both within and without, lamentation, and song, and woe. Understand by within the Song of Solomon that follows, who says: The king has brought me into his chamber. And the forty-fourth (45th) psalm, in which it is written: All the glory of the king's daughter is within. But without is whatever is read in the letter, and is seen in the bark, and is not held in the marrow of the spirit. And so, both according to the letter and according to tropology, in all the books of the prophets a lament is written over those who repent after sins; a song over those who, stained by no filth of sins, are worthy of canticle and praise; woe over those who do not repent, but according to the hardness of their heart treasure up for themselves wrath in the day of wrath.

Consider and observe, my hearer, that if God had given a hope to Sodom and to her fellows, He would not have overthrown them with fire and brimstone, the sign of the last day of the world, but would have delivered them over to one of the kingdoms to be chastised. As it is written that when Jeremiah caused the nations and kingdoms to drink the cup of wrath, he said concerning each one of the cities, that after they shall drink the cup, I will turn back the captivity of Elam, of Tyre, of Zidon, of the children of Ammon, and of Moab, and of Edom. Concerning each one of these kingdoms he said:—In the last days I well turn back her captivity. Now we see that Tyre was inhabited, and was opulent after she had wandered seventy years, and after she had received the reward of her harlotries and after she had committed fornication with all kingdoms. And she took the harp, and played it sweetly, and multiplied her music. And also the region of Elam is inhabited and opulent. And with regard to Babylon Jeremiah said:—Babylon shall fall, and shall not rise. And lo! unto this day does it continue in desolation, and will do so for ever. And also about Jerusalem he said:—The virgin of Israel shall fall, and shall not rise again. She is forsaken upon the ground and there is none to raise her up. For if the prophecy is true which Jeremiah spoke about Babylon, also that about Jerusalem is true and worthy of faith. And Isaiah said unto Jerusalem:—I will not again be wroth with thee, nor will I reprove thee. Of a truth He will not again be wroth with her, nor will He reprove her for ever; for that which is in desolation He will not reprove, nor will she provoke him to wrath.

If, then, the apostle, who was a chosen vessel separated unto the gospel of Christ, by reason of the pricks of the flesh and the allurements of vice keeps his body and brings it into subjection, lest when he has preached to others he may himself be a cast away; and yet, for all that, sees another law in his members warring against the law of his mind, and bringing him into captivity to the law of sin; if after nakedness, fasting, hunger, imprisonment, scourging and other torments, he turns back to himself and cries, "Oh, wretched man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death?" do you fancy that you ought to lay aside apprehension? See to it that God say not some day of you, "The virgin of Israel is fallen, and there is none to raise her up." I will say it boldly: God can do all things, but the virgin who has fallen will not be raised up. He may indeed relieve one who is defiled from the penalty of her sin, but he will not give her a crown. Let us fear lest in us also prophecy be fulfilled, "Good virgins shall faint." Notice that it is good virgins who are spoken of, for there are bad ones as well. "Whoever looks on a woman," the Lord says, "to lust after her has committed adultery with her already in his heart." So that virginity may be lost even by a thought. Such are evil virgins in the flesh, not in the spirit; foolish virgins, who, having no oil, are shut out by the bridegroom.

But if, as we have said, the lament is over those who repent, and repentance restores health to the wound, how is it said according to the Seventy: The house of Israel has fallen, it will rise no more. The virgin Israel has strayed in her land, there is no one to raise her up? This can be resolved thus: after the house of Israel has collapsed by its own will, it will by no means recover its former dignity; after the virgin Israel has strayed in her land, she will no longer be able to find one to raise her up. And consider the proper meanings of the words. He who is a house, and is counted in the crowd, is said to fall. But he who is of the number of the virgins, if he strays, even for a light sin, will not be able to be raised up; not that he is not raised up, but the virgin Israel is by no means raised up, and the Lord of Israel will by no means rise again. For the glory is not the same of him who has always followed the Lord and of him who has wandered from the flock and afterwards been carried back on the shoulders of the good shepherd. Hence the Lord also says through another prophet: I prefer the repentance of a sinner rather than his death. Repentance becomes better not when compared with the purest holiness and the Church of Christ — which has no wrinkle nor spot —, but when compared with death and the underworld. We say these things, not in order to take away, with Novatus, the hope of repentance, but in order to make more fearful, and therefore anxious, those who, with the door of repentance open, while they hope for the future, lose the present, and who, though they could have remained without a wound, carelessly receive a wound, so as afterwards to be tormented by pain. There are many mansions with my Father, and star differs from star in brightness; so also is the resurrection of the dead, the saints shining like the sun and the moon, the evening star and the morning star. But those who have repented after sin will be made equal to other stars, according to the diversity of their merits.

For thus says the Lord God: The city from which a thousand went out, there shall be left in it a hundred; and from which a hundred went out, there shall be left in it ten, in the house of Israel. LXX: likewise. The divine word gives the reasons why the house of Israel, falling, does not rise again, and the virgin Israel, straying, or cast down upon the land, has no one to raise her up. The city, he says, from which a thousand went out, there shall be left in it a hundred; and from which a hundred went out, there shall be left in it ten, in the house of Israel; so that where once there had been a multitude, because of the excessive devastation scarcely a tenth part remains. And lest, clinging wholly to the letter, we leave the mysteries of numbers untouched: that the number seven is holy the sabbath also proves, on which God rested from all his works. And he commands that no servile work be done on it, except only those things which pertain to the soul, and that we should not carry burdens on it. Hence also in the wilderness the man who had gathered wood on the sabbath day, things that are to burn, is condemned by the sentence of the Lord. And seven weeks complete the number of holy Pentecost, and the jubilee year of remission and of the sounding trumpets is woven from this number. In the seventh month also tabernacles are pitched, and the Hebrew, when he has served six years, is set free in the seventh year. Secular philosophy also knows this, and the books of the physicians, of whom Galen, most eloquent and most learned, wrote three books, κρίσεων καὶ τῶν κριτικῶν ἡμερῶν (On Crises and Critical Days), in which, showing the power of the number seven, he says that the most burning fevers are broken on the seventh day; or, if the quantity of noxious humour and phlegm has been so great that it has by no means been consumed by the heat of the first week, the last day of the second week is awaited, that is, the fourteenth. But if, to speak with Hippocrates, the νόσος (the disease) has overcome this one, they pass on to the twenty-first day, that is, to the end of the third week; the days having been so established from the beginning of the world that all labours and troubles come to rest at the seventh number. Finally, the captivity of the people of Israel and the overthrow of the temple were also completed in the seventieth year of desolation, and seven stars are said to be wandering, according to the number of the days. Of the mysteries of this number Cicero tells more fully in the Dream of Scipio; and the Timaeus of Plato is a most obscure book, which is not made plainer even by the golden mouth of Cicero. Just as, therefore, the number seven has its own mystery, so the number that is held in unity, and is enclosed by the majesty of the one God, is sanctified and perfect and, so to speak, the true number. Hence the Son says: I am in the Father, and the Father in me, and, wishing all to be one with the Father, he speaks to him: Father, grant that, as I and you are one, so these also may be one in us. The first blessedness, therefore, is to be in the first number, which is one and true; the second in the second, that is, in the decad; the third in the third, that is, in the hecatontad. For as the decad is completed by the tenth unit, so the hecatontad is built from ten decads. The fourth number, which is contained in the thousand, consists of ten hecatontads. When, therefore, someone has repented, from the thousand and the fourth number he scarcely returns to the hundred and the third number. Again, he who is in the hundred scarcely returns to the second number, that of the first decad; and so it comes about that the house of Israel which had fallen cannot rise again, and the virgin Israel which had strayed has no one in the land to raise her up, because he who has once departed from unity, and has lost that glory of the purest virginity — of which the Apostle says: For I am jealous for you with the jealousy of God, and I have resolved to present you as a chaste virgin to one husband, to Christ, in which there is no spot nor wrinkle —, will not be able to recover his former state and the blessedness of unity, and it will scarcely be granted him to return from a thousand to a hundred, and to go back from a hundred to ten. I have said these things briefly, lest I should seem in this section to have fled tropology altogether because of the difficulty of the numbers.

For thus says the Lord to the house of Israel: Seek me, and you shall live; and do not seek Bethel, and do not enter into Gilgal, and do not pass over to Beersheba; for Gilgal shall be led captive, and Bethel shall be useless. LXX: For thus says the Lord to the house of Israel: Seek me, and you shall live; and do not seek Bethel, and do not go into Gilgal, and do not pass over upon the well of the oath; for Gilgal shall be led captive, and Bethel shall be as though it were not. It is the custom of the Scriptures always to join glad things to adverse ones, and after God has threatened sad things, he calls to repentance those whom he has frightened, according to that which we read in Isaiah: Woe, sinful nation, a people full of offences, a most wicked seed, unjust sons. And when he had said: Your land is deserted, your cities consumed with fire, strangers will devour your regions before you, he speaks to them, promising better things: Wash yourselves, be clean; take away your wickednesses from your souls, learn to do good, seek judgment, judge for the orphan, justify the widow; and come, let us dispute, says the Lord. Just as, therefore, in Isaiah he supports with gentle speech those whom he had frightened with a severe voice, so also in this prophet, to those to whom he had said: The house of Israel has fallen, it will not again rise; the virgin Israel has strayed in the land, there is no one to raise her up. Now he speaks to them and says: To the house of Israel, that is, to the ten tribes, Seek me and you shall live, since in that you do not seek me, you are dead. And when you have sought, you will find; and when you have found, you will live.

And do not seek Bethel, in which was the golden calf, and Gilgal, the place of idolatry, of which I have also said above: All their wickedness is in Gilgal. And you shall not pass over to Beersheba. Beautifully he says: you shall not pass over to Beersheba, that is, to the well of the oath, where the tribe of Judah, whenever it went astray, had been accustomed to worship idols. But Israel raged in the worship of images to such a degree that, by no means content with its own idols, it passed over to those of others. Finally, Gilgal, he says, shall be led captive, and Bethel shall be useless, or not subsisting at all, when the idols in it have been overthrown. But of Beersheba he was altogether silent, because when the ten tribes were conquered, the city by the name of Beersheba, which was in the tribe of Judah at that time, was neither taken nor destroyed. And at the same time it must be noticed that the LXX translators in the present place translated the name Beersheba, saying: The well of the oath, and in later passages they set down the name itself: Your God lives, O Dan, and the way of Beersheba lives. And they set down the way of Beersheba because from Israel they went by a long journey to the farthest borders of Judah, which were in Gerar and adjoined the Egyptian wilderness, in order to worship idols. It is, moreover, the place in which Abraham dwelt; and from the fact that he and Abimelech, after seven sheep had been given, swore to a mutual covenant, it was called the well of the oath, or the well of the seventh, because of the number of the seven sheep. For Sabe signifies both. And according to the laws of allegory he commands the house of Israel, that is, those who promise themselves the knowledge of God, not to seek Bethel, and not to enter into Gilgal, and not to pass over, or go up, to the well of the oath, but rather to seek God and live in him. And they seek Bethel, which is interpreted house of God, who say: The temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord; and they trust in buildings, of which the Lord spoke to the disciples: Days will come in which there will not be left a stone upon a stone that will not be destroyed. And they enter into Gilgal who after the coming of Christ desire to be circumcised again. For in Gilgal the people was circumcised a second time. Hence the place itself also received its name, because the Lord took away from them the reproach of Egypt. And you shall not pass over, he says, to Beersheba, or to the well of the oath, lest you think those to be the borders of Judea which Scripture once, according to the letter, had promised, from Dan to Beersheba. Nor should you say any longer with the prophet: God is known in Judea, his name is great in Israel, but you should hear with the apostles: Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world, because Gilgal also, that is, the circumcision of the flesh, will be led captive by the true circumcision of the heart. And Bethel, which you think the house of God, will not subsist, or, as I think better, returns useless, that is, auen, so that it is by no means called the house of God, but is called the useless house, or the house of the idol. Another interpretation: he seeks Bethel who follows only the letter that kills, and does not seek in the words the sense, which is God; and he enters into Gilgal who strives after greater revelations, promising himself the knowledge of things above; and he passes over, or goes up, to the well from which the Samaritan woman, desiring to draw waters that could not satisfy thirst, did not know him from whose belly proceed rivers of water springing up into eternal life.

Therefore, while there is time, look to the true and eternal salvation, and, since the end of the world is now at hand, out of fear of God turn your minds to God. Let not your powerless and vain dominion in the world over the just and the meek delight you. Remember that in the fields the tares and the darnel have dominion over the cultivated and fruitful corn, and you should not say that evils happen because your gods are not worshiped by us. But you should realize that this is God's anger, this is God's censure, so that he who is not recognized for his blessings may at least be recognized for his judgments. "Seek God, and your soul shall live." Acknowledge God even though it is late. For Christ advises and teaches this, saying, "Now this is everlasting life, that they may know you the only true God and him whom you have sent, Jesus Christ." Believe him who by no means deceives. Believe him who has foretold that all these things would come to pass. Believe him who will give the reward of eternal life to those who believe. Believe him who by the fires of Gehenna will inflict eternal punishments on the disbelieving.
Treatise V. An Address to Demetrianus 23

Seek the Lord and live, lest perhaps the house of Joseph be burned like fire; and it will devour, and there will be no one to quench Bethel. LXX: Seek the Lord and live, lest perhaps the house of Joseph be kindled like fire; and it devour it, and there be no one to quench the house of Israel. Just as it is said in the person of God: Seek me, and you shall live, so the prophet speaks about the Lord, that they should seek him and live. For in seeking the Lord they begin to live; but if they have not sought him, and for that reason have not lived, at once the house of Joseph will be kindled like fire. By it we ought to understand, because of Jeroboam, who was of the tribe of Ephraim and of the house of Joseph, the ten tribes, which are called Israel and, from the greater part of the people, possessed the former name. But the two tribes which were ruled by the stock of David, who was of the tribe of Judah, were called Judah, and possessed Jerusalem, in which was the temple of God. And when the house of Joseph has been kindled, it will devour and consume Bethel, of which I have said above: Do not seek Bethel, and there will be no one to quench it, since it will have been set on fire by its own kings. In place of Bethel, in the LXX is read the house of Israel, since they translated the sense rather than the word; so that, as King Jeroboam succeeded, and all the kings who thereafter succeeded him in the rule, the ten tribes, which are called Israel, burn. This is the fire which is kindled, or shines out, and inflames the house of Joseph, so that Bethel is consumed; of which it is said elsewhere: Walk in the light of your fire, and in the flame which you have kindled. And since we have often referred the house of Joseph — because of Jeroboam, who separated the people of God from the stock of David, and made golden cows in Dan and in Bethel, and said: We have no part in David, nor inheritance in the son of Jesse — to the person of the heretics, who with polished speech have fashioned comely and beautiful and, so to speak, golden images, and adore the works of their own hands, and under the appearance of cows promise themselves an image of agriculture, it is said to them: Seek the Lord, and live, him who says: I am the way, and the truth, and the life, so that, after they have walked in him and found the truth, those who before were dead may then begin to live. And unless they do this, they will be burned by the ardours of the devil, and none will be able to be found among their princes, who themselves also have been kindled by the heretical fire, who could put out the flame that devours all things, and especially Bethel, which assumes for itself the false name of the house of God.

You who turn judgment into wormwood and leave righteousness on the earth; him who makes Arcturus and Orion, and turns darkness into morning, and changes day into night. Who calls the waters of the sea and pours them out upon the face of the earth: the Lord is his name. Who smiles devastation upon the strong, and brings plundering upon the mighty. LXX: Who makes judgment on high and has set righteousness on the earth; who makes all things, and transforms them, and turns the shadow of death into morning, and darkens the day into night. Who calls the water of the sea and pours it out upon the face of the earth: the Lord God Almighty is his name. Who divides crushing upon strength, and brings misery upon the fortress. In this place the common edition disagrees greatly with the Hebrew truth, as the prudent reader at once understands, without our reminder, from what we have set forth. Let us therefore expound first according to the Hebrews, and afterwards, if we have deserved it, with Christ opening the way, let us say what seems to us in the translation of the LXX. The house of Joseph, that is, the house of Ephraim, and for that reason the royal house, and Bethel, or, as the LXX translated, the house of Israel, that is, both kings and peoples, both worshippers and idols alike, will be overthrown, who by unjust judgment provoked God to anger. And they turned the sweetness of judgment into the bitterness of wormwood, which is a kind of most bitter herb, taking up iniquity and leaving righteousness.

Let us speak also according to the LXX: God makes judgment on high, when he judges truth and renders to each according to his work; and everyone who is an imitator of God, and desires to be his son, and to be perfect, as his Father who dwells in heaven is perfect, makes judgment on high, and does not imitate that judge who did not fear God, and did not respect man, and by the perversity of his judgment did not lift his sentence up to heaven, but dragged it down to the depths. And as for what follows: And has set righteousness on the earth, we ought to take it according to this, that he gave us Christ, his righteousness, and did not cast it away but set it down on the earth, so that, all iniquity being overcome, he might make us heavenly from earthly. I think that the Gentile poet also stole from this place, who, discoursing on the simplicity and blessedness of country folk, added: "Justice, leaving the earth, made her last steps among them."

When I think of the past tempest, and of the present calm, I cease not saying, "Blessed be God, who maketh all things, and changeth them; who hath brought light out of darkness; who leadeth to the gates of hell, and bringeth back; who chastiseth, but killeth not." And this I desire you too to repeat constantly, and never to desist. For if He hath benefitted us by deeds, what pardon shall we deserve, if we do not requite Him even by words. Therefore, I exhort that we never cease to give Him thanks; since if we are grateful for the former benefits, it is plain that we shall enjoy others also, which are greater. Let us say, then, continually, Blessed be God, who hath permitted us to spread before you in security the accustomed table, whilst He hath also granted you to hear our word with assurance of safety! Blessed be God, that we no longer run hither flying from the danger without, but only from desire to hear; that we no longer meet one another with agony, trembling, and anxious thoughts; but with much confidence, having shaken off all our fear. Our condition, indeed, on former days was nothing better than that of those who are tossed up and down in the midst of the deep; and expecting shipwreck every hour. We were scared all day long by innumerable rumours, and disturbed and agitated on every side; and were every day busy and curious to know who had come from the court? what news he had brought? and whether what was reported was true or false? Our nights too we passed without sleep, and whilst we looked upon the city, we wept over it, as if it were on the eve of its destruction.

See how highly God has honored us, in committing to us so excellent a frame. I made heaven and earth, He says, and to you I give the power of creation. Make your earth heaven. For it is in thy power. "I am He that maketh and transformeth all things" (Amos v. 8, Sept.), saith God of Himself. And He hath given to men a similar power; as a painter, being an affectionate father, teaches his own art to his son. I formed thy body beautiful, he says, but I give thee the power of forming something better. Make thy soul beautiful. I said, "Let the earth bring forth grass, and every fruitful tree." Do thou also say, Let this earth bring forth its proper fruit, and what thou willest to produce will be produced. "I make the summer and the cloud. I create the lightning and the wind." I formed the dragon, that is, the devil, to make sport with him. Nor have I grudged thee the like power. Thou, if thou wilt, canst sport with him, and bind him as thou wouldest a sparrow. I make the sun to rise upon the evil and the good: do thou imitate Me, by imparting of that is thine to the good and the evil. When mocked I bear with it, and do good to those who mock Me: do thou imitate Me, as thou canst. I do good, not to be requited; do thou imitate Me, and do good, not to be repaid.

But what this righteousness is, the following verse shows: Him who makes Arcturus and Orion, and turns darkness into morning, and changes day into night. He of whom he had said above: Forming the mountains, and creating the wind, and announcing to man his speech, making the morning mist, and stepping upon the high places of the earth: the Lord God of hosts is his name, he it is who is the Creator of Arcturus, which in Hebrew is called Chima, and by Symmachus and Theodotion is rendered εἰς πλειάδα (the Pleiades), which is commonly called Boötes. And as for what follows, Orion, which in Hebrew is called Chasil, Symmachus translated it absolutely as stars, Theodotion as the evening star. But the Hebrew who instructed us in the holy Scriptures thinks that Chasil means splendour, and signifies in general the shining stars. But when we hear Arcturus and Orion, we ought not to follow the fables of the poets and the ridiculous and monstrous lies with which they try to defame even heaven and to set the reward of debauchery among the stars, saying: "He scans Arcturus and the rainy Hyades and the twin Triones, and Orion armed with gold"; but we ought to know that the Hebrew names, which among them are called otherwise, have been carried over into our language by the terms of the Gentile fables, since we cannot understand what is said except through those terms which we have learned by use and drunk in with error. Hence also in the book of Kings the Greeks translated the Hebrew Raphaim as titans, which is a most celebrated fable among the heathen, from which they write γιγαντομαχίας (battles of the giants) in praise of the gods; and the Typhoean shafts, and Mount Etna placed upon Enceladus, at whose movement Trinacria trembles. But this God, the Creator of all things, who makes Arcturus and Orion, changes night into day and day into night, and filters the most bitter waters of the sea, suspended by the heat of the upper air, and distils them into the sweet taste of the rains, like a medicinal cupping-glass, which by the heat of its upper round draws moisture and blood upward; from which we learn whence the rains come.

But in saying: Making all things and transforming them, they comprehend Arcturus and Orion in one word, neglecting to carry over the proper sense of the names into the Greek language. And God transforms all things when he makes heavenly things from earthly, and bestows on men the likeness of angels; when the moon will glow with the brightness of the sun, and the sun will have sevenfold light; when man, animal and weak and corruptible, is transformed into one spiritual and strong and incorrupt, changing his glory, not his nature; when those who understand will shine like the splendour of the firmament, and what is written will be fulfilled: One is the glory of the sun, another the glory of the moon, another the glory of the stars. For star differs from star in brightness; so also is the resurrection of the dead; when every creature will be set free from the slavery of corruption into the liberty of the glory of the sons of God. This God who transforms all things also changes the shadow of death into light, when those who sat in darkness and the shadow of death saw a great light, and those who were sons of night and of darkness became sons of light and sons of the day. This is the God who also turns the day into darkness, the day of those who said: Crucify, crucify him, take such a one from the earth; when from the sixth hour, as a type of Jewish blindness, the day was turned into night. And not only according to the letter but also according to a higher understanding, the light which rose for them in the law and the prophets was turned into darkness, since they do not know what they read, what they hear, so that there is fulfilled concerning them what is written: Let their eyes be darkened, lest they see, and bend their back always. This God calls to himself the water of the sea and pours it out upon the face of the earth, making righteous men out of sinners. To expound this, for the sake of brevity let us set down only one example. Paul the Apostle, like a violent whirlwind and a savage tempest and the flood of a swelling sea, was persecuting the Church of God and striving to crush it. Being called by God, he was poured out upon the face of the whole earth, to preach the Gospel from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum, and to build not upon another's foundation, where there had already been preaching, but to press on as far as the Spains, and to run from the Red Sea, nay rather from ocean to ocean, imitating his Lord and the sun of righteousness, of whom we read: His going forth is from the highest heaven, and his course to its highest point, so that the earth gave out before him sooner than his zeal for preaching.

What, then, is your opinion about that section of the statement that follows, "He brings about rain upon the just and the unjust"? Surely he who gives, gives when he wishes and gives where he wishes, either by arranging the well- ordered nature or by lavishly bestowing his own munificence. And in case you contemplate also casting aside this statement, in keeping with the madness of your impiety, listen to the prophet testifying about this truth: "He who calls for the waters of the sea and pours them out upon the face of the earth. The Lord is his name."

And as for what follows: Who smiles devastation upon the strong, he returns to the present time. And the order is: he who is the Creator of all things also threatens captivity upon Samaria, and brings plundering upon the mighty, since it turns judgment into wormwood and leaves righteousness on the earth. Where we have said, who smiles, Aquila translated ὁ μειδιῶν. And μειδίαμα is properly said of what we can call a smiling, when someone is angry and, with his lips parted a little, pretends to smile, so as to show the greatness of his anger.

This God also divides crushing upon strength, so as to make weak those who are wickedly strong, and so that they can imitate the Apostle, who says: When I am weak, then I am stronger. For the sons of this world are more prudent than the sons of light in their own generation. The strength of the body is the weakness of the soul, and again the strength of the soul is the weakness of the body. Therefore the Lord, who dispenses all things by reason and does all things by true judgment, divides crushing upon the strong enemy, so as to bring misery upon the fortress which raises itself up against the knowledge of God. Of which we also read in Proverbs: The wise man entered strong cities and destroyed the fortress in which the ungodly trusted. This he does indeed against all worldly strength, but properly against the heretics, who try to strengthen the falsity of their dogmas with arguments and sophisms and the dialectical art. But the wise man destroys it, and, helped by the aid of God, shows every fortress to be most vain, so as to bring misery upon it, and, when its pride has been bowed down, he can say with the Apostle: Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from the body of this death?

They take the two sons as types of two peoples, the elder Jewish, the younger Christian.… But if I show that the Jew does not fit the type represented by the elder son, it will be admitted, in consequence, that the Christian is not typified by the younger. Admittedly, the Jew is called a "son" and an "elder son" since he is first by adoption, and although he resents the Christian's reconciliation with God his Father (this is a point which our opponents seize upon most eagerly), yet the statement "Behold, how many years I serve you and I have never transgressed your commandment" cannot be one which the Jew makes to the Father. For when was Judah not a transgressor of the law? "Hearing with the ear and not hearing, holding in hate him who reproves at the gates and scorning holy speech."

They hated him who rebukes in the gate, and abhorred him who speaks perfectly. LXX: They hated him who reproves in the gates, and abhorred the holy word. These upon whom God smiles devastation, and brings plundering upon them, who are strong in evil and mighty to oppress, hated him who rebukes in the gate, that is, in court: either me, or the other prophets who have been sent to them; and him who speaks perfectly, or the immaculate word, as Symmachus translated, or the holy speech, as Theodotion and the LXX rendered. That the judgments of the people took place in the gate, according to the ancient custom of the Jews, we have both often read and frequently explained, so that neither would the farmer coming to a case be frightened by the throng of the city and its novel aspect, nor would the inhabitant of the city hasten far from the city and seek the conveyance of beasts of burden. This much let us say according to the letter. But it is a great sin to hate him who rebukes, especially if he rebukes you not out of hatred but out of love; if alone with you alone; if with another brother taken along; if afterwards in the presence of the Church; so that he may be seen to bring the charge not from a desire to disparage, but for your amendment. We often read in the Scriptures of double gates, of death and of life, of vices and of virtues, as in that place in the psalms: You who lift me up from the gates of death, that I may announce all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion. There is no doubt that he signifies the Church: the lofty Mount Zion, and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and the multitude of angels, and the Church of the firstborn, who are written in heaven. He who has been lifted up in the gates of Zion will not be able to fear the gates of death, of which the Lord spoke to Peter: Upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. The gates of virtue we learn plainly in another psalm: Open to me the gates of righteousness; having entered into them, I will confess to the Lord. This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous shall enter into it. Finally, Wisdom too, in the gates of the city, said boldly: As long as the innocent have held to righteousness, they will not be put to shame. Therefore I think that the gates of the city, that is, of the soul that believes in Christ, are the virtues through which Christ enters into those who believe. And since it is not written in which gates they hated him who rebukes, whether in the evil or in the good, let us refer it to both. The prophet reproves sinners standing in the gates of vices, and for that reason he is held in detestation by them. Or certainly the prophet himself stands in the gates and beginnings of the virtues, and is hated by those whom he rebukes; and it is not enough for sinners to hate him who reproves, or rebukes, in the gates, unless they also abhor the holy word that is brought forth from his mouth. For he who does not receive the prophet does not receive him who sent him. But if they abhorred the holy word, or him who spoke perfectly — moreover, the holy word is the Lord Jesus, of whom it is said: You will not give your holy one to see corruption —, all the Jews, saying anathema to Jesus, abhor the word of God, which is both perfect and holy and immaculate. For to the sinner piety is an abomination. And whatever we have said of the Jews can be referred both to the heathen and to the heretics, of whom the former abhor all the holy Scriptures, in which is the word of God; the latter, while they perversely understand what they read, set up an abomination in the house of God.

Therefore, because you plundered the poor man and took choice spoil from him, you shall build houses of squared stone and shall not dwell in them; you shall plant most lovely vineyards and shall not drink their wine. For I have known your many crimes and your strong sins, enemies of the just, taking a gift and pressing down the poor in the gate; therefore the prudent man shall keep silent at that time, for it is an evil time. LXX: Therefore, because you struck the poor with the fist, and received choice gifts from them, you have built houses of hewn stones, and you shall not dwell in them; you have planted desirable vineyards, and you shall not drink their wine; for I have known your many impieties and your strong sins; trampling the just, receiving exchanges, and turning aside the poor in the gates; therefore he who understands shall be silent at that time, for it is an evil time. Lest Israel should perhaps think that it was being handed over to the enemy for punishment on account of idolatry alone, he joins to it also the other things which it committed once the religion of the truth had been lost. You plundered the poor man, he says, so as to take from him who scarcely had what was necessary for his sustenance, and whatever you saw that was precious and beautiful you handed over to your own uses. Hence also from the price of the things which you seized and took from the poor man you built houses of squared stone, so that, while despoiling men, you might clothe walls with marble; and because you built them out of plunder, and prepared them not only for dwelling and shelter, which human frailty requires, but for beauty and delights, you shall not dwell in them, carried off by sudden captivity or by death. You also planted most lovely vineyards, providing for future drinking, and you shall not drink wine from them, because I have known all your crimes and sins, and strong sins, which have provoked my wrath. You are the enemies of righteousness, or of every just man, and you receive gifts and press down the poor in judgment.

We can say this very thing of the heretics as well, who plunder the poor man, or strike his head with a clenched hand: for this is what κατεκονδύλιζον means in Greek, according to what we read above, striking the poor upon the head. For the heretics strike none but the poor man, who cannot withstand the threat, and not in his other members, but in the ruling part of the heart and in the truth of faith. The poor, I think, are those who, content with a simple faith, are unable to answer the malice of the heretics. But whatever good work they have also prepared as gifts for God, unless they resist the adversaries, they will lose in the time of battle and contest; and these adversaries, by the composition and structure of words, build houses for themselves so that they may remain safe and secure. But they shall not dwell in them, when these have been destroyed and overturned by churchmen. And they not only build houses, but also plant most lovely and desirable vineyards, so as to counterfeit the mysteries of Christ; but they shall not drink wine from them, except that which is the incurable fury of dragons. For the Lord waited for these vineyards to bring forth fruit, and they brought forth not grapes but thorns or wild grapes, not judgment but a cry, with which they blaspheme against their God with insane mouth. And therefore they shall not dwell in their houses, and shall not drink the wine of the vineyards which they had planted, because the Lord has known their many impieties.

And this you may learn from what He Himself says thereupon by the mouth of the holy prophets; "Therefore because you have bruised the heads of the poor, and taken from them chosen gifts, you shall build houses of carved stone, but you shall not dwell therein: and you shall plant desirable vineyards, but you shall not drink of their wine. For I know your many wickednesses, and mighty are your sins." And again, "Woe unto those who add house to house, and join field to field, that they may take away something from their neighbour. Will you dwell alone in the earth? For these things have been heard in the ears of the Lord of hosts. For though your houses be many, they shall be a desolation: though they be great and fair, there shall be none to inhabit them. For the ground that ten yoke of oxen till shall produce one pitcher full: and he that sows six artabae shall gather three measures," Although therefore houses and fields may be the fruit of the oppression of others, yet these, He says, shall lie waste, without inhabitants, and shall yield no profit whatsoever to those who will act wickedly, because the just wrath of God is poured out upon them. In every way therefore there is no profit in covetousness.
Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

Here knowledge is not to be understood according to what we read elsewhere: The Lord knew those who are his, but in the sense that nothing is hidden from God, and that he knows all the secrets of sinners. I have known, he says, many impieties, which are not only many but also strong and oppressing, or trampling on righteousness itself, or on him who is just. And you receive, he says, exchange, for which all likewise translated ἐξίλασμα, that is, propitiation, and we said gift; but ἄλλαγμα, according to the idiom of the Scriptures, means a price, as we also read in the Gospel: Or what exchange shall a man give for his soul? They also turned aside the poor in the gates, or, as Symmachus translated, oppressed them, so as to sell a sentence for a price against the truth of judgment, falling into that which is written: Gifts blind the eyes even of the wise. These the heretics receive, so as to turn the severity of the Scriptures, which announce torments to sinners, into blessedness; and while they promise every prosperity to the rich, toward the poor alone they are fierce and severe.

Therefore he who is poor and prudent, when he sees that the judge has been bought, shall keep silent at that time, for it is an evil time. Or certainly it is to be understood thus: What use is it now, when your captivity is near, to enumerate your sins, when there is no longer any remedy and a hostile army surrounds the walls of your cities?

When therefore a churchman, prudent and understanding, comes to know that there are many impieties in that which is called the house of God, and not only many but also strong, and such as can oppress righteousness, and that the madness of the teachers has gone so far that they take a price in judgment and do everything for gifts, and also shun the poor in the gates and disdain to hear them, let him be silent at that time, lest he give what is holy to dogs and cast pearls before swine, who would turn and trample them; and let him imitate Jeremiah, who says: I sat alone, because I was filled with bitterness. And that in the psalms: I am alone until I pass over.

For when a man rules his own self—and that counts for more than to govern others—his heart is in the hand of God, and God turns it where he wills. No wonder if he turns it to the good, perfect goodness is his. And so let us be in the hand of God that we may seek the good, that incorruptible and immutable good of which the prophet Amos says, "Seek good and not evil, that you may live, and so the Lord God almighty will be with you, as you have said, 'We have hated evil and loved good.' " And so, where the good God is, there are the good things that David desired to see and believed that he would see, even as he says, "I believe I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living." They indeed are the good things that endure always, that cannot be destroyed by change of time or of age.

Let us hurry to him in whom is that highest good, since he is goodness itself. He is the patience of Israel calling you to repentance, so you will not come to judgment but may receive the remission of sins. "Repent," he says. He is the one of whom the prophet Amos cries, "Seek you good." He is the highest good, for he needs nothing and abounds in all things. Well may he abound, for in him dwells bodily the fullness of divinity. Well may he abound, of whose fullness we have all received, and in whom we have been filled, as the Evangelist says.

And so, where the good God is, there are the good things that David desired to see and believed that he would see, even as he says, "I believe I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living.(Ps. 27:13)"' They indeed are the good things that endure always, that cannot be destroyed by change of time or of age.

All these things can also be fitted to the heretics, so that, abandoning the error which they have invented, they may return to the Church, and hate their former dogmas, and love the truth of the Lord in the Church, and exercise true judgment in the gates of vices and virtues, leaving the former and passing over to the latter; and that those who have been able to escape from the jaws of the devil may hope for mercy. But according to the LXX, with the order changed, the reading of the present section can be rendered more plainly thus: As you have said, We have hated evil things and loved good things, so seek good and not evil, that you may live; and as the Lord God Almighty is with you, so render judgment in the gates, that the Lord God Almighty may have mercy on the remnant of Joseph.

Seek good and not evil, that you may live, and the Lord God of hosts will be with you, as you have said: Hate evil and love good, and establish judgment in the gates, if perhaps the Lord God of hosts may have mercy on the remnant of Joseph. LXX: Seek good and not evil, that you may live; and so the Lord God Almighty will be with you, as you have said: We have hated evil things and loved good things; and render judgment in the gates, that the Lord God may have mercy on those who are left of Joseph. You say that God is with you because you are sons of Abraham; hear what follows: If you are sons of Abraham, do the works of your father. What are the works of your father Abraham? Love good and not evil. It is a great sin not only to do evil but also to love it. Many sin, and when the heat of pleasure is spent they are stung by their conscience, and they repent of their sin. But he who not only does not grieve that he has done what is evil, but even glories in his crime, fulfils that which is written: The sinner, when he has come into the depth of impiety, despises. Seek therefore good and not evil. For if you seek good, in the very act of seeking good you at once repel evil. But you would never seek good unless you first repelled evil, fulfilling the words of the psalmist, who says: Turn away from evil and do good. And when you have sought good and avoided evil, then you will live in him who says: I am the life. He seeks good who believes in him who speaks in the Gospel: I am the good shepherd. He repels evil who flees from him of whom it is written: The world is set in the evil one. And in the Lord's prayer he says: Deliver us from evil. And when you have sought good, he says, and not evil, and have lived, then the Lord God of hosts will be with you, as you had said that he was with you for this reason, that you were born of Abraham.

Seek good and not evil, that you may live, and so it will be the Lord God the Almighty with you; in the manner that you said, We have hated evil and loved good, and establish judgment in the gates, so that the Lord God the Almighty may have mercy on the remnant of Joseph. Therefore, in the manner you have spoken, he says, seek good and not evil, so that you may gain well-being by living and being saved, and the Lord God, who has authority over all, may be with you. And establish judgment in the gates, that is, become upright judges; not recording an unjust vote against the weaker; not misrepresenting the power of the just; nor indeed striking the heads of the poor; nor turning aside the way of the humble, so that God may henceforth have mercy on those left from Joseph from the captivities that have already occurred. Therefore, it is necessary to think rightly, and to correct our own minds, so that we must think the things pleasing to God, and achieve virtue, and cling to the ways of justice, and be wise guardians of uprightness; for thus we will have the God of all with us and defending us.

It was the old custom that the elders should sit at the gate to make out by judicial trial the quarrels of persons at strife, in order that they should never enter the city at variance and should dwell there in harmony. And hence the Lord says by the prophet, "Establish judgment at the gate."
MORALS ON THE BOOK OF JOB 4:21.32

Nor is it enough to seek good and not to seek evil, unless you have ἐπιείκησιν (equity) in both, so that first you hate evil and then love good. He hates evil who is not only not overcome by pleasure, but hates the works of pleasure; and he loves good who does what is good not unwillingly, nor from necessity or fear of the laws, but because it is good, so that he has as the reward of his good work his own conscience and the love which he bears toward the good. Hence the Apostle too says: God loves, he says, a cheerful giver. For not every almsgiving pleases God, but only that which is offered with cheerfulness. And when you have hated evil and loved good, establish judgment in the gates, of which it was spoken above, so that, iniquity being driven out, truth may return. And if you do this, perhaps the Lord God Almighty will have mercy on the remnant of Joseph, those of the tribe of Ephraim and of the ten tribes who were able to escape captivity.
And again it signifies Ephraim, that is, the ten tribes. For as I have already said before, since Ephraim came from Joseph, for this reason he is also signified by his father's name.

Therefore thus says the Lord God of hosts, the Ruler: In all the streets there shall be wailing, and in all the places that are outside it shall be said: Woe, woe. And they shall call the farmer to mourning, and to wailing those who know how to wail. And in all the vineyards there shall be wailing, for I will pass through the midst of you, says the Lord. LXX: Therefore thus says the Lord God Almighty: In all the streets wailing, and in all the ways it shall be said: Woe, woe. The farmer shall be called to mourning, and to wailing those who know lamentation, and in all the ways wailing, for I will pass through the midst of you, says the Lord. I commanded you to seek good and not evil, that you might live, and that the Lord might be with you. And again I added, lest you should say that you had been warned only once: Hate evil and love good, and restore judgment in the gates, you who hated him who rebuked in the gate, that the Lord may have mercy on the remnant of Joseph. And because you would not do it, trampling on my commandments, and you turned a retreating shoulder to me, therefore thus says the Lord God Almighty, who is the Lord of hosts. Everywhere lamentation, everywhere sadness. The farmers shall be called to mourning, and those who know how to lead the dirge, after the custom of the province, so as to stir up tears, shall be called, so that the wailing and mourning shall be, not in all the streets, as was said above, but in the vineyards, so that where there was once the matter of gladness, there may be the source of tears. And all these things shall come to pass, because I will pass through, he says, the midst of you. The Hebrew word I will pass through, which in their language is said eebor, whenever it is placed in the holy Scriptures in the person of God, is to be taken as a punishment, meaning that he does not remain among them but passes through and leaves them. Hence also in other places, according to the translation of Aquila, when God is angry, he calls his fury and wrath ἀνυπερθεσίαν (no postponement).

All these things can be referred to the heretics, so that, because they would not do this and that which is just, there may be wailing in all their streets. Wide indeed and spacious is the way that leads to death, and each of the heretics and of the gentiles has his streets in their fables and fictions; to which it is fittingly added: And in all the places that are outside it shall be said: Woe, woe. For those who are in the Church will not hear woe, which is the last of punishments; but if perhaps they have sinned, a lamentation will be taken up over them. And it shall be said outside, or in all the ways: Woe, woe, for this reason, that they do not have the one way that leads to life, which is the king's way, but crooked and perverse ways, turning aside to the right and to the left, since they do not hear the Lord saying: Do not be overmuch just, and: Perverse are the ways which are on the left. And they fall into a double woe, of the flesh and of the spirit, of the present age and of the age to come; whereas, on the contrary, the churchmen hear: Rejoice, again I say, rejoice. But the farmer too is called to mourning — for the heretics have their own farmers, in whose fields thistles and thorns spring up —, and to wailing are called those who know how to wail, whether for their own sins or for those of others; although we can also take this in a good sense, that a churchman who is able to call others to repentance should imitate his Lord, who says: We have lamented, and you have not wailed; and that he should wail for the heretics, as Samuel once wailed for Saul, king of Israel. And the Apostle says that he mourns over those who have not repented.

And in all the vineyards there shall be wailing, for their vineyards are the vineyards of Sodom. And instead of the wine of gladness, which gladdens the heart of man, they have brought forth the wine of dragons and the incurable fury of asps. And they will suffer all these things, because the Lord will pass through their midst, so as not to dwell among them, nor to say: I will dwell in them, and walk among them, and: Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age.

Perhaps we will understand what has been written if we deal with a Gospel text spoken by the Savior, which expresses it in this way: "Work while it is day. The night comes when no one can work." He has named here as this age the day—but of necessity I have added the word here, for I know that in other passages other meanings are revealed—so he has called this age the day, but the darkness and the night the consummation because of punishments. For "why do you desire the Day of the Lord? And it is darkness and not light," says the prophet Amos. If you can envision after the consummation of the world what the gloom is, a gloom that pursues nearly all of the race of humans who are punished for sins. The atmosphere will become dark at that time, and no longer can anyone ever give glory to God, since the Word has given orders to the righteous saying, go, "my people, enter into your rooms, shut the door, hide yourself for a little season, until the force of my anger has passed away."

Woe to those who desire the day of the Lord: to what end is it for you? That day of the Lord is darkness and not light; as if a man should flee from the face of a lion, and a bear should meet him, and he should enter the house and lean with his hand upon the wall, and a snake should bite him. Is not the day of the Lord darkness and not light? And gloom and no brightness in it? LXX: Woe to those who desire the day of the Lord: to what end is this day of the Lord for you? And it is darkness and not light. As if a man should flee from the face of a lion, and a bear should fall upon him, and he should go into the house and lean with his hands upon the wall, and a snake should bite him. Is not the day of the Lord darkness and not light? And gloom, and it has no brightness. Lest the Tekoite prophet, who was of the tribe of Judah, should seem to neglect the men of his own tribe altogether and to address his word to the ten tribes alone, the prophecy is now directed to both kingdoms, that is, to Judah and Israel; this can be understood from many other things indeed, but especially from what follows: Woe to you who are wealthy in Zion, and trust in the mountain of Samaria. Woe therefore to Judah and Israel, who say: Let the day come, let the foretold captivity come, provided that the restoration also which is promised through the prophets follows. For there is not so much evil in the injury of captivity as there is good in the things which the Lord promises after the captivity.
