To them the prophet replied that they were waiting in vain, after the seventy years of the Babylonian captivity, for what is to come a long time afterwards, at the coming of the Son of God; for desolation and poverty and innumerable miseries will follow them. For to those who flee, he says, from the face of Nebuchadnezzar the lion, Ahasuerus will come to meet them, under whom the history of Esther is told; or, when the empire of the Assyrians and Chaldeans has been destroyed, the Medes and Persians will rise up. And when you have returned in the reign of Cyrus, and at the command of Darius have begun to build the house of the Lord, and have put all your confidence in the temple, so that you rest in it and lean your weary hands upon the walls, then will come Alexander, king of the Macedonians, or Antiochus surnamed Ἐπιφανὴς (Epiphanes), who will stay in the temple and bite you like a snake, not outside in Babylon and in Susa, but within the borders of the holy land. By these things it is proved that the day which you long for is not one of light and joy, but of darkness and sadness. These things we have said briefly according to the history, so as not to leave the opinion of the Jews wholly untouched.

But no one doubts that all our writers understand the day of darkness as the day of judgment, of which Zephaniah also writes: Near is the great day of the Lord, it is near and exceedingly swift: the voice of the day of the Lord is bitter and hard. And Isaiah: Behold, the incurable day of the Lord is coming, of fury and wrath, to make the whole world a desert, and to destroy the sinners out of it. And at the same time the confidence of the proud is shaken off, who, in order to appear just before men, are accustomed to await the day of judgment and to say: Would that the Lord might come, would that it were granted us to be dissolved and to be with Christ, imitating the Pharisee who spoke in the Gospel: God, I thank you that I am not like other men, robbers, unjust, adulterers, or like this publican. I fast twice in the week, I give tithes of all that I possess. For by this very fact, that they desire the day of the Lord and do not dread it, they are judged worthy of punishment, because no man is without sin, and the stars are unclean before him. And he has shut up all things under sin, that he may have mercy on all. Since therefore no one can pass judgment on the judgment of God, and we are to render an account even for an idle word, and Job daily offered sacrifices for his sons, lest perhaps they should think something perverse against the Lord, what rashness it is to hear with the Corinthians: Without us you reign, and would that you did reign, that we also might reign with you. Certainly, even if their own conscience did not sting them, they ought to have imitated Paul, who says: Who is made to stumble, and I do not burn? And they ought to have been anxious for all, lest, as lovers of themselves, they should desire the torments of others so that they themselves might reign, as if someone wished his own country to be captured and his city overthrown, so that he alone might enjoy the friendship of the victors. We are accustomed to say in straits and tribulations: Would that I might depart from the body and be freed from the miseries of this age, not knowing that so long as we dwell in this flesh we have a place for repentance; but if we have departed, we shall hear that word of the prophet: But in hell who will confess to you? This is the sadness of the world, which leads to death, by which the Apostle does not wish him to perish who had committed fornication with his father's wife; by which also the unhappy Judas perished, who, swallowed up by excessive sadness, joined murder to betrayal, and a murder worse than all murders, so that where he thought there was a remedy, and the death of hanging an end of his evils, there he found the lion and the bear and the snake.

Since there were some buoyed up by audacity and temerity who resisted the prophetic oracles, raging against them, calling the divine pronouncements false and demanding the fulfillment of the prophecies, the Lord declares these people lamentable for longing to see darkness instead of light. Those who long to see the fulfillment of prophecy, he is saying, are no different from a person fleeing an attacking lion and after that running into a bear, or fearfully going into a house and, with one's soul in the grip of panic, putting a hand on the wall and being bitten by a venomous snake. In other words, as that person on that day sees darkness and not a gleam of light, so these people will be given over to deep darkness on the day of punishment.

Yet here a question arises: why do the saints desire the day of the Lord, when the prophet says, “Woe to those who desire the day of the Lord” (Amos 5:18)? For we know that the day of the Lord is the condemnation of the wicked, as we have already said. And what need was there for the prophet to say, “Woe to those who desire the day of the Lord,” when no wicked person is found who either desires his own death or the day of the Lord, since he fears being condemned in it? And because what the prophet said is true, we must investigate what it signifies. Indeed, the condemnation of the wicked is their sins: whoever therefore desires to go to bed with a prostitute, desires his own condemnation; whoever desires to get drunk, desires his own condemnation; whoever desires to steal a horse or an ox or anything like that, desires his own condemnation; whoever desires to inflict some harm on his neighbor, desires his own condemnation. Therefore, since the condemnation of the wicked will be the day of judgment, whoever desires to commit those crimes for which he will be condemned on the day of judgment, desires the day of the Lord, that is, he desires his own condemnation.

By these names there seem to me to be signified either various punishments or the devil himself, who is rightly called both lion and bear and snake. And when we think that we hear Isaiah saying: Go, my people, into your chambers; shut the door, hide yourself for a little while until the wrath of the Lord passes, and that we are as it were in our own house, as it were resting in hell, then the snake will bite us, which in the present place is called Nahas, and in Job is called Leviathan, about whose nature and manifold terror we learn more fully in that book itself. But in the gloom and darkness, which are the opposites of brightness and light, the diversity of torments is set forth.

I am pierced by one wound and tortured with much grief, the bond of bitterness does not permit the tongue to perform its function, and it is easier to weep than to talk. Lo, one affliction comes upon another affliction and contrition upon contrition, "as if a man were to flee from a lion, and a bear should meet him," or howl at being struck by a scorpion, "and a snake should bite him," so completely am I dejected and afflicted with the misery of sorrow. I confess, madam, that every time I try to write to you about the passing of our lady Basilla of blessed memory, I am overcome with bitterness and experience a dullness in my mind, a heaviness in my sense and slowness in my tongue, because while I was occupied with grief, my mind was moved by death.

This brings us to a conclusion on another matter of great importance. The observances regarding sacrifices, sabbaths, new moons, and all such things prescribed by the Jewish way of life of that day—they are not essential. Even when they were observed they could make no great contribution to virtue; nor when neglected could they make the excellent person worthless or degrade in any way the sanctity of his soul. People of old, while still on earth, manifested by their piety a way of life that rivals the way the angels live. Yet they followed none of these observances, they slew no beasts in sacrifice, they kept no fast, they made no display of fasting. They were so pleasing to God that they surpassed this fallen human nature of ours and, by the lives they lived, drew the whole world to a knowledge of God.

I have hated and cast away your festivals, and I will not take in the odour of your gatherings. And if you bring me your whole burnt offerings and your gifts, I will not accept them, and I will not regard the vows of your fatlings. LXX: I have held in hatred and rejected your festivals, nor will I smell in your assemblies. And if you offer me holocausts and sacrifices, I will not accept them, and I will not regard the saving offering of your presence. This is said properly against the tribe of Judah, and against those who had migrated from Israel to the ceremonies of God, and nevertheless did not depart from the high places, and worshipped idols, and polluted the sacrifices of God by the greatness of their sins. For I never think that he would have said of the offerings of calves which they offered in Dan and in Bethel: If you offer me your whole burnt offerings and your gifts, I will not accept them. But God hates, and not only hates but also has cast away, the festivals of those who flee the lion and run into the bear, and enter the house and are bitten by the serpent, because they do not celebrate the festivals of God but their own festivals, as the Lord says: I have hated and cast away your festivals. And he does not accept the gathering and the odour of men of this kind, nor does he hold it for an odour of sweet fragrance, and he detests all their gifts, and does not regard their fattest vows. This indeed will happen not only to the men of that time, but to us as well, if we commit similar offences, and think that we offer to God what has been gained by plunder and perjuries and crimes, and that we redeem our sins, when we have read that Zacchaeus restored fourfold whatever he had seized, and of what he had gained honestly offered half his substance. For he could not offer as gifts to God what had been wrongly gained, unless he first restored it to its owners, and afterwards fulfilled what is written: Honour the Lord from your just labours, and: The ransom of a man's soul is his own riches; for God does not accept vows from the hire of a harlot. On the contrary, the just man can say: Let my prayer be directed as incense in your sight. This prayer was turned into sin for Judas the betrayer, for it did not have a good odour, but he said by his deed: My scars have putrefied and are corrupted, because of my foolishness. All these things we can say of the heretics as well, who, while they flee the lion, run into the bear, and having entered the house which they think is the Church of God, lean upon walls which they themselves have made, and are bitten by the serpent; whose light and day darkness and gloom snatch away, so that the darkness is palpable and their firstborn are slain. God hates their sacrifices and casts them away from himself, and whenever they have gathered under the name of the Lord, he detests their stench and shuts his nostrils. But in speaking of hating and casting away and not smelling, he speaks by a human likeness, so that we may come to know the disposition of God through our own words. And if they offer holocausts, or seem to fast, to give alms, to profess chastity, which are the true holocausts, the Lord does not accept these, nor does he deign to look upon their fattest victims. For he judges not the greatness of the sacrifices but the merits and motives of those who offer. Hence also the widow in the Gospel, who had cast two mites into the treasury, is preferred by the Savior to all those who believed that they were offering the fattest vows and victims full of marrow, giving little out of much, since she had offered all that she had. Are these things said more plainly and more truly, after the coming of the Lord, to the people of the Jews, who, though the temple and the altar have been destroyed, believe that they offer victims? God hates and casts away their festivals, and does not take in the odour of their gathering, when, gathered together, they say: Crucify, crucify such a one, and: His blood be upon us and upon our children. And if they offer holocausts in the synagogues, and gifts in the councils of Satan, and their fattest vows, the Lord does not regard them, just as he did not regard the gifts of Cain. They worship the one God well indeed, and offer rightly, but in this they are not regarded, that they do not divide their confession into the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit. But our gifts, that is, those of the Church, which we offer from our firstfruits, God regards, as once he regarded the sacrifices of Abel.

The difference, however, between the two services is very great: for the Saviour of all offers as a priest to God the Father the confession of our faith, and the "torrent of the sweet spiritual savour:"—for "God is a Spirit: and they that worship Him must worship in spirit and in truth." But the bloody sacrifices which they offer are not well-pleasing to God. For He even said to them, "I have hated, and have rejected your festivals, and I will not smell at your solemn assemblies. Because even though you bring Me whole burnt offerings and sacrifices, I will not accept them, nor will I regard the salvation of your appearance. Take away from Me the sounding of your praises: nor will I hear the psalmody of your instruments." Understand therefore that He says, that He hated their festivals, and that as well their praises as their sacrifices were rejected by Him. And yet God rejoices in being praised; but not by impure mouths, nor by a defiled tongue: for it is written in the book of Psalms, "But to the sinner God has said, Why do you declare My commandments, and take My covenant in your mouth; whereas you have hated instruction, and have cast out My words behind you? And again He said, "Add no more to tread My court: if you bring fine wheaten flour, it is in vain: and your spices are an abomination to Me." Why therefore, O Pharisee, do you murmur at those things being expelled from the sacred courts which were employed for the legal sacrifices, when the appointed time now summoned men to a life better than types, and to true justification by faith in Christ, Who is Himself the truth.
Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

The word would be especially fitting for those from Judah and Benjamin. For the tribes in Samaria to the worship of idols being wholly attached, they were found to be very slothful and greatly negligent of the laws given through Moses; but those in Jerusalem sacrificed on the high places to Baal and offered libations to the host of heaven, yet in addition to this they pretended to take care to show reverence for the law, and to be eager to fulfill both sacrifices and feasts. But that the Creator of all things has hated these things, he also made clear through the voice of Isaiah, saying, "Hear the word of the Lord, you rulers of Sodom; attend to the law of God, you people of Gomorrah. What is the multitude of your sacrifices to me, says the Lord? I am full of the burnt offerings of rams, and the fat of lambs and the blood of bulls and goats I do not desire, not even should you come to appear before me. For who has sought these things from your hands? You shall not continue to tread my court. If you bring fine flour, it is in vain; incense is an abomination to me. Your new moons and your Sabbaths and the great day I do not tolerate; fasting and idleness and your feasts my soul hates; you have become to me a surfeit." We say that the preceding words depend on this thought. For he says, I have hated and cast off your feasts, and I would not praise your sacrifices, nor would I ever reckon as a fragrant aroma the whole burnt offerings and the offerings for salvation.

And besides, before His coming He refused the sacrifices of the people, while they frequently offered them, when they sinned against Him, and thought He was to be appeased by sacrifices, but not by repentance. For thus He speaks: "Why dost thou bring to me frankincense from Saba, and cinnamon from a remote land? Your burnt-offerings are not acceptable, and your sacrifices are not sweet to me." And afterwards: "Gather your burnt-offerings, together with your sacrifices, and eat flesh. For I did not command you, when I brought you out of the land of Egypt, concerning burnt-offerings and sacrifices." And He says by Isaiah: "To what purpose do ye bring me a multitude of sacrifices? saith the Lord. I am full of the burnt-offerings of rams, and I will not accept the fat of lambs, and the blood of bulls and of goats. Nor do you come and appear before me; for who hath required these things at your hands? Do not go on to tread my courts any more. If you bring me fine flour, it is vain: incense is an abomination unto me: your new moons, and your Sabbaths, and your great day, I cannot bear them: your fasts, and your rests, and your feasts, my soul hateth them; I am over-full of them." And He says by another: "Depart from me; the sound of thine hymns, and the psalms of thy musical instruments, I will not hear." And Samuel says to Saul, when he thought to sacrifice: "Obedience is better than sacrifice, and hearkening than the fat of rams. For, behold, the Lord does not so much delight in sacrifice, as in obeying Him."
Constitutions of the Holy Apostles Book 6

What shall I say to those who worship Astarate or Chemosh, the abomination of the Sidions, or the likeness of a star, a god a little above them to these idolaters, but yet a creature and a piece of workmanship, when I myself either do not worship two of those into whose united name I am baptized, or else worship my fellow servants, for they are fellow servants, even if a little higher in the scale; for differences must exist among fellow servants.

Take away from me the tumult of your songs, and the canticles of your lyre I will not hear. LXX: Remove from me the sound of your songs, and the psalm of your instruments I will not hear. The beautiful canticles of the Levites, with which they praised God, he calls a tumult and a confused sound, because praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner, and they had been accustomed to offer these same things to idols as well. The prayer of the Jews also, and the psalms which they sing in the synagogues, and the composed praise of the heretics, are a tumult to the Lord and, so to speak, the grunting of a swine and the braying of asses, to whose cries the works of Israel are rather compared. But the psalm and the songs, the lyre and the instruments, take either according to the letter in the people of Israel, things which were once done as an image of things to come, or according to the spirit in us and in the heretics: if we direct them with good works, they are heard by the Lord; if with evil works, he shuts his ears and does not deign to hear the canticles of the ungodly.

And judgment shall be revealed as water, and justice as a mighty torrent. LXX: And judgment shall roll as water, and justice as an impassable torrent. As water, if it slides down a slope, lays bare what it had covered before and makes it lie open to the eyes of all, so the judgment and justice of God, which he once judged concerning his own people, will lie open to all and will be borne along like a most mighty torrent. Whatever it seizes, it drags with it, and it suffers nothing to withstand it. But according to the Seventy the judgment of the worst men rolls about like water, because it does not stand in one opinion but is carried about by every wind of doctrine, disapproving what it had approved, and thinking what it had praised before to be worth nothing. Their justifications are compared not to rivers and the purest springs, but to muddy and miry torrents, which have no waters of their own but waters gathered from rocks and brambles and crags. Whoever wishes to cross them will at once be swept headlong, and, his feet overturned, he will not be able to say: He set my feet upon a rock; for he treads upon sands, which have no foundation, and when he has been in peril he will say, according to the Hebrews: The torrent has passed over my soul. On the contrary, we read of the just, whose judgment does not roll like water and whose justice is not borne along like an impassable torrent: The thoughts of the just are judgments.

And judgment shall roll down as water, and righteousness as an impassable torrent. The righteous verdict against them will be like an impassable torrent, that is, dragging away what falls into it and sparing nothing. For when God drives someone into destruction and troubles, who is the one who will save? Who is the one who will help and deliver from judgment? Or what way will there be, by which if one passed through, he might be outside of the evils? None at all. "For who will turn back the high hand?" And, "If he shuts a man in, who can open it?" according to what is written.

And it is no difficult thing to see, that the message of the Gospel preaching, being small at first, was soon to leap forth as it were unto great increase, inasmuch as God had foretold of it by the voice of Isaiah, "that the whole earth has been filled with the knowledge of the Lord, as the deep waters that cover the seas." For the preaching of salvation is everywhere poured forth like a sea, and its onward course is irresistible. And this too the God of all clearly told us by the voice of the prophet, "And judgment shall roll as the waters, and righteousness as an impassable flood." For He gives the names of judgment and righteousness to the gospel message, and grants us the assurance that it shall roll over the world like waters and as a flood, whoso rushing streams, as it violently pours along, no man can stay.
Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

This Moses whom they refused, saying, Who made thee a ruler and a judge? the same did God send to be a ruler and a deliverer by the hand of the angel which appeared to him in the bush.  He brought them out, after that he had showed wonders and signs in the land of Egypt, and in the Red sea, and in the wilderness forty years.  This is that Moses, which said unto the children of Israel, A prophet shall the Lord your God raise up unto you of your brethren, like unto me; him shall ye hear.  This is he, that was in the church in the wilderness with the angel which spake to him in the mount Sina, and with our fathers: who received the lively oracles to give unto us:  To whom our fathers would not obey, but thrust him from them, and in their hearts turned back again into Egypt,  Saying unto Aaron, Make us gods to go before us: for as for this Moses, which brought us out of the land of Egypt, we wot not what is become of him.  And they made a calf in those days, and offered sacrifice unto the idol, and rejoiced in the works of their own hands.  Then God turned, and gave them up to worship the host of heaven; as it is written in the book of the prophets, O ye house of Israel, have ye offered to me slain beasts and sacrifices by the space of forty years in the wilderness?  Yea, ye took up the tabernacle of Moloch, and the star of your god Remphan, figures which ye made to worship them: and I will carry you away beyond Babylon. [Amos 5:25-27]

Did you offer victims and sacrifice to me in the desert for forty years, house of Israel? And you carried the tabernacle of your Moloch and the image of your idols, the star of your god, which you made for yourselves. And I will make you migrate beyond Damascus, said the Lord: the God of hosts is his name. LXX: Did you offer victims and sacrificial beasts to me in the wilderness for forty years, house of Israel, and you took up the tabernacle of Melchom, and the star of your god Repham, their figures which you made for yourselves. And I will carry you over beyond Damascus, says the Lord: God Almighty is his name. From this place we learn that all the victims and sacrifices which Israel offered in the desert it offered not to God but to Moloch its king, whose tabernacles they carried, and that they venerated the image of their idols and statues. And what this image or idol is, he shows in the words that follow: The star of your god, which in Hebrew is called chocab, that is, of Lucifer, whom the Saracens worship to this day. For this reason the Lord made them migrate beyond Damascus, that is, to the Assyrians and Chaldeans, the Lord whose omnipotence is shown from the fact that he is the Lord God of hosts.

That we may understand it so, Stephen, the first martyr of the Gospel, worthy of his name, relates in the history of the apostles: And they made a calf in those days, and offered a victim to the image, and rejoiced in the works of their hands. But God turned, and gave them up to serve the host of heaven, as it is written in the book of the prophets: Did you offer sacrificial beasts or victims to me for forty years in the desert, house of Israel? And you took up the tabernacle of Moloch, and the star of your god Rhepham, the figures which you made to worship them, and I will carry you over beyond Babylon. Nor must the first martyr be thought to have erred because, where it is written in the prophet, Beyond Damascus, he said, Beyond Babylon. For he set down the sense rather than the word, since they were led beyond Damascus into Babylon, or beyond Babylon. But in the place where Luke put Μολὸχ and where in the Hebrew is written Melchechem, Aquila and the LXX translated Μελχὸμ, Symmachus and Theodotion, of your king. Likewise, where Repham is read in the Seventy, Aquila and Symmachus, transferring the Hebrew word itself, put Chion, Theodotion ἀμαύρωσιν, that is, obscurity. Again, for Sochoth Aquila translated συσκιασμοὺς, that is, tabernacles, Symmachus and the Seventy, tabernacle, Theodotion, vision. And this is to be observed in all the holy Scriptures: that the apostles and apostolic men, in setting down testimonies from the Old Testament, consider not the words but the sense, and do not tread in the same footprints of the expressions, provided they do not depart from the meaning.

We ask how they offered victims and sacrifice in the desert not to God but to their king, whom they call Lucifer? From the time when they transformed the gold into the head of a calf, saying: These are your gods, Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, everything they did is shown to have been done not for God but for idols. And as for our reading that afterwards they offered certain things to the Lord, they did it not willingly but out of fear of punishment, and because of the slaughter of those who fell on account of the idols; but the Lord regards not the things that are offered but the will of those who offer. Finally, whenever there was occasion, they always returned in heart to Egypt, longing for the garlic and onions and cucumbers and the flesh of Egypt, and despising the manna that was given from heaven.

But whatever is said according to the letter against the people of the Jews, refer all of it to those who worship idols under the name of Christ, and who, inventing perverse dogmas for themselves, carry the tabernacle of their king the devil, and the image of their statues and idols. For they do not worship one idol, but according to the variety of their doctrine they adore different gods, and the star of their god. Since he is an angel of Satan, he transforms himself into an angel of light, and falls from heaven like lightning, and the antichrist imitates Christ. And he fittingly added: Which you made for yourselves. For they did not receive these things from God, but fashioned them out of their own mind.

Therefore the Lord will make them migrate beyond Damascus, so that they may not drink the blood of the Lord, but may pass over into Babylon and hear through the prophet: Babylon is a golden cup, making all the nations drunk. For Damascus, as we have often said, means drinking blood, or the blood of sackcloth, so that through repentance they may be called forth to drink the blood of the Lord.

[Passage quoted, Amos. iv. 12—v. 2.]

God now proclaiming the Christ by name the seventh time is said to "strengthen the thunder" and "to create the wind," the proclamation of the Gospel being called thunder from its being heard by all men, and similarly the spirit that Christ breathed on His apostles is meant; and also the Saviour's sojourn among men has clearly fulfilled the prophecy in which God is said to make "morning" and "mist" together, morning for those that receive salvation, but for the Jews that disbelieve in Him the contrary. On whom also Scripture foretells an extreme curse, adding a lamentation for the Jewish race, which actually overtook them immediately after their impiety against our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ. For of a truth from that day to this the House of Israel has fallen, and the vision once shewn by God and the rejection have been brought to pass, concerning the falling of their house in Jerusalem, and against their whole state, that it should not be possible for any one to lift them up, who will never more be lifted up. "There is," he says, "therefore no one to lift her up." For since they did not accept the Christ of God when He came, perforce He left them and turned to all the Gentiles, telling the cause of his turning, when He said with tears, as if almost apologizing:

"Jerusalem, Jerusalem, which killeth the prophets, and stonest them which are sent unto her, how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a bird gathereth her nestlings under her wings, and ye would not: behold, your house is left unto you desolate."
The Proof of the Gospel, Book 4, Chapter 16
6: Jesus' miracle was performed in the district of Samaria, to which country also belonged one of the lepers. Samaria, however, had revolted from Israel, carrying with it the disaffected nine tribes, which having been alienated by the prophet Ahijah, Jeroboam settled in Samaria. Besides, the Samaritans were always pleased with the mountains and the wells of their ancestors. Thus, in the Gospel of John, the woman of Samaria, when conversing with the Lord at the well, says, "No doubt yours are greater," and again, "Our fathers worshiped in this mountain, but you say that Jerusalem is the place where men ought to worship." Accordingly, he who said "woe unto them that trust in the mountain of Samaria," promising now to restore that very region, purposely requests the men "to go and show themselves to the priests," because these were to be found only there where the temple was, submitting the Samaritan to the Jew, inasmuch as "salvation was of the Jews," whether to the Israelite or the Samaritan.

Now that Samaria is to be understood of the heresies is proved both in the prophet Hosea and in many other places, and especially by that testimony: Woe to those who despise Zion and who trust in the mountain of Samaria; they have gathered as a vintage the chiefs of the nations; for all heretics despise 'Sion' [Zion], which means 'watchtower' and is referred to the Church, and they trust in the mountain of Samaria, namely in the pride of perverse doctrines which they think sublime, and through these frauds of preaching they gather as a vintage and lay waste the chiefs of the nations, so that, by the marvel of their doctrines, they draw all the powerful among the Gentiles into heretical error.

Woe to you who are wealthy in Zion, and trust in the mountain of Samaria; you nobles, heads of the peoples, entering with pomp the house of Israel. LXX: Woe to those who despise Zion, and trust in the mountain of Samaria; they have gathered the vintage of the firstfruits of the nations, and have gone in for themselves. To Zion, as we said above, and to the mountain of Samaria, that is, to the two tribes, which were called Judah, and to the ten, which were called by the name of Israel, the prophet's word is directed; and especially to those who in each people are nobles and princes, and give themselves to delights after the example of that rich man clothed in purple, who rejoiced in feasting and was lifted up into such pride that he did not deign to look at Lazarus, full of sores, before his door, and did not grant him even what was going to be wasted from his table. These are the heads of the peoples, who trust in riches, and are wealthy in Zion, and have confidence in the mountain of Samaria, and enter with pomp the house of Israel, so that the body shows the swelling of the mind, and they seem like the litters carried in processions. But according to the laws of tropology and the LXX translators, Zion is referred to the Church, of which we read it written: You who lift me up from the gates of death, that I may declare all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion. But the mountain of Samaria, on account of the pride and boasting in the keeping of God's commandments, is understood of the heretics, who despise the Church, because God chose the weak things of the world, to confound the strong, and the foolish things, to destroy the wisdom of the wise and reject the understanding of the prudent. These have gathered the vintage of the firstfruits of the nations, so that under the Christian name they might bring them into their own winepresses, where the grape is not trodden but ruined, where not new wine is pressed out but poison. And they have gone in for themselves. He said well, for themselves; for they did not go in in the Lord, but went in for themselves. Otherwise, as regards God they have rather gone out, while they withdraw from the Church. And what follows, house of Israel, according to the Seventy is to be read at the beginning of the following section; according to the Hebrews, at the end of this one, which we have expounded.

Pass over to Calneh, and see, and go from there to Hamath the great, and go down to Gath of the Philistines, and to all the best kingdoms of these, whether their border is wider than your border. You who are set apart for the evil day, and draw near to the throne of iniquity, who sleep on beds of ivory, and wanton on your couches, who eat the lamb from the flock, and calves from the midst of the herd, who sing to the sound of the psaltery: Like David they thought they had instruments of song, drinking wine in bowls, and they are anointed with the best ointment, and they suffered nothing over the breaking of Joseph. LXX: House of Israel, pass over, all of you, and see, into Calneh, and pass on from there into Hamath Rabba, and go down into Gath of the foreigners, the best of all these kingdoms, whether their borders are larger than your borders, you who come to the evil day, who draw near and touch false sabbaths, who sleep on beds of ivory, and abound in delights on your couches, and eat kids from the flocks and suckling calves from the midst of the herds, who clap to the sound of the instruments; they thought them as things standing, and not as things fleeing; who drink strained wine, and are anointed with the first ointments, and suffered nothing over the breaking of Joseph. Pass over, all of you, to Calneh, which is now called Ctesiphon, and pass over, all of you. Who are these all? Surely those of whom he had spoken above: Nobles, heads of the peoples, and you who are wealthy in Zion, and trust in the mountain of Samaria. You therefore, pass over into the city of Persia, and observe carefully, and from there go on to Hamath the great, which is now named Antioch. And he calls it great to distinguish it from the lesser Hamath, which is called Epiphania. Hence even to this day, for those going to Mesopotamia, the first stopping-place is called Emmas, a corrupted word indeed, but one keeping traces of the former name; its region is called Riblah, in which, in the presence of Nebuchadnezzar, the sons of Zedekiah king of Judea were killed, and his eyes were blinded. And go down, he says, to Gath of the Philistines. You who dwell on mount Zion and on the mountain of Samaria, go down to the Philistines, who live in the plains, and to all the best kingdoms of these, which lie under different cities, Gaza and Ashkelon, Azotus, Ekron and Gath, and see whether their border is wider than your border, whether you or they hold the larger provinces; you, I say, you of the people of Israel, who are set apart for the evil day, namely for the day of captivity, and draw near to the throne of iniquity, going to the unjust judge, the Babylonian king.

All that we have said according to the truth of the history, let us now transfer, according to the LXX translators, to the cloud of allegory. House of Israel, you who have withdrawn from me, who trust in the mountain of Samaria, who have gathered the vintage of the firstfruits of the nations, pass over and see, and go on to the very many walls, for this is what Hamath Rabba means; and from there go gently down into the winepress of those who fall while drinking: for this is what Gath and the Philistines signify. And contemplate everything, and especially the best kingdoms, or the best cities out of all the kingdoms; and consider whether their borders are more than yours. For if we wish to treat it in the mind and to examine the philosophy of all the nations, of the Egyptians, the Indians and the Persians, we shall find their borders narrower than the borders of the holy Scriptures: Into all indeed the earth their sound has gone out, and their words to the ends of the world.

Those to whom he had said above: House of Israel, pass over, all of you, and see, from what sort of vices they are bidden to pass over to better things, the following words describe: Who come to the evil day, preparing for themselves by their own vice an evil day; not that any day is evil, but that each one prepares evil for himself, according to what we read in Ecclesiastes: Do not say, The former days were better for me than these, for you do not ask about this in wisdom; for it is foolish to lay it on the times, since it is in our power to make for ourselves either a good day or an evil one. These draw near to and touch false sabbaths. For just as there is what is called circumcision of the flesh and circumcision of the heart, and there are Jews openly and in secret, of whom the one kind is rejected and the other approved, so there are sabbaths of the Lord that are holy and rest upon truth, and others that are not holy and are false, which follow the idleness of the letter that kills.

Let us not be careless, dearly beloved, in dealing with matters concerning our salvation; recognizing instead the troubles that could come from that evil source, let us avoid the harm it produces. After all, we are warned against intemperance not only in the new dispensation by its greater attention to right thinking, its more frequent struggles and greater effort, its many rewards and ineffable consolations. Not even people living under the old law were permitted to indulge themselves in that way, even though they were sitting in the dark dependent upon tapers and were brought forward gradually into the light, like children being weaned off milk. Lest you think I am idly finding fault with intemperance in what I say, listen to what the prophet says: "Woe to those who fall on evil days in sleeping on beds of ivory, luxuriating on their couches, living on a diet of goats picked from the flocks and suckling calves from the herds, and drinking strained wines, anointed with precious unguents—like men treating this as a lasting city, and not seeking one to come." Do you see the heavy accusation the prophet levels against intemperance in charging the Jews with these faults of stupidity, sensuality and daily gluttony? I mean, note the accuracy of the words: after attacking their gluttony and their drinking to excess, he added, "like men treating this as a lasting city, and not seeking one to come," all but stating that their satisfaction got as far as lips and palate, and they went on to nothing better. Pleasure however, is brief and fleeting, whereas pain never lets up and has no end. The truth of this comes from experience, the true meaning of lasting realities—"like men treating this as a lasting city"—and fleeting things—"not seeking one to come"—that is, not lasting for a moment.

Since therefore the Jews, separating themselves from worldly things, devoted not themselves to spiritual things, to temperance, and gentleness, and hearing the divine word, but did the very opposite, feasting, drinking, indulging in excess and luxury; on this account it is, that the prophet condemns them. For he says, "Woe to them that come to an evil day," and, in continuation, "that make a Sabbath of lies." He shows by that which follows how their Sabbath became unprofitable. How then did they make it unprofitable? By their working wickedness, living in luxury, drinking, and doing numberless other base and vile acts. And that this charge is true, hear what follows; for he intimates that which I am affirming, by that which he immediately adds, saying: "That lie upon beds of ivory, and stretch themselves upon their couches, and eat the lambs out of the flock, and the calves out of the midst of the stall; that drink refined wine, and anoint themselves with the chief ointments," (Amos vi. 4, 6.)

Thou didst receive the Sabbath that thou mightest purify thy soul from wickedness; but thou hast increased wickedness. For what can be worse than this effeminacy—this "sleeping upon beds of ivory?" The other sins, as drinking, covetousness, or prodigality, may be accompanied with some small amount of pleasure; but the sleeping on beds of ivory, what pleasure is there in it? Is more refreshing or sweeter sleep brought to us by the beauty of the couch? Nay, rather this beauty is more burdensome and more troublesome to us, if we reflect upon the matter. For whenever thou dost consider that while thou art sleeping on an ivory couch, another fellow-creature is not even able to enjoy the certainty of having bread to eat, will not conscience condemn thee and rise up to accuse this wrong?
Four Discourses on the Rich Man and Lazarus, Discourse 1

Though you are about to suffer this, you now sleep on beds of ivory and wanton on soft couches, so as to couple lust with sleep. You eat not to drive away hunger and to sustain the human body, but for delights and luxury, so that whatever is tender and fat in the flocks and in the herds you make ready for your gullet; for you the lust of the genitals and of the throat, and a paunch seething with food, are not enough unless you soothe your ears with the songs of pipes and psaltery and lyre, so that what David did for the worship of God, devising the orders of the Levites and the varieties of instruments, you turn to pleasure and luxury.

And what follows, You who sleep upon beds of ivory, we can interpret thus: he who is an athlete of the Lord, and is trained for wrestling, and prepares himself against the adverse powers, sleeps on the bare ground, imitating Jacob; and he puts at his head the stone which the builders rejected, and which has become the head of the corner. But those who give themselves to delights and luxury, and do everything for the sake of the belly, sleep on beds made of the ivory of a dead animal, and cling to unclean bones; and because vices seem beautiful and delight with their present sheen, they rest on their couches and are weighed down by the heaviest sleep. These do not eat solid and athletic food, by which the strength of wrestlers is reinforced, but soft and tender food, and of the left-hand side, such as are kids from the flocks and fattened calves, very tender, indeed still fed on milk, for this is what μοσχάρια γαλαθηνὰ means.

They also clap with their hands to the voice and sound of the instruments, so that all their works look for pleasure, and they do nothing except what they provide for the belly and for lust. Nor let the prudent reader at once object to us this, and how it is written: Let the rivers clap with their hands, and: All nations, clap your hands, and: Shout for joy to God our helper. For there they are said to clap not to the sound of instruments, but to have one accord in the praise of God. After the voice of the instruments he added: They thought them as things standing, and not as things fleeing. For the things of the world and all bodies, according to Epicurus, flow and pass away moment by moment, and nothing stands firm in its own state, but all things either grow or decrease, and, in the manner of the waters of torrents, slide headlong. Hence we also read in secular literature: "But meanwhile time flies, flies beyond recall." And in another place: "Alas, Postumus, Postumus, the fleeting years slip by." For nothing is more fleeting than the world and the things of the world. While we hold them we lose them, and through infancy, boyhood, youth, and manhood, and the age that grows heavy, and ripe age, and the last years of old age, the seven stages into which Philo divides human life, we are changed, and we run, and unawares we arrive at the boundaries of death.

This most beautiful sense, in which it is said: They thought them as things standing, and not as things fleeing, is not found in the Hebrew, but in its place is written: Like David they thought they had instruments of song. Hence it seems to me to have been added by the translators, who in the description of luxury brought forth a maxim of this kind against vices and pleasures, so that they did not translate what was written, but added from their own what seemed good to them, or rather changed it.

And you drink wine in bowls, not to sate thirst but to overwhelm the mind. And you are anointed, not with the purest oil to soothe the labours of the body, but with the most costly ointments. And while you abound in these delights, if you see any of the people perishing, you are moved by no pity over their slaughter, but you despise them as brute animals and as beasts perishing in their own gore. This same sense the prophet Ezekiel also sets down under the example of the shepherds: Who eat the milk of the sheep, and are clothed with the wool, and devour whatever is choicest, and do not heal the wounded, do not bind up the broken, do not seek the perishing.

And what follows, Who drink strained wine, can properly be referred to the heretics, who approve some Scriptures and reject others, wishing to drink strained wines, although in the holy Scriptures nothing is muddy and miry, but all is most pure, from the water above. These are anointed with the first ointments who, not having the perfumer's art, without any knowledge of the Scriptures, and of the traditions and teaching of the apostles, claim for themselves the dignity of the priesthood, and say that they are the anointed of the Lord, and contaminate the purest oil with the dregs of their own understanding. And while they do these things to the slaughter of those whom they have deceived, they are tormented by no grief, but rejoice in the deaths of others and take delight in the blood of the wretched.

There is nothing else to see happening everywhere in the world except disorder, unheralded war, unrestrained wrath and savagery exceeding all barbaric inhumanity, and there is no one suffering "by the collapse of Joseph." We bite and we devour one another, and then we have been destroyed by one another, providing pleasure to the enemies of piety.

And if I may speak of those who have undertaken the direction of souls, how many there are today who reveal their lack of the requisite qualities! Only with a feeling of pain can I speak of this subject at all -- how they melt down in the furnace of their covetousness the insults endured by Christ, the spittle, the scourging, the nails, the lance, the cross, his death itself, and squander them in the pursuit of shameful gain. The very price of the world's redemption is bundled into their purses; and only in this do they differ from Judas Iscariot, that he reckoned the total value of these things at a paltry sum of money, while they, with a more ravening greed, demand riches beyond counting. They display an insatiable passion for gains that they constantly fear to lose, and bewail after they have lost. In this love of money they find their rest, provided they are ever free from the anxiety of securing, or even further increasing, what they have acquired. Neither the peril of souls nor their salvation gives them any concern. They are certainly devoid of the maternal instinct. Grown fat, gross, bloated to excess on the heritage of the crucified Christ, "about the ruin of Joseph they do not care at all."
Sermons on the Song of Songs, Sermon 10

Therefore now they shall migrate at the head of those who migrate, and the faction of the wanton shall be taken away. The Lord God has sworn by his soul; says the Lord God of hosts: I detest the pride of Jacob, and I hate his houses, and I will deliver up the city with its inhabitants. And if ten men remain in one house, they too shall die; and his kinsman shall take him up, and shall burn him, to carry the bones out of the house, and he shall say to the one who is in the inner rooms of the house: Is anyone still with you? And he will answer: It is the end; and he will say to him: Be silent, and do not remember the name of the Lord. LXX: Therefore now they shall be captives from the beginning of the mighty, and the neighing of horses shall be taken away from Ephraim; for the Lord has sworn by himself, says the Lord God of powers: For I will abominate all the insolence of Jacob, and I hate his regions, and I will take away the city with all its inhabitants. And it shall be, if ten men remain in one house, and they die; and his household shall take them up, and shall try to carry their bones out of the house; and they shall say to those who are over the house: Is anyone still with you? And he will say: By no means; and he will say: Be silent, do not name the name of the Lord. For the reasons above which the prophetic word describes — of those who sleep on beds of ivory, and wanton on their couches, and eat lambs from the flock and calves from the midst of the herd, and sing to the sound of the psaltery, and drink in bowls, and are anointed with the best ointment, and moreover suffer nothing over the breaking of his people, which was begotten of the stock of Joseph — the Lord now threatens and says: Because they have done this and this, now they shall migrate at the head of those who migrate. And the sense is: The punishment is by no means put off into the future, nor is it prophesied of ages long after; what now presses upon them, what is now about to come, my word foretells: that they will go at the beginning of those who migrate, namely the princes and the powerful, to whom he had said above: Hear this word, you fat cows, who are on the mountain of Samaria. And again: Woe to you who are wealthy in Zion, and trust in the mountain of Samaria; you nobles, heads of the peoples, entering with pomp the house of Israel. You who are first in riches will be the first to bear the yoke of captivity, according to what is written in Ezekiel: Begin from my sanctuary. Not from the saints, as most people think, but from the overthrow of the temple, which was holy. The mighty indeed shall suffer torments mightily, and from him to whom more is entrusted, more will be required. And there shall be taken away, he says, the faction of the wanton, who had one accord in seizing pleasures, and practised revels and shared feasts; these will be taken away together, so that those whose luxury was one may have one punishment. For this the LXX translated, the neighing of the horse shall be taken away from Ephraim, which is not found in the Hebrew, and will be discussed at length by us when we begin to weave the tropology.

We have drawn the slender lines of the history; now let us set our hand to the allegory. The princes of the heretics, who for the sake of their delights devoured my people and suffered nothing over the breaking of Joseph, will be the first to be led to punishment, and the neighing of the horse will be taken away from Ephraim, which in the holy Scriptures is taken in two ways: either for the pride and power of those who neigh, or for the greatness of lust. For pride and the conspiracy of the wicked, as there: Some in chariots, and some in horses, and: A horse is deceitful for safety. And the kings of Israel are commanded not to multiply horses for themselves. And in the book of Job the voice of the horse is compared to the blast of the trumpet. In Zechariah too we read, what is confirmed by the testimony of the Gospel and is referred to the presence of the Savior: Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion, proclaim, daughter of Jerusalem. Behold, your king comes to you, just and a Savior, himself meek, and mounting upon a she-ass and the foal of a she-ass; and he will destroy the four-horse chariots from Ephraim, and the horses from Jerusalem. But for the greatness of lust and the unbridled desire for intercourse, as in Jeremiah, who, describing the luxurious and the adulterers, added: Each one neighed after his neighbour's wife. Such horses the coming of Christ and the wrath of God hamstring.

And the Lord swears by himself, since he has no one greater by whom to swear, that he detests all the insolences of the heretics and hates all their regions. For whatever they say is an insult, and worthy of the hatred of God. And he swears that he will take away the city and their meeting-places with those who dwell in them, namely both the people and the teachers, and that, even if ten men remain — men who, had they been in Sodom and Gomorrah, the fire would by no means have come down upon those cities — all will die that death which leads to Tartarus, of which Ezekiel writes: The soul that sins, it shall die.

The Lord has sworn by himself, or, as we read in the Hebrew, by his soul, according to what is written in Isaiah: Your new moons and sabbaths and feast days my soul hates, not that God has a soul, but that he speaks with human affections. Nor is it surprising if he is said to have a soul, since he testifies that he has the other members too, which are lower than the soul, feet and hands and belly, and the other limbs. But if those who deny that Christ had a human soul, and say instead that in the human body God was in place of the soul, should raise this against us, let them hear that in Christ the substance of a soul is shown, just as the members of his body also had substance. But in God the Father, just as the other things that are spoken of are not members, but by their names a diversity of operations is indicated, so also the soul is not substantial, but an affection of the inner mind and the seat of thoughts, through which God indicates his will. Has sworn, therefore, the Lord, the God of hosts, that is, Sabaoth — for which the Seventy translated, of powers — that he detests the pride of Jacob and hates his houses. Here, following the preceding section, where it is written: And they suffered nothing over the breaking of Joseph, take Jacob either as the ten tribes, or certainly as the whole house of the twelve tribes. And he has sworn that he will deliver up the city with its inhabitants, either Samaria, or certainly Jerusalem, or both in common. This we can refer to the time of the Lord Savior, after whose coming and passion God detested all the pride, or the insult, of Jacob, with which they cried out that he was the son of a carpenter, and a Samaritan, and had a demon. For this reason Jerusalem with its inhabitants was delivered up to the Roman armies.

And the wrath of God raged against them to such a degree that, even if ten men remain in one house, they too die, and a kinsman, or a neighbour, burns the corpses of the dead to carry the bones out of his house, because, for the crowds of the dying, whole bodies cannot be carried out. And when the one who has grown weary of carrying them away asks the one who is in the inner rooms of the house whether any remain whom he should hand over to him, and he answers: It is the end, I no longer have anyone to hand over to you for burial; then, before he can swear that he has none, the one who had asked, who was outside and had learned that there were none, commands him and says: Be silent, and do not remember the name of the Lord. He records this in order to show that not even when driven by the weight and necessity of evils are they willing to confess the name of the Lord, and that the name of God had come into such oblivion among Israel that Israel does not deign to hear his name even in a simple oath.

The passage involves deep obscurity from the viewpoint of commentary. It resembles the part in Genesis where there is mention of the treaty that Laban and Jacob made with each other about ownership of the offspring of the sheep, one man owning some, the other owning others. While that is obscure in its expression, the sense gains clarity in the course of comment. Now it is necessary to expound the sense of this passage as well, whose reference is not clearly expressed. His intention, in fact, is to cite a proof of the devastation affecting them in that it was very extreme. In many cases scarcely ten will be left from a large household of many members, the rest being done away with in various ways through the war.

Their bones are buried by their kinsmen and their household, of whom it is said: Let the dead bury their own dead. And he who is outside, and does not enter the house of the dead, but rather casts the dead out, commands the one who burns the dead, and dissolves them into ashes, and crushes their bones, to be silent and not to stain the most pure name of God with a dead mouth. For God says to the sinner: Why do you declare my justices, and take up my covenant through your mouth? Hence we too must take care that we do not, being dead, bury the dead, but rather that, living, we lead forth to life those who are dead. If we do not do this, we are commanded and told, Be silent, because we are judged unworthy of the name of God.

For behold, the Lord will command, and he will strike the greater house with ruins, and the lesser house with rents. Can horses run on rocks, or can there be ploughing with wild oxen? For you have turned judgment into bitterness, and the fruit of righteousness into wormwood. You who rejoice in nothing, who say: Did we not by our own strength take horns for ourselves? For behold, I will raise up against you, house of Israel, says the Lord God of hosts, a nation; and they will crush you from the entrance of Hamath to the torrent of the desert. LXX: Therefore behold, the Lord will command, and he will strike the great house with ruins, and the small house with rents. Will horses give chase on rocks, will they keep silent toward the females? For you have turned judgment into fury, and the fruit of righteousness into bitterness. You who rejoice over no good word, who says: Did we not have horns by our own strength? For behold, I will raise up against you, house of Israel, says the Lord God of powers, a nation; and they will crush you, so that you do not enter into Hamath, and as far as the torrent of the west. Because you have leapt into such madness that even in the time of death, with evils hanging over you, you were unwilling to name the name of the Lord, therefore the Lord will command, and he will strike the greater house with ruins, and the lesser house with rents. If he commands, how does he strike? If he strikes, how does he command? But in commanding and giving orders to his ministers, he himself is seen to strike. Just as, when the Father commands and the Son performs, he who commanded himself does it, and that little verse is fulfilled: He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created. For all things indeed were made through him, and without him nothing was made that was made. And in Egypt the Lord testifies that he himself killed the firstborn, who are reported to have been slain by the destroyer. So too in the present place the Lord commands, and he himself, through his ministers, strikes the greater house with ruins, that is, the ten tribes, which were called Israel, and the lesser house with rents, the two tribes, which were ruled by the stock of the house of David. And note the particular character of each. Israel, because it had sinned more greatly, is struck with ruins and handed over to perpetual captivity. But the house of Judah, in which the temple was, and which had sinned in part, is held in a captivity of seventy years, and is not struck with ruins but with rents. For a house that is rent can be mended; ruins call not so much for restoration as for building anew.

Some, according to anagogy, think that the great house and the lesser house signify the Jewish people and the Church gathered from the Gentiles. For they are called great because of the fathers, and the law, and the prophets; we lesser, because we were without the covenant and the commandments of God, of whom we also read in the Song of Songs: My sister is little, and she has no breasts. This house, great and small, gathered into the one household of God, if it does not keep discipline and does not do the commandments of God, will be struck with ruins and rents. Whenever, therefore, the house of God, which is the Church, collapses and is torn, whether in persecutions or in heresies and schisms, it shows the hand of God striking; and if we wish to escape it, let us hear and follow the example of the comparison.

The ruins and rents of these two houses he compares to horses and wild oxen: the former cannot run on rocks; the latter are so untamed that they do not take the yoke on their necks, and, being forest cattle, because of their wildness they refuse to cleave the earth with the ploughshare. But you, though horses and wild oxen cannot change their nature, have changed the nature of God, so as to make the sweet one bitter and to turn the fruit of his righteousness into wormwood, which is a most bitter herb.

Horses cannot give chase on rocks. The rock is Christ, who granted to his apostles that they too should be called rocks: You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church. Whoever is on these rocks, the adverse powers, which are called horses, of which we spoke above, will not be able to pursue him, their courses being hindered and they falling on every single rock. Let us come also to the other comparison, according to our custom, discussing the edition of the LXX translators, lest, if we cling wholly to the Hebrew, we should seem to have mocked the diligence of the reader, and, by keeping silent about the common edition, to have set it out to no purpose. Or will they keep silent, he says, among the females: there is no doubt that he means the horses, of which he had said above: Will horses give chase on rocks. These horses, that is, the opposing powers, which go mad for the females, do not dare to approach when they see a manly spirit strengthened by the might of God. But when they see an effeminate mind, enervated by ointments and luxuries and turned to womanish softness, at once they go mad, cannot hold themselves back, and are wild with lust. There follows: For you have turned judgment into fury. He turns judgment into fury who judges in anger; and though the Lord says: You shall not accept a person in judgment, and in another place: You shall not pity the poor man in judgment, and: For the judgment is God's, such a man comes down to judge with an angry mind; indeed, though he does not know the case nor understand the truth of the judgment, he decides beforehand what sentence he ought to pass; the fruit of righteousness too, which is most sweet, he turns into bitterness. What we have said of one virtue, let us understand also of the rest, prudence, fortitude, temperance: whoever is angry will not be able to gather their fruits, and when he does gather them, they will be bitter. Hence it is said in Isaiah: Woe to those who call sweet bitter, and bitter sweet. This is said by those who in judging consider not the cases but the persons, and turn the fruit of Christ's righteousness, which is most sweet, into bitterness. Whoever, therefore, in judging is led either by kinship or by friendship, or, on the other hand, by hostile hatred or by enmities, perverts the judgment of Christ, who is righteousness, and turns his fruit into bitterness.

Whence also we say that the holy men are just and that they are made pleasing to God after their sins not only through their merits but through the mercy of him to whom every creature is subject and stands in need of his mercy. Let heretics hear, who are lifted up by pride and say, "We have taken unto us horns by our own strength." Let them listen to what Moab heard said to him: "We have heard the pride of Moab, he is exceedingly proud. 'His haughtiness and his arrogance and his pride and the loftiness of his heart I know,' says the Lord, 'because his strength is not according to the loftiness thereof.' "

You who rejoice in nothing, either in idols and golden calves, which are nothing, as Esther says to the Lord: Do not hand over your sceptre to those who are not, or in nothingness and falsehood. You who think that by your own strength you took horns, and kings and power, with which to toss your enemies.

Those who do this rejoice in no good word, or in vain, as Symmachus translated, that is, ἀλόγως, and, lifted up in pride, they say: Did we not have horns by our own strength? Whereas, on the contrary, the just man glories in the Lord and says: In you we will toss our enemies with the horn. And in the same place: For I will not hope in my bow, and my sword will not save me. Hence also in Exodus, according to the Hebrew and the edition of Aquila, we read: And Moses did not know that the appearance of his face was horned, he who could truly say: In you I toss my enemies with the horn. We read also in another place: And he will exalt the horn of his people, and: He has exalted the horn of his Christ, and of the horn of the altar, and of the clean and horned animals, which alone are offered to God, whose interpretation belongs not to this occasion.

Because, therefore, you have done these things, behold, I will raise up against you, O great house and lesser house, which are to be struck with ruins and rents; that is, O house of Israel and all the twelve tribes, the most savage nation of the Assyrians and Chaldeans, to crush and overthrow you from beginning to end, from head to tail; from the borders of your land which look toward the sun, to the torrent of the desert, or of the west, as the LXX translated, that is, from Hamath to Rhinocorura, between which and Pelusium the stream of the Nile, or the torrent coming from the wilderness, enters the sea. We said above that Hamath is Epiphania, which took its name from Antiochus, whose surname was Ἐπιφανὴς (Epiphanes). But those who think that the house of Israel here signifies the ten tribes will not be able to explain how it can be said in a threat against the ten tribes that they are to be crushed from Epiphania to the borders of Egypt, within which borders not the ten tribes only, but all twelve are enclosed, among which were also Judah and Benjamin.

Because of these great sins and the utmost pride, which speaks iniquity against God and sets its mouth on high, the Lord God Almighty says that he will raise up a most savage nation, to crush and grind them down, or rather to forbid them to enter into Hamath, and as far as the torrent of the west. Hamath means wall, or walled. They were therefore forbidden by this most savage nation, to which the punishments had been entrusted, to flee for refuge to the fortified city, which is the heavenly Jerusalem, lest they enter and be saved; after the manner of that section which we read in Genesis, where God placed the Cherubim and the flaming sword which turns to guard the way of the tree of life, so that he who had been cast out of paradise might by no means enter there unworthy. And what follows: As far as the torrent of the west, we shall interpret from the sixty-seventh (68th) psalm, in which it is written: Sing to the Lord, sing a psalm to his name; make a way for him who ascends above the sunset. The Lord is his name. For unless evil works have set in us, Christ will not ascend above us. And when they have set, and we have Christ as our charioteer, then, as we advance and go on to better things, it will be commanded us in the same psalm: Sing to God, sing psalms to the Lord, who ascends above the heaven of heaven toward the east. Hence also in the mysteries we first renounce him who is in the west, and who dies to us together with our sins, and so, turned toward the east, we enter into a covenant with the sun of righteousness and promise that we will serve him. For the torrent of the west, Symmachus translated a valley of the plain, Theodotion the torrent of Arabia, Aquila the torrent which is in the level ground. By these words it is shown that those who are shut out from the walled city can by no means be fortified against sins, nor do they reach the torrent of the plain and the level ground, or of the desert, which is called the torrent of pleasure, according to what we read: You will give them to drink from the torrent of your pleasure.
7: These things the Lord God showed me: and behold, the maker of the locust at the beginning of the shoots of the late rain, and behold, the late one, afterwards the king's shearer. And it came to pass, when it had finished eating the grass of the land, I said: O Lord God, be merciful, I beseech you; who will raise up Jacob, for he is very small? The Lord had pity over this: It shall not be, said the Lord. LXX: Thus the Lord showed me: And behold, a brood of locusts was coming in the morning; and behold, one cankerworm, Gog the king. And it will be, if it has finished devouring the hay of the land, and I said: O Lord God, be merciful; who will raise up Jacob, since he is small? Repent, O Lord, over this; and this shall not be, says the Lord. The prophetic word foretells not only the things which are to come many ages later, but also things near at hand, which follow immediately upon the prophecy. For we men are accustomed to think much more about ourselves than about posterity, as Hezekiah says: Let there be peace in my days. This is so that those who see fulfilled in fact what was announced beforehand may be converted to the worship of God, in whose prophets is the truth of divination. The Lord therefore shows that Sennacherib king of the Assyrians, with a boundless multitude of his army, like a locust shearing everything, would come at the beginning of the late rain, when Israel was in need of the utmost mercy of God Almighty; and the maker and creator of this locust is the Lord. This locust comes at the beginning of the late rain, when all things are green and every field is in labour, and the blossoms of the various trees burst out into fruits of their own kind. And to show in one word what I mean, the blossoms of the trees and the blades of the crops promise an abundance of all things. These locusts, which were flying in early spring, were followed by a countless cankerworm, which came after the late rain and was called the shearer, or the shearing, of the king, because it laid everything waste and left nothing at all of green grass on the earth. This shearer, or shearing, Isaiah calls a sharp razor, which shaved off all the hairs and locks of the body of Israel. And when, he says, I was in doubt what this razor might be, he at once added: the king of the Assyrians. The razor, therefore, and the king's shearer is the army of the Chaldeans, which like the cankerworm ravaged everything, and consumed not only the crops but the trees, the hay and the stubble.

The LXX translators seem to me to have understood the Hebrew word gozi, which means shearer or shearing, as Gog, taking the letter zai for uau, and to have compared the countless multitude of the cankerworm to Gog, a most savage nation, which is described as about to lay waste the land of Judea. But what Aquila meant to say with Behold, the late one after the king of Gaza, since Gaza is called Aza in the Hebrew word, I do not well understand, unless perhaps he set down the very word gozi, and it was gradually corrupted by error into Gaza. Let us speak also spiritually: those who after works of righteousness — of which it is said in the prophet: Sow for yourselves in righteousness, and break up fresh ground for yourselves; and do not sow upon thorns — have committed grave sins, upon them is brought the brood, or generation, of locusts coming in the morning, when, as the darkness of night passes, they begin to recognize their own sins; and because they have not repented, the cankerworm is brought on, which is called Gog, the king; and Gog is rendered in our language roof, a certain proud and arrogant strength.

It is, after all, the practice of the prophets and the just to grieve not only for themselves but also for the rest of humankind. If you're inclined to check that, you will find them all giving evidence of this compassion—for example, you can listen to Jeremiah, "Who will pour water on my head, and provide a fountain of tears for my eyes?" or Ezekiel, "Alas, Lord, you will destroy what remains of Israel?" or Daniel lamenting in these words, "You have made us few in number by comparison with the Gentiles," or Amos, "Think better of this, Lord."

And it came to pass, when the cankerworm that had come after the locust had finished eating the grass of the land, and the prophet understood what he was seeing, he turns to prayer and says: O Lord God, be merciful, I beseech you. I do not wish my words to be fulfilled in the overthrow of my people; I do not wish to have been chosen from the number of the shepherds for this, that I should announce the ruin of the ten tribes. For who will be able to raise up Jacob, except you alone? When you strike him down, there is no one to raise him up. Jacob is very small, and destroyed by the frequent incursions of enemies.

And when it has consumed the hay and the stubble of our land, whoever are saints among the people will pray for pardon and will say: O Lord God, be merciful. For who else will be able to raise up Jacob? Which of the physicians can heal the αἱμοῤῥοῦσαν (the woman with the issue of blood), except you alone, at the touch of whose fringe health at once returns? For Jacob is very small, or of small number, because no traces of virtues, or only a few, have remained in them.

And as he prayed and poured out the tears of the inner man, the Lord had pity over this and answered: I will not destroy the whole race of Israel; a remnant will be saved. Or certainly it is to be taken thus: he beheld two things to come together, first the locust, then the cankerworm. For both he entreated the Lord, and he is heard in one only, so that the cankerworm should not lay everything waste to utter destruction; but the locust, flying about, devours some things and leaves others untouched.

Repent, O Lord, over this which you threatened that you would do to your people. But the repenting of God in the Scriptures we ought to understand in the same way as his sleep and his anger: not that God repents or changes his sentence, he who speaks through the prophet: I am God, and I do not change, and to whom we say: But you are the selfsame, and your years will not fail; but that, when we are converted to better things, he too repents of his sentence, so that he neither pays the just man the rewards he promised, if he turns aside to iniquity, nor the sinner the punishments he threatened, if he is converted to salvation. It is said to him who is about to repent: Give no sleep to your eyes, nor slumber to your eyelids, that you may be freed like a little doe from the nets, and like a bird from the snares. If such a one has at first despised the commandments of the Lord, and afterwards, set in straits, begins to wake up, he rouses the Lord, who for him is sleeping, and says: Arise, why do you sleep, O Lord? On the other hand, those who have stored up wrath for themselves in the day of wrath will feel God angry. But if they choose repentance, the wrath will be turned into mercy, and according to our disturbances and our virtues the Lord will change in either direction, toward punishment or toward clemency.

These things the Lord God showed me, and behold, the Lord God was calling judgment to fire; and it devoured the great deep and ate up a part as well. And I said: O Lord God, be still, I beseech you; who will raise up Jacob, for he is very small? The Lord had pity over this: But this too shall not be, said the Lord God. LXX: Thus the Lord God showed me, and behold, the Lord God called judgment in fire, and it devoured the great deep, and ate up a part; and I said: O Lord God, cease; who will raise up Jacob, since he is very small? Repent, O Lord, over this; and this shall not come to be, says the Lord God. First the Lord showed the prophet the maker of the locusts at the beginning of the shoots of the late rain, and after the late rain the shearer king, or the king's shearer, and, to render word for word, the shearing of king Sennacherib, by which he sheared and laid waste everything of the ten tribes. Now the same Lord shows Nebuchadnezzar, or rather calls him and commands him to come against Judah and Jerusalem. And he calls him so that he may set the temple and Jerusalem on fire, and execute judgment in fire upon that which was once his people. And when the fire had come to judgment, to fulfil the Lord's command, it devoured the great deep, and ate up a part as well: all the cities of Judah, and the Lord's part, which was called his temple.

But since, once and for all, following the prophet Hosea and the psalmist, who says: The sons of Ephraim, bending and shooting the bow, turned back in the day of battle, we have referred the ten tribes, which were called Israel, to the person of the heretics, and the two, over which Judah presided, to the Church and the sinners of the Church, who confess indeed the right faith, but because of the filth of their vices need flames to purge them; therefore the Lord now shows that he calls judgment to fire, so that the fire may prove of what sort each one's work is, and that may be fulfilled which is written: Walk in the light of your fire, and in the flame which you have kindled. Hence it is said also to Babylon: You have coals of fire, you will sit upon them, they will be a help to you. And in the psalm the deceitful tongue, full of lies, is said to need purging by the fire of coals: What shall be given you, or what shall be added to you, against a deceitful tongue? The sharp arrows of the mighty, with desolating coals. Of these coals of the altar, the desolating coal is taken up with the tongs of the two testaments, and purges the unclean lips of Isaiah, so that he can prophesy the word of the Lord. The fire, then, called to judgment, first devours the deep, that is, all kinds of sins, wood, hay, stubble, and afterwards eats up a part as well, that is, it reaches his saints, who are reckoned as the Lord's own possession and in his portion; for it is time for judgment to begin from the house of the Lord. And in Ezekiel it is commanded to those who are to inflict the punishments: Begin from my saints. And in the Apostle we read: If anyone's work burns, he will suffer loss, but he himself will be saved, yet so as through fire.

And when we have all been in sin, and have lain prostrate before the truth of the sentence, the Lord will have mercy on us, and because we are very small, he will raise us up at the time of the resurrection, or he will raise up through virtues us who lay in vices; the Lord promising this and saying: But this too shall not be.
