And he said well: But this too, because above he had already said: This shall not be. Not, indeed, to the end will he be angry, nor for ever will he threaten. He has not dealt with us according to our sins, nor repaid us according to our iniquities. As far as the east is from the west, so far has he removed our iniquities from us. As a father has pity on his sons, so the Lord has had pity on those who fear him.

And when the prophet had seen this, he said to the Lord, not as above: Be merciful, I beseech you, but: Be still, or cease, so that by his prayers he might obtain that he whom he had already seen begin should cease, especially since there is no other who can raise up Jacob, fallen and very small and humbled, except the Lord, who is able to bring back into the land of Judah those taken captive and carried off into Chaldea.

I will also proclaim confidently that there is someone who cannot be affected very much by the "hammer of the whole earth." And since the example was offered of a perceptible "hammer," I will seek a material stronger than the "hammer" which does not feel the blows from it. In searching for it I find it too in what was written: "Behold a man standing above the adamant walls, and in his adamant." History records about "adamant" that it is stronger than every "hammer" striking it, remaining unbroken and unyielding. Even if the "hammer," the devil, stands above, and the serpent, who "as an indomitable anvil," may position himself below, still "adamant" endures nothing when it is resting "in the hand of the Lord" and in his regard. Thus the two opposites to this "adamant" are the "hammer" and the immovable "anvil." Yet there is indeed among the nations a much-used proverb in the common language concerning those who are pressed by anxieties and extremely bad situations; they say, "They are 'between a hammer and an anvil.' " Still you can say that this refers to the devil and the serpent, who are always signified by names of this sort in the Scriptures for a variety of purposes. And you can say that the holy person, who is an "adamant wall" or is "adamant in the hand of the Lord," is not affected either by the "hammer" or by the "anvil," but the more one is struck, the brighter will his virtue shine.

These things the Lord showed me: And behold, the Lord standing upon a plastered wall, and in his hand a mason's trowel. And the Lord said to me: What do you see, Amos? And I said: A mason's trowel. And the Lord said: Behold, I will set a trowel in the midst of my people Israel. I will not again overlay it, and the high places of the idol shall be demolished, and the sanctuaries of Israel shall be made desolate; and I will rise up against the house of Jeroboam with the sword. LXX: Thus the Lord showed me: And behold, a man was standing upon a wall of adamant, and in his hand adamant. And the Lord said to me: What do you see, Amos? And I said: Adamant. And the Lord said to me: Behold, I will cast adamant into the midst of my people Israel. I will by no means again pass him by, and the altars of laughter shall be scattered, and the sacrifices of Israel shall be made desolate, and I will rise up against the house of Jeroboam with the sword. Before we discuss the adamant, which Symmachus and the LXX gave for what is written in the Hebrew as enach, it must be said briefly that Aquila rendered this word γάνωσιν and Theodotion τηκόμενον, of which the one means tinning and the other melting, so that that frying pan which we read of in Ezekiel, in which is signified the frying of the people hemmed in by siege, may be shown, through the word tinning, also in the ten tribes and in the reign of Jeroboam — who was the grandson of Jehu, under whom this prophecy is seen —. The Lord, then, is seen standing upon a wall tinned, or plastered, and in his hand tinning, or a mason's trowel, with which walls are usually overlaid, and receive not only beauty but also strength against the harm of the rains and the very frequent storms.

We have said as best we could what has been handed down to us by the Hebrews according to the truth of the history; let us pass to anagogy, setting down a few words from Xenocrates, who wrote on the natures of stones and gems: "Adamant is a stone of its own name, which in Latin we can call untamable, because it yields to no material, not even to iron. For if it is placed on an anvil and struck with a heavy blow of the hammer, the anvil and the hammer receive damage before the adamant is broken. And though fire tames all things and consumes all metals, it renders the adamant harder, so that the force of excessive heat does not blunt even the smallest corner of it. I have seen also in gold an adamant the size of a millet grain, and though the gold around it is worn away by long use and great age, the adamant alone is not worn down, and it cannot be diminished by any file, but on the contrary wears down the file, and furrows with lines whatever it touches. This stone, most hard and untamable, is dissolved by the blood of goats alone, and put into hot blood, it loses its strength. It is small and unsightly, having the colour of rust and the brilliance of crystal. And four kinds of adamant are described: the first is Indian, the second Arabian, the third Macedonian, the fourth Cyprian, possessing more or less hardness according to the character of the regions. It is said also, like electrum, to detect poisons and to resist the arts of sorcerers". Such is the Lord and Savior, who, though he was in the form of God, did not think it robbery to be equal to God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, made in the likeness of men, and found in bearing as a man; humbling himself, made obedient unto death, and the death of the cross. Of whom Isaiah writes: He has no form nor comeliness; we saw him, and there was no beauty, despised and the last of men, a man of sorrows, and knowing how to bear infirmity. He stands upon the wall of adamant, that is, upon his saints and apostles, to whom he granted that they too should be called adamants, and, overcome by no one, should say: Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or the sword? And again: I am sure that neither death nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor things present, nor things to come, nor strength, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus our Lord. Peter too was a most strong adamant: the gates of hell did not prevail against him. This man and Lord, who stands upon the wall of adamant, has in his hand the adamant, which, unless it is held by the hand of God and fortified by his help, loses all its strength, as the Lord says in the Gospel: No one can snatch out of the hand of my Father. And he is so robust that it is said to him: If you pass through fire, the flame will not burn you; and the more he is beaten by temptations, the stronger he becomes, and for the name of the Savior he rejoices amid the scourges. And though he can be overcome by no one, he is dissolved by the heat of deadly lust alone. For this is said to be the nature of the blood of goats and of the goat himself, that he is most hot for lust, and that what fire cannot tame, his blood alone dissolves.

Jesus would lead his detractors to the point of judging themselves, saying, "What do the vinedressers deserve?" They decided concerning themselves, saying, "Let him destroy the evil ones with evil." Then he explained this, saying, "Have you not read that 'the stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner?' " What stone? That which is known to be lead. For see, he has said, "I am setting a plumb line in the midst of the sons of Israel." To show that he himself was this stone, he said concerning it, "Whoever knocks against that stone will be broken to pieces, but it will crush and destroy whomever it falls upon." The leaders of the people were gathered together against him and wanted his downfall because his teaching did not please them. But he said, "It will crush and destroy whomever it falls upon," because he had resisted idolatry, among other things. For "the stone that struck the image has become a great mountain, and the entire earth has been filled with it."

The Lord therefore sets an adamant of this kind in the midst of his people Israel, and no longer passes him by, nor does he leave off, so that the altars, which deserve laughter and derision, are scattered, and he strikes with the sword and overthrows all the mysteries of the heretics and the house of Jeroboam, who first divided the people of God.

We read in Ezekiel that the Lord threatens that, when storm and hail arise, he will by no means plaster or clothe the wall of Israel, but will let it be broken up by the rains. Hence now too he of whom it is written, He shall be called the builder of the wall, himself the cornerstone and the builder of the house, says that he will lay down the trowel in the midst of his people Israel, and make it cease and lie idle, so that he will by no means again overlay it, and clothe and protect it with his help.

And when the Lord, the trowel ceasing, has withdrawn his protection and, so to speak, the clothing of the wall, then the high places of the idols, which in Hebrew are called bamoth, will be demolished, and the sanctuaries of the ten tribes will be made desolate, so that Dan and Bethel are destroyed, in which the golden calves were worshipped.

All that we have interpreted concerning Amaziah, and Jeroboam, and Israel, and Amos must be referred τροπολογικῶς (tropologically) to the heretics, whose priest Amaziah is accustomed at times to send to Jeroboam, the heretical king and patron of heretics, and to accuse holy men and heralds of the faith before him, and to order the teachers not to preach in Israel, lest they act against the king's will, because Bethel, that is, the house of God, and the false Church is the sanctuary of the king and the house of the kingdom. For they are accustomed to say: The emperor is in communion with us; and if anyone resists them, they at once bring the slanderous charge: So you act against the emperor? You despise the commands of the Augustus? And yet let us consider that many Christian kings who have persecuted the Church of God, and tried to establish the Arian impiety in the whole world, outdo Jeroboam king of Israel in wickedness. For he despised the commands of the false priest, and would give no answer to his prompting. But these, with their many Amaziahs as their priests, by hunger and want, by prisons and exiles, have put to death the prophet Amos and the priests of the Lord.

And Amaziah the priest of Bethel sent to Jeroboam king of Israel, saying: Amos has rebelled against you in the midst of the house of Israel. The land will not be able to bear all his words. For thus says Amos: Jeroboam shall die by the sword, and Israel shall go captive out of his land. And Amaziah said to Amos: You who see, go, flee into the land of Judah, and eat bread there, and there you shall prophesy; and in Bethel you shall not again prophesy any more, because it is the sanctuary of the king and it is the house of the kingdom. LXX: And Amaziah sent the priests of Bethel to Jeroboam king of Israel, saying: Amos is making gatherings against you in the midst of the house of Israel; the land will not be able to bear all his words. For thus says Amos: Jeroboam shall die by the sword. But Israel shall be led captive out of his land. And Amaziah said to Amos: You who see, go out, withdraw into the land of Judah, and live there, and there you shall prophesy; but in Bethel you shall not again prophesy any more, because it is the sanctuary of the king, and the house of the kingdom. It is a proverb of Solomon, or rather a command: Do not rebuke the wicked, lest they hate you. And on the contrary he gave a precept about the good: Rebuke a wise man, and he will love you. In another place also: He who rebukes, he says, the ways of a man will have more favor than he who speaks what pleases. And so Amos too spoke to the people out of a desire for their amendment, and from the words of God threatened terrible things, so that they might repent, return to God and forsake their idols. Then the priest of Bethel, in which was the golden calf that Jeroboam the son of Nebat and the others who had succeeded him in the rule had set up, sends to Jeroboam, the grandson of Jehu, someone to report to him, saying: Amos has rebelled against you, or, is making gatherings and assemblies in the midst of your kingdom, Israel; and he says such great things that the land of your kingdom cannot bear his words. And he dares to send to the king of Israel as though he were a high priest, fearing that if the people should be converted to the worship of God, he would lose the glory of his priesthood. And though he had heard two things, the high places for idols will be demolished, or the altars of laughter, and the sanctuaries, or ceremonies, of Israel will be laid waste, and I will rise up against the house of Jeroboam with the sword, because the idols over which Amaziah the priest presided were to be utterly destroyed, and God would rise up against Jeroboam with the sword unless he repented, he sends no word about the wrong done to himself, so that he may seem to grieve only over the insult to the king.

For thus, he says, says Amos. You are wrong, slanderer. For in all his words the prophet does not speak as though from himself, but always sets at the head: Thus says the Lord. Therefore he makes out that the prophet Amos said what the Lord spoke, so as to provoke the king the more to vengeance. What are the things that Amos says? Jeroboam shall die by the sword. In this too you lie: for he did not say: He shall die; for if he had said this, it would seem that he did not admit repentance; but he said that the Lord will rise up against the house of Jeroboam with the sword, threatening punishment, not inflicting it. Nor does he say: Jeroboam shall die by the sword, but: I will rise up against the house of Jeroboam with the sword. For Jeroboam did not die by the sword, but his house, that is, his son Zechariah, was destroyed when God struck him. And Israel, he says, shall go captive out of his land; add the rest too: if he does not repent.

Moreover Jeroboam, despising the utterly empty messages of Amaziah, would give no answer to what he had sent him; whereupon Amaziah takes upon himself the authority of the priestly eminence, and speaks to Amos: You who see, go, flee into the land of Judah. The prophets, as we have often said, were formerly called seers, because they beheld with the eyes of the heart the things they said were to come. The prudent reader may ask why he calls him a seer, and by the prophetic name, the man whom he compels to leave the land of Israel. To him the answer must be either that he says it in mockery, κατὰ ἀντίφρασιν (by antiphrasis), since everything Amos says is a lie, or that he saw there were many among the people who listened to him gladly; for which reason he also reported to the king: Amos is making gatherings against you; he does not dare to do him an open injury, lest he seem to offend those who listen to him. Go, he says, into the land of Judah, in which you were born, where madmen are gladly listened to, and eat your bread there, or live there, or at any rate practise your art there, by which you may find yourself food, and prophesy there, because you have many there whom you are used to leading astray; but in Bethel, in which I am priest, you shall not prophesy any more, because it is the sanctuary of the king and the house of the kingdom. And this he says as a false priest, flattering the royal eminence, so that he does not say: It is the sanctuary of our God, and the house of the idol, but the sanctuary of the king and the house of the kingdom; for all who worship false gods have this custom, to ascribe their own pride to kings, so that what they themselves do may seem to have been done by the king.

Amos also said, "I was no prophet, nor the son of a prophet, but only a herdsman, a gatherer of sycamore fruit. And God took me." But he did not say this to exalt himself, but to stop their mouths that suspected him as no prophet, and to show that he is no deceiver, nor says of his own mind the things which he says.

And Amos answered, and said to Amaziah: I am not a prophet, and I am not the son of a prophet, but I am a shepherd plucking sycamores. And the Lord took me when I was following the flock, and said to me: Go, prophesy to my people Israel. And now hear the word of the Lord: You say: You shall not prophesy over Israel, and you shall not drip upon the house of the idol. Therefore thus said the Lord: Your wife shall commit fornication in the city, and your sons and your daughters shall fall by the sword, and your ground shall be measured with the line, and you shall die in a polluted land, and Israel shall go captive out of his land. LXX: And Amos answered, and said to Amaziah: I was not a prophet, nor the son of a prophet, but a herder plucking sycamines. And the Lord took me from the sheep, and the Lord said to me: Go, and prophesy over my people Israel. And now hear the word of the Lord: You say: Do not prophesy over Israel, and do not gather hearers against the house of Jacob. Therefore thus says the Lord: Your wife shall commit fornication in the city, and your sons and your daughters shall fall by the sword, and your land shall be divided with the line, and you shall die in an unclean land; but Israel shall be led captive out of his land. What Scripture records that the blessed apostles did, when the scribes and Pharisees warned them not to teach in the name of Jesus, and they answered, saying: We must obey God rather than men, we recognize that the prophet Amos also did: when the high priest of the idols ordered him not to prophesy in Bethel, he not only prophesies, and shows that he fears God who sends him more than the man who forbids him, but boldly and freely announces punishments to the very man who tried to forbid him and to hinder the word of God. Not only, he says, am I not a prophet, or, was not — of which the one belongs to humility, the other to truth — nor the son of a prophet, descended from a prophetic stock, but when I was a herdsman and was stripping blackberries from the brambles, the Lord took me as I followed the flocks. For herdsman, which in Hebrew is called boger, Aquila and Symmachus and Theodotion and the Fifth edition translated βουκόλον, one who pastures herds of cattle, not sheep. The Seventy alone said αἰπόλον, which properly means a herder of goats, ἀπὸ τοῦ αἰπολίου, which indeed means a flock that lives on the heights, to show that flocks of goats always climb rocks and rough crags and higher places. But since he adds: And the Lord took me ἐκ τῶν προβάτων, that is, from the flocks, he seems rather to mean sheep than goats, although we read at the beginning of Leviticus that both sheep and goats are designated by the name of flocks. For thus the Lord speaks: If you offer ἀπὸ τῶν προβάτων, that is, from the flocks to the Lord, a lamb or a kid, and a sheep or a goat. Moreover, what he says, plucking sycamines, which Aquila translated searching sycamores, and Symmachus having sycamores, some explain in this way, holding that sycamines is the name of a kind of tree that grows in the plains of Palestine and bears wild figs; and these, if they are not plucked, produce very bitter little figs and are spoiled by gnats. To us, however, since the wilderness in which Amos lived produces no tree of this kind, it seems rather that he means brambles, which bear blackberries and relieve the hunger and want of herders. However the reader may wish to take it, this must be said: that the Lord took up a lowly and rustic herder, and sent him to his people Israel, and commanded him to go out from his own land and proceed to Samaria, and there prophesy the things that are to come.

How good it is to raise up eyes of faith to the power of this worker, the Holy Spirit, and to look here and there at our ancestors in the Old and New Testaments. With the eyes of my faith open, I gaze on David, on Amos, on Daniel, on Peter, on Paul, on Matthew—and I am filled with a desire to behold the nature of this worker, the Holy Spirit. But I fall short. The Spirit filled a boy who played upon the harp, and made him a psalmist; on a shepherd and herdsman who pruned sycamore trees, and made him a prophet; on a child given to abstinence, and made him a judge of his elders; on a fisherman, and made him a preacher; on one who persecuted the church, and made him the teacher of the Gentiles; on a tax collector, and made him an Evangelist. What a skilled worker this Spirit is! There is no question of delay in learning what the Spirit teaches us. No sooner does the Spirit touch our minds in regard to anything than we are taught; the Spirit's very touch is teaching. The Spirit changes the human heart in a moment, filling it with light. Suddenly we are no longer what we were; suddenly we are something we never used to be.

If the spirit of prophecy had always been present to the prophets, the prophet Amos when asked would never have said, "I am no prophet"; he even adds, "neither a prophet's son, but I am a herdsman and a gatherer of sycamore fruit." How then was he no prophet who foretold so many true things concerning the future? Or in what way was he a prophet if he at the time disowned the truth concerning himself? At the moment that he was called in question, he felt that the spirit of prophecy was not with him. He bore true testimony concerning himself in saying, "I am not a prophet." Yet he added afterward, "Now therefore hear the word of the Lord. Therefore thus said the Lord, 'Your wife shall be a harlot in the city, and your sons and your daughters shall fall by the sword, and your land shall be divided by line, and you shall die in a polluted land.' " By these words of the prophet it is plainly shown that while he was bearing that testimony about himself he was filled, and on the instant rewarded with the spirit of prophecy, because he humbly acknowledged himself to be no prophet.
MORALS ON THE BOOK OF JOB 1:2.89

"And Amaziah sends, etc." In fact, since the prophet had received the order to prophesy beside the temple of the idols, so that his words might be heard not only by the ten tribes but also by the people living around, Amaziah, the priest of the temple, thinks that if these words were addressed to the people for some time, inevitably they would have been afraid and would not have come to worship the idols anymore, and therefore he would have lost authority. So he sends his complaint to excite the reaction of the king against the prophet, asking that either he was executed or expelled from that place. But since the king was afraid to harm the prophet, Amaziah dares say to the prophet by mocking him and laughing at him—in fact, the word seer is used with scorn: "Go, flee away to the land of Judah." That is, there you will be treated justly by receiving the wage for your role as a prophet, because those of the house of Judah are accustomed to taking care of their prophets. This priest of the demons had believed that the prophet had taken up his task as if it was an ordinary job, that is, to make a living as he himself had done. He imagined that the motive of Amos was to stuff himself with food. But the prophet answered, according to the Greek text, "I was no prophet, nor a prophet's son." That is, I have not learned this profession as a trade nor have I inherited it from my fathers, but it is the work of divine grace that is given to those who seek after God. "I was a goat herder and dug around sycamore trees." Other versions read, "I looked for the fruits of the sycamore trees," or "I scraped the wild fig trees," or "I made incisions on the fruits of the sycamores." This meaning is, sometimes I pastured goats and sheep as well, sometimes I tilled the ground by digging and raking and irrigating around the trees. By mentioning the sycamore trees, which are wild fig trees, he refers to all trees.

According to tropology, Amaziah the priest means strong and rigid, because, rebellious and fierce, he forbids the churchman and true prophet to bring forth the words and the teaching of God, and prohibits him from correcting the erring people. His wife, the false Church, will lie open to the fornication of all, and his sons and daughters, whom he wickedly begot in error, will be struck by the Lord's sword; his ground too and all his possession will be the portion of demons, and he himself will die in a polluted land, which does not have God as its inhabitant but is contaminated by the many errors of a depraved religion; and all the people who take to themselves the false name of Israel will go captive out of their land, so as not to serve God, but to submit their necks to the yoke of heretics and demons.

Since, therefore, he says, when the Lord commands me to speak, you, Amaziah, say to me: You shall not prophesy over Israel, and you shall not drip upon the house of the idol, hear what the Lord threatens against you. For house of the idol, in the Hebrew is written beth isaac, that is, house of laughter, for Isaac means laughter; which the LXX translated house of Jacob, understanding one name in place of another, and not the thing. Again, where we have put: And you shall not drip, Symmachus translated: you shall not rebuke. Now that the prophets drip is an idiom of the Scriptures, because they do not bring on the whole wrath of God at once, but announce it in small drops by their threatening.

Because, therefore, you said to me: You shall not prophesy, your wife shall commit fornication in the city; which Symmachus translated better, πορνευθήσεται, not that she herself will commit fornication, but that, in the passive voice, violated by others, she will suffer fornication. And it is a great grief and an incredible disgrace when a husband, in the middle of the city, with everyone present, cannot prevent the outrage done to his wife. Your sons also, he says, and your daughters shall fall by the sword. The grief over a violated daughter is not so great as over a defiled wife, nor the grief over a slain wife so great as over slaughtered children. For a husband would more willingly have his wife killed than defiled. Nor is this enough for the outrage, unless his land too is divided with the line by the enemy, and receives new tillers. Amaziah himself also, who now glories in the power of the priesthood, will by no means die in his own land, but, led into captivity, will die in a land polluted with idols; and he will not die before he sees the people he had deceived enslaved and captive.
8: But if we choose to read a fowler's vessel instead of a hook for fruit, this must be said: that as a fowler, with birdlime or nets, draws down to the earth birds that fly through the air and range on high, so the Lord, through Sennacherib or Nebuchadnezzar, whom we now understand as the fowlers, seized, bound, carried away and killed his people, who were formerly free and lofty through their observance of the law. For not unjustly are nets spread for birds. And this is to be referred not only to the time of the Babylonian captivity, but also to the coming of the Lord the Savior, when they said: Away with such a one from the earth; crucify him, crucify him; and they lost the wings of the dove. And the end came upon them, and the final captivity, and God spared them no longer.

These things the Lord God showed me: And behold, a hook for fruit, and he said: What do you see, Amos? And I said: A hook for fruit. And the Lord said to me: The end has come upon my people Israel; I will not again pass him by any more, and the hinges of the temple shall creak in that day, says the Lord God; many shall die, in every place silence shall be cast. LXX: Thus the Lord God showed me: And behold, a fowler's vessel. And he said: What do you see, Amos? And I said: A fowler's vessel. And the Lord said to me: The end has come upon my people Israel; I will not again pass him by any more; and the ceilings of the temple shall howl in that day, says the Lord God. Many will be falling: in every place I will cast silence. What Jeremiah sees under the figure of the rod of watchings, or of the nut, because God kept watch over the sins of his people, lest, as though with eyes shut and blinking, he should not see their offenses, this Amos now beholds against Judah and Israel alike under the appearance of a hook, which in Hebrew is called chelub and is turned by the LXX into a fowler's vessel; whereas a fowler is properly called moces, as we read above in this same prophet: If a bird will fall upon the earth without a fowler. And the sense is: As the branches of trees are drawn down with a hook to pick the fruit, so I have drawn near the time of captivity.

And that we may know that this is what we say, God himself explains what the vision he had shown the prophet signifies: The end has come upon my people Israel. And what follows: I will not again pass him by any more, signifies this: that he will no longer pass over the iniquities of his people, nor neglect them, nor allow their crimes to pass unpunished.

And lest he seem to speak only of the ten tribes, he added: The hinges of the temple shall creak, or the ceilings, in that day, says the Lord. This, however, is to be taken ὑπερβολικῶς (hyperbolically): so heavy a weight of evils will press down that even the very hinges of the gates and the lofty ceilings will howl and feel an incredible devastation, when many will die and, the inhabitants being captured or killed, silence will be cast in every place.

And the hinges of the temple howled, or the ceilings of the temple, collapsing upon the slain people. And in every place silence has been cast, the Jews having Moses and the prophets, but not having the Word of God; reading the letter and losing the spirit, when their table was made into a snare, and into a recompense, and into a ruin; and their eyes were darkened, so that they should not see; and their ears were stopped, so that they should not hear; and their back was bowed down, so that they should not look up to heaven, but, with that woman of the Gospel who had a spirit of infirmity, should always be bent toward the earth. And the wrath of God was poured out upon them, and the fury of his wrath seized them, so that their habitation became desolate, and there was no inhabitant in their tents; when this was fulfilled: Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will send a famine upon the land; not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the word of the Lord; about which, if we reach that point, we must speak more fully later on. We, then, seeing that God did not spare the natural branches, let us fear to suffer the same things, and let us avoid the fowler's snares, and say to the Lord: Do not be silent, nor hold yourself back, O God, and do not keep silence from me, and I shall become like those who go down into the pit. Over the whole world the silence of the Jews has been cast: wherever they are, they mutter rather than speak; and though their blasphemy against the Lord the Savior reaches even to heaven, all interpretation of the Scriptures is mute and silent, and does not set its ears to hearing.

And this indeed we sometimes see done also by perverse teachers and rulers, who without the fear of God lord it over the clergy, of whom Jeremiah speaks: Their clergy will not profit them; who think that gain is godliness, and, sitting in the temple as money-changers, set out doves, not in cages but in chairs, as though they were teachers, selling the gifts of the Holy Spirit; who make the measure smaller and greater, so that to the poor they speak either little or nothing, but to the rich, and to those from whom they pursue gain, they speak in the manner of public orators at very great length. And for money they crush and trample the heads of the poor, and thrust into greedy throats, not the grain of the Lord, which strengthens the heart of man, but refuse and the vilest dust; selling even these things that are of no value, although the Lord commanded the apostles: Freely you have received, freely give.

Hear this, you who crush the poor and make the needy of the land fail, saying: When will the month pass, and we shall sell our wares, and the sabbath, and we shall open the grain, that we may diminish the measure and increase the shekel; and put in deceitful balances, that we may possess the needy for silver, and the poor for shoes, and sell the refuse of the grain. LXX: Hear these things, you who crush the poor in the morning, and oppress the needy from the land, who say: When will the month pass by, and we shall trade; and the sabbaths, and we shall open the granary, to make the measure smaller and the weight greater; and let us make an unjust balance, that we may possess the poor for money, and the needy for shoes, and trade in every sale. Lest the hook for fruit and the fowler's vessel should seem to have been shown in vain, and the captivity to threaten as near through these signs, the causes of God's offense are briefly described. O you, Judah, O you, Israel, hear what crimes you have committed: rising by night, instead of prayer and hymns to God, you have a zeal for oppressing, or crushing, the poor, so that, worn out with hunger and want, they may be removed from the land.

You who wait for the Kalends, to trade and to heap interest upon interest, and for the sabbaths, to open the granaries and give out grain, meaning to receive more back, and who turn the solemn feasts of God to your own profit for the sake of shameful gain; who make the measure smaller in selling goods, and the weights greater in receiving them, and the balance unjust, so that you may possess the poor man's money, and hold men so cheap that you fulfill what I said of you above: Because you sold the righteous for silver, and the poor for shoes; you have leapt into such a frenzy for gain that you sell to the poor not grain, by eating which men's bodies are sustained, but the refuse and sweepings of the grain, mixing dust and chaff with the wheat.

[Passage quoted, Amos viii. 7-12.]

THIS prophecy foretells the pride, insolence and rebellion of the Jews against our Saviour, and says that the Lord sware against the presumption of Jacob, that their insolence against Him should never be forgotten, and that their land and its inhabitants should undergo suffering and mourning, and that no more as before should they be punished a little while and then restored, but that this judgment should last for ever. For He says, "Complete destruction shall come upon them," meaning that wrath in the time of the Roman Empire would attack them, that a river should rise on them as on men who before were lifted up.

And then after this anger of God against them, their state, He says, will again "Come down like the river of Egypt."

By which I think is meant, that the ancient glories of the Jews once so lofty, so prized by God, and as it were exalted on high, will become like the state of the heathen nations, which flow and pass by like a river, and will go from height to depth.
The Proof of the Gospel, Book 10, Chapter 6

And he swears that he will not forget their works even to the end; for the proud God resists, but gives grace to the humble; but that he holds in memory all the sins they have committed, and brings them even to the end and the time of judgment. Hence the penitent pray: Do not remember our former iniquities; especially since against the proud the earth itself is moved, or troubled, and mourns, not the tenant and the stranger, but its inhabitant; and its consummation rises up like a river, and goes down like the stream of Egypt, so that he who repents rises with the climbing river, but he who persists in his offenses goes down like the river of Egypt and, entering the sea, is swallowed up. And by this he shows that the pride of Jacob, against which the Lord swears, is to be devoured by eternal punishments.

The Lord has sworn against the pride of Jacob: If I shall have forgotten all their works even to the end. Shall not the earth be moved over this, and every inhabitant of it mourn, and it rise up wholly like a river, and be cast out, and flow away like the brook of Egypt? LXX: The Lord has sworn against the pride of Jacob: If he will forget all your works to the end. And over these things shall not the earth be troubled, and every inhabitant of it mourn, and its consummation rise up like a stream, and go down like the river of Egypt? Scripture quite often records the Lord swearing. First, in Genesis, the angel of the Lord called Abraham a second time from heaven, saying: By myself I have sworn, says the Lord, because you have done this thing, and have not spared your dearest son, blessing I will bless you, and multiplying I will multiply you like the stars of heaven, and like the sand that is on the shore of the sea. And in the hundred and ninth (110th) psalm: The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent; you are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek. Discussing this, whoever he is who wrote the epistle to the Hebrews says: Since he had no one greater by whom to swear, he swore by himself. And in this same prophet we read above: The Lord has sworn by his holiness, or by his holy ones, that behold, days will come upon you, and they will take you up with weapons, or with poles, and the rest. He, then, who had earlier sworn by his holiness, or by his holy ones, now swears against the pride of Jacob, so that if they do not believe him when he threatens, they may believe him when he swears, after the likeness of men, who take up an oath when their simple words are not believed. Nor is it surprising if God is said to swear, since he sleeps with those who sleep and keeps watch with those who keep watch, and is said to be angry with those who have stored up wrath for themselves in the day of wrath.

And He next tells what will happen at the time of the saving Passion, "In that day," He says, saith the Lord, "the sun shall set at midday, and the light shall be darkened on the earth at daytime," and this was plainly fulfilled, when our Lord was lifted up, according to the Gospel:

"And there was darkness over all the earth from the sixth hour even to the ninth hour, and about the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani."
The Proof of the Gospel, Book 10, Chapter 6

For that lamp shone and they did not by it seek the Lord their God. And its light shone in the darkness and the darkness did not comprehend it. And the lamp was set up on the lamp-stand and those who were in the house did not see its light. And what then means this, that the lamp was set up on the lamp-stand? Clearly His being raised up upon the cross. And by this all the house was made dark over them. For when they crucified Him, the light was darkened from them, and shone amongst the Gentiles, because that from the time of the sixth hour (of the day) on which they crucified Him even unto the ninth hour there was darkness in all the land of Israel. And the sun set in midday and the land was darkened in the shining daytime, as is written in Zechariah the Prophet:—It shall come to pass in that day, saith the Lord, I will cause the sun to set in midday, and will make dark the land in the shining daytime.

HOW THE PROPHECY AGREES WITH THE GOSPEL, CONCERNING THE DARKENING OF THE SUN AND CERTAIN OTHER THINGS. — Since at the Lord’s first coming it was foretold that the sun would be darkened at his passion, at the very hour when it is proved to have happened, that is, at midday, for therefore it is written in the prophet Amos: “And it shall come to pass in that day, says the Lord, I will cause the sun to go down at noon, and I will darken the earth in the clear day” (Amos 8:9). On that day, therefore, from the sixth hour the sun was darkened until the ninth hour, and therefore the prophecy of the aforementioned prophet was fulfilled. The image of this event, which is to occur at the Lord’s second coming, was shown in the Lord’s passion; for at the end, when the Lord begins to come to judge the world, the heavenly lights will be released from their service, as the Lord says: “In those days the sun shall be darkened, and the moon shall not give her light” (Matt. 24:29). Joel the prophet has not omitted this either, so that, being signified by many, it may without doubt be believed to be fulfilled. For therefore he said: “The sun shall be turned into darkness and the moon into blood, before the great and revealing day of the Lord comes” (Joel 2:31). As far as appears, this more fittingly belongs to the second coming; for then it will be openly revealed to all, as Scripture says: “Then every eye shall see him, and all the tribes of the earth shall mourn over him, and those who crucified him” (Rev. 1:7). Therefore, if in both comings it is contained that the sun shall be darkened in those days, what is that day on which Scripture rings that the sun and moon shall be increased? For among other things Isaiah says: “And there shall be upon every high mountain, and upon every high hill, streams running with water in that day, when many shall perish and when the towers shall fall. And the light of the moon shall be as the light of the sun, and the light of the sun shall be sevenfold, in the day when the Lord shall heal the brokenness of his people” (Isa. 30:25–26), and so forth. What day can be understood, on which the Lord promised to heal the brokenness of his people? I think this is the day which Zacharias, the father of John, pointed out when he said: “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for he has visited and performed the redemption of his people. And he has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of David his servant, as he spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets, who have been since the world began, that he would deliver us from our enemies and from the hand of all who hate us, to perform mercy with our fathers” (Luke 1:68–72). And Simeon, among other things, said: “This child is set for the fall and for the rise of many in Israel” (Luke 2:34). This fall is that of the scribes and Pharisees and the rulers of the Jews, whom the prophet signified by the towers. These, therefore, falling through unbelief, others rose up by believing, who had previously seemed weak and sick through negligence. Where the Savior says: “For judgment I have come into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (Jn. 9:39); so that those who by the practice and knowledge of the Law seem to be lights may be blinded through unbelief, but the blind, that is, the unlearned or publicans, may see by believing. Their weaknesses the prophet foretold that the Savior would bear (Isa. 53:11). And so at this time of the Savior it came to pass, as we read in the Gospel, that “he took our infirmities and bore our diseases” (Matt. 8:17). All these things indeed were completed and fulfilled in the Savior’s passion: for therefore the salvation of the human race, both in heaven above and in the lower regions, was both redeemed and confirmed, since the prophecy of the aforementioned Zacharias encompasses both. For here above they were freed from the crushing of enemies by the intervention of mercy; and there below, in the underworld, when they were snatched from Tartarus. For all who hoped in the promised Christ were awaiting his coming, that, death having been conquered, they might be freed from Hades. Therefore he said: “To perform mercy with our fathers.” If anyone, however, understands this salvation also to be contained in the second coming, yet in both comings, especially in the second, the sun will be turned into darkness and the moon will not give her brightness: how then shall we perceive the sun and moon to be increased on the day when the Lord will visit his people, when in both times, in which the liberation of the people was begun and completed, we read that the sun and moon are not diminished but darkened? Unless, clearly, we understand the sun and moon to be compared to the saints; just as in another place we read that the saints are made equal to the heavenly lights, with the Apostle Paul preaching that among these men the saints in this world appear as luminaries. And in the Gospel: “Then the righteous shall shine like the sun” (Matt. 13:43). For the Lord calls righteous works “light”: therefore he says, “Let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:16). Those, therefore, who, having left all that is theirs, follow the Lord for the sake of righteousness and holiness, are compared to the sun and moon as being honored sevenfold; as the Lord says: “There is no one who leaves house, or wife, or children, or fields, who will not receive seven times as much in this age” (see Luke 18:29–30). Those, then, who are now honored sevenfold can be understood to be believed in the future to become seven degrees brighter than the rest; so that their resurrection is compared to the sun and moon, while that of the others is like the stars. Therefore the brightness of the saints, which is honored sevenfold here, obtains another sevenfold in the resurrection, so that one who here has the brightness of the moon will receive the brightness of the sun in the future; and one who here is compared to the sun will be believed then to receive seven times as much. Therefore the prophet Isaiah foretold that by comparison with the sun and moon the merits of the saints would be increased, and not without reason. For if the Lord himself is called the Sun of righteousness, and the saints will be like him, as the Apostle John says: “When he appears, we shall be like him” (1 Jn. 3:2), then fittingly the saints are signified in the sun, yet the aforementioned prophet shows the sun to be greater than the moon by seven degrees For when it shows that the moon, like the light of the sun, will exist in the future, but the sun will be seven times as great; it certainly means, in the manner of speaking, that the moon will be increased sevenfold more than the sun, so that the moon will then be such as the sun is now: although the reasoning here concerns the saints, under this explanation of the luminaries it has nevertheless partly revealed their measure, so that after the increase of the sun and the moon, a saint will again be as much greater as the sun once was; and as much as one saint now differs from another saint, so much will one differ from another in the future after the reward.
QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 105: ON THE DARKENING OF THE SUN

And it shall be in that day, says the Lord: The sun shall set at midday, and I will make the earth grow dark in the day of light; and I will turn your festivals into mourning and all your songs into lamentation; and I will bring sackcloth upon every back of yours and baldness upon every head; and I will make it like the mourning for an only son, and its last end like a bitter day. LXX: And it shall be in that day, says the Lord God: The sun shall set at midday, and the light shall grow dark upon the earth in the day; and I will turn your solemnities into mourning and all your songs into lamentation; and I will bring sackcloth upon every loin and baldness upon every head; and I will make it like the mourning for a beloved one, and those who are with him like a day of grief. By that day he means the day of captivity, when both peoples will be led away to the Assyrians and the Chaldeans; for whom, from the greatness of their sorrow, the sun will set at midday, and while the light is clear for all, darkness will fill everything; when their festivals and all their songs were turned into mourning and lamentation, and upon every back, or loins, they were girded with haircloth, and, according to the custom of mourners of old, they had baldness on their heads, which we read that Job also did at the deaths of his children. And so great will be the greatness of the mourning and sorrow that it will surpass the grief for an only son, dying, and very dear to his mother, and all things will be filled with lamentation and bitterness. We can also understand this passage of the Lord's passion, when the sun at the sixth hour drew back its rays and did not dare to look upon its Lord hanging on the cross; when, as darkness filled everything, their festivals and songs, with Vespasian and Titus prevailing, were changed into mourning and lamentation; when all things were filled with tears and remorse and haircloth, and their heads had baldness, which before, adorned with the long hair of the Nazirites, had grown their locks for the Lord. Then the first-born son of God, the people of Israel, which had laid its hand upon the Only-begotten and true Son of God, was handed over to eternal mourning; and its last end, or those who were with it, were filled with bitterness. Now therefore, while they have darkness, who drove back the sun of righteousness, we who sat in darkness and in the shadow of death have seen a great light, and their whole festival has been transferred to the mysteries of the Church, so that while they weep, we sing praises together to the Lord.

And some are commanded to "be angry" after a wholesome fashion, but with our own selves, and with evil thoughts that arise, and "not to sin," viz., by bringing them to a bad issue. Finally, the next verse explains this to be the meaning more clearly: "The things you say in your hearts, be sorry for them on your beds:" i.e., whatever you think of in your hearts when sudden and nervous excitements rush in on you, correct and amend with wholesome sorrow, lying as it were on a bed of rest, and removing by the moderating influence of counsel all noise and disturbance of wrath. Lastly, the blessed Apostle, when he made use of the testimony of this verse, and said, "Be ye angry and sin not," added, "Let not the sun go down upon your wrath, neither give place to the devil." If it is dangerous for the sun of righteousness to go down upon our wrath, and if when we are angry we straightway give place to the devil in our hearts, how is it that above he charges us to be angry, saying, "Be ye angry, and sin not"? Does he not evidently mean this: be ye angry with your faults and your tempers, lest, if you acquiesce in them, Christ, the sun of righteousness, may on account of your anger begin to go down on your darkened minds, and when He departs you may furnish a place for the devil in your hearts?

And of this sun God clearly makes mention by the prophet, when He says, "But to those that fear my name the sun of righteousness shall arise with healing in His wings." And this again is said to "go down" at midday on sinners and false prophets, and those who are angry, when the prophet says, "Their sun is gone down at noon." And at any rate "tropically" the mind, that is the nou=j or reason, which is fairly called the sun because it looks over all the thoughts and discernings of the heart, should not be put out by the sin of anger: lest when it "goes down" the shadows of disturbance, together with the devil their author, fill all the feelings of our hearts, and, overwhelmed by the shadows of wrath, as in a murky night, we know not what we ought to do. In this sense it is that we have brought forward this passage of the Apostle, handed down to us by the teaching of the elders, because it was needful, even at the risk of a somewhat lengthy discourse, to show how they felt with regard to anger, for they do not permit it even for a moment to effect an entrance into our heart: observing with the utmost care that saying of the gospel: "Whosoever is angry with his brother is in danger of the judgment." But if it be lawful to be angry up till sunset, the surfeit of our wrath and the vengeance of our anger will be able to give full play to passion and dangerous excitement before that sun inclines towards its setting.
The Twelve Books on the Institutes of the Coenobia, Book 8, Chapters 9-10

In relation to Christ's death, it is said: "The sun shall go down at midday." At midday, the sun falls for the Jews. When Christ was at the highest point of His power, that is, after the resurrection and the ascension, the Jews were blinded.

Let us keep [the Feast of Annunciation] with psalms and hymns and spiritual songs. From ancient times Israel kept their festival, but then it was with unleavened bread and bitter herbs, of which the prophet says, "I will turn their feasts into afflictions and lamentation and their joy into shame." But our afflictions our Lord has assured us he will turn into joy by the fruits of repentance.
ON THE ANNUNCIATION TO THE HOLY VIRGIN MARY 2

Suspended, then, and fastened to his cross Christ cried out to God the Father in a loud voice and willingly laid down his life. In that same hour there was an earthquake, and the veil of the temple that separated the two tabernacles was cut in two, and the sun was suddenly withdrawn, and from the sixth hour until the ninth hour there was darkness. The prophet Amos bears witness to this. "And it shall come to pass in that day, says the Lord, that the sun shall go down at midday, and the day shall be darkened of light. And I will turn your feasts into mourning and all your songs into lamentation."

This prophecy was thus fulfilled, and it goes on to say:

"And I will turn your feasts into mourning, and all your song into lamentation. And I will bring sackcloth on all loins, and baldness on every head: And I will make him as grief for a dear one, and them with him as a day of pain. Behold, the days come, saith the Lord, that I will send famine upon the earth, not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the word of the Lord," etc.

And all this prophecy of what would result from their insolence against the Christ has been clearly proved to have taken place after their plot against our Saviour. For it was not before it, but afterwards from that day to this that God turned their feasts into mourning, despoiled them of their famous mother-city, and destroyed the holy Temple therein when Titus and Vespasian were Emperors of Rome, so that they could no longer go up to keep their feasts and sacred meetings. I need not say that a famine of hearing the Word of the Lord has overtaken them all, in return for their rejection of the Word of God; since with one voice they refused Him, so He refuses them.
The Proof of the Gospel, Book 10, Chapter 6

They, instead of a belt, are girded with ropes and haircloth; to us, with the apostles, it is said: Let your loins be girded, and burning lamps in your hands. We are girded with the truth of Christ, fulfilling what is written: Stand, having your loins girded in truth. But they, instead of truth, are girt about with the lie of the devil. Our head, of which the Savior speaks: But even the hairs of your head are numbered, has perpetual hair, and in our head, who is Christ, we possess strength to kill the lion. But they slept on the knees of the harlot synagogue, and, shaved bare as the devil sheared them, lost the power of the head, losing together with their strength their eyes, of which it is written in Ecclesiastes: The eyes of the wise man are in his head, but he who is a fool walks in darkness. Their companions pass their days in mourning; our comrades are clothed with the garment of gladness.

But this also, which he says, "about thirty years old", must be considered. "Joseph was thirty years old" when he was released from his chains and, having interpreted the dream of Pharaoh, was made ruler of Egypt, and in the time of plenty gathered wheat, so that in the time of famine he might have what he could distribute. I think that the thirty years of Joseph went before, as a type of the thirty years of the Savior. For this Joseph gathered not such wheat as that Joseph in Egypt, but true and heavenly wheat, so that, the wheat having been gathered in the time of plenty, he might have what he could distribute when famine had been sent into Egypt, "not a famine of bread nor a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the word of God". And so he gathers from the prophets, from the law, from the apostles the words of abundance, so that when now no more books are written, nor is any new instrument composed, nor are apostles sent, then he may distribute those things which had been brought together by Jesus into the storehouses of the apostles — that is, into their souls and the souls of all the saints — and may nourish Egypt, imperiled by famine, and especially his brothers, of whom it is written: "I will declare your name to my brothers, in the midst of the church I will sing to you". Other men too have words of patience and words of justice and the words of the remaining virtues; this is the wheat which Joseph distributed to the Egyptians. But the grain which he gives to his brothers, that is, to his disciples, is another kind, from the land of Goshen, from that land which looks toward the east: the wheat of the Gospel, the wheat of the apostles.
HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 28

It is prophesied, "Their young men will die by the sword, and their sons and daughters will perish in famine." Those who hindered Jesus from teaching have not simply perished by the sword. But now, after the advent of the Lord, a more profound famine has come upon them. It is "not a famine of bread or thirst of water, but a famine of hearing the Word of the Lord." For the "Lord almighty" no longer "speaks" with them. This famine portends that prophecy would cease. And why do I say prophecy? The Lord ceased teaching them. Even if they bear the title sage a thousand times with them, the Word of the Lord is still not among them, since the verse has been fulfilled: "The Lord took away from Judea and Jerusalem the strong man and strong woman, the giant and the strong man, and the soldier and judge and prophet and diviner and elder and captain of fifty and the admirable adviser and master builder and intelligent pupil." For he is no longer able to say, "Like a master builder I laid a foundation." The builders have passed over, have come to the church, have laid the foundation, Jesus Christ. Those who came after them have also built on him.

The unreliability of excessive wealth may edify even to the point of eliciting contempt of corporal riches. Wealth is unstable. It is like a wave accustomed to change back and forth due to the violence of the wind. One might suppose that the people of Israel are rich, since they have the adoption of sons and divine worship, the promises and the patriarchs. However, they have become poor because of their sin against the Lord. "But they that seek the Lord shall not be deprived of any good." They have lacked nourishment in a certain way and have suffered hunger. For when they had put to death the bread of life, a hunger for the bread came upon them. A chastisement for the thirst was imposed on them, but "the hunger was not for sensible bread or the thirst for water, but a hunger to hear the Word of God." Therefore "they have wanted and have suffered hunger."

We harm both soul and body if we are guilty of lack of moderation to them both by fattening one beyond need or by causing them to waste away from starvation.… The Lord of all once admonished the Jewish people … by way of extreme indignation in the words, "I will deal you not a famine of bread nor a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the Word of the Lord," to teach us that while one famine can torture the body, the other famine affects the soul. This very thing that the Lord threatened to inflict on them by way of punishment we now of our own volition secure for ourselves despite God's show of care for us and his provision for us, through the advice of mentors, as well as the reading of Scriptures.

Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will send a famine into the land, not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the word of the Lord. And they shall be moved from sea to sea, and from the north to the east they shall go about seeking the word of the Lord, and shall not find it. In that day the beautiful virgins shall fail, and the young men, in thirst, who swear by the sin of Samaria, and say: Your god lives, Dan, and the way of Beersheba lives; and they shall fall and shall not rise again any longer. LXX: Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord God, and I will send forth a famine upon the land, not a famine of bread nor a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the word of the Lord. And the waters shall be moved from sea to sea, and from the North to the East they shall go about seeking the word of the Lord, and shall not find it. In that day the beautiful virgins shall fail, and the youths, in thirst, who swear by the propitiation of Samaria; who say: Your god lives, Dan, and your god lives, Beersheba; and they shall fall and shall not rise again any more. 'Waters' are not found in the Hebrew; and 'propitiation', which we have rendered 'sin', and which is called asamath by the Hebrews, signifies an idol, which is the beginning of sins. Ancient history, Latin as well as Greek, and that of all the barbarian nations, relates that nothing is harder than famine, which often compels the besieged to feed on human flesh and to rage against their own nature, so that parents do not spare their little children, and marital affection tears apart the limbs of a wife once loved. If the famine of bodies does this, what must be said of the famine of souls? This famine, on the day of the Lord's resurrection, overwhelmed the people of the Jews, and joined to the famine was a most burning thirst, since they did not have the bread which came down from heaven, nor those waters which flowed from the belly of Jesus. The law has been taken away from them, and the prophets have fallen silent in eternal silence; they are moved from sea to sea, and from the British Ocean to the Atlantic Ocean, that is, from the west to the south, and from the north to the east, wanderers through the whole world, and they are not able to find the word of God. At this place we shall ask the Jews what day they think is signified, in which they are to endure a famine of hearing the word of God, especially since they read the Scriptures and follow the lowliness of the letter? To them we press home that what was foretold is a famine of spiritual understanding, in which Christ is discerned, and the passion and resurrection of the Lord are found. They go around the world and seek the word of the Lord and do not find it, because they denied the Word of the Lord, which came to pass in the hands of all the prophets, which in the beginning was with the Father, which was made flesh and dwelt among us.

But the Lord sends a famine into the land upon those who savor earthly things; and a famine not of bread, and a thirst not of water, but of hearing the word of the Lord, when on account of the sins of the people teaching fails in the churches; and from sea to sea, that is, from salt and most bitter waves they come as far as the sea; not meeting with rivers, nor with most sweet and varied springs, but running back again to bitter things; and from the north to the east, desiring to forsake the north, which is the harshest wind and is called 'the right-hand wind' by the ignorant, and to reach the east, which they will not be able to find, because they do not go by a straight road but wander about by devious paths, and, not keeping to the king's road, are led along winding turns.

And when the virgins fail, the young men too will fail, who had previously conquered the world; and they will fail for this reason, because they swear by the idol of Samaria, which we always take as standing for the heretics, as this same prophet says: Woe to those who despise Zion, and trust in the mountain of Samaria. For the heretics despise the Church of the Lord and trust in the falsity of their own dogmas, raising themselves up against the knowledge of God, having split his people, and saying: We have no portion in David, nor inheritance in the son of Jesse. If anyone, therefore, swears by the sin of Samaria and says: Your god lives, Dan, and the way of Beersheba lives, he will fall and will not be able to rise again any longer. The tribe of Dan could not find a possession in the farthest borders of the Jews, as is written in the book of Judges, and Dan is interpreted 'judgment'. Beersheba, according to the variety of accents, is rendered into our language 'well of the oath', or 'well of plenty', and 'of the seventh'. Therefore the heretics too will thirst at the farthest borders of the holy Scriptures, despising the judgment of God and desiring the way of Beersheba, which was in the tribe of Judah; and, desiring to imitate many mysteries of the Church, they say that they are sated and filled. These the apostle Paul reproaches: Already you are sated, already you have become rich; and they swear in the name of the Lord; and, once fallen, since they consider the gods of the idols to be their god, they will not rise again any more. But those who are willing to repent, and do not say: Your god lives, Dan, and the way of Beersheba lives, will hear through Jeremiah: Shall he who falls not rise again, or he who has turned away not return.

In that time the beautiful virgins failed, and the young men, or the chosen ones and teachers — for this is what baurim means —, failed in thirst. They interpret the beautiful virgins as the synagogues, and the chosen ones as the masters of the people. And since these have failed, they teach that the curses of Deuteronomy have been fulfilled in the Jewish people.

In that time the virgin souls will fail, which the Apostle calls uncorrupted; and he desires them to possess everlasting chastity, writing to the Corinthians: For I betrothed you to one husband, to present a chaste virgin to Christ. But I fear lest, as the serpent seduced Eve by his cunning, so your minds should be corrupted and fall away from the simplicity which is in Christ. And if all virgins were beautiful or good, he would never have said: The good virgins will fail; but he set down 'good' to distinguish them from bad virgins, the good being those who are holy in body and in spirit. The bad virgins are the five foolish ones, who did not prepare oil for their lamps. The good and comely virgins are those who had the light of the virtues and entered the bridegroom's chamber. But the virgins will fail, because they will not find the word of the Lord. From this we understand that when teaching is lacking in the churches, modesty perishes, chastity dies, all the virtues depart, because they have not eaten the word of the Lord; and whoever has eaten it, fattened with its food, will hear through Solomon: The righteous man eating satisfies his soul, but the souls of the ungodly hunger. And David, who had reached the old age of Abraham, sang freely: I have been young, and have grown old, and I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed seeking bread. How many martyrs in persecutions perished of hunger, and lacked grain and these nourishments of the body. Therefore he speaks of that bread which came down from heaven, which whoever eats will be able neither to hunger nor to thirst.

These chosen ones and teachers swore by the idol of Samaria, that is, by the golden calves, and said: Your god lives, Dan, at the borders of the land of Judea, where Paneas now is, and where at that time the golden calf was worshipped, and the way of Beersheba lives, because they travelled there by a long and seldom-taken journey, on account of the kings of Judah, the righteous and the unrighteous alike. And because they did this, they will therefore fall and will not rise again any more, that is, they will not recover the state which they had had before.
